tracks.title: HCP layer coverage, conformance, MCP binding, and the agent-memory flow
tracks.summary:
Coverage is complete at the operation level. Every HCP context and governance operation has a task, and so do the delegations endpoints and the revocation notice. A few HCP acts have no task, among them keeping both entries in a conflict and declining a proposal, which have no HTTP endpoint in HCP either. The HTTP and MCP bindings are deliberately not carried. HCP's MCP binding (section 10), and 10.5 above all, is never cited: no spec says the access token must stay out of a model's context, though the family puts the token in the payload. Questions 44, 45 and 47 appear in no spec. Only their titles are in PR #1380's description, and their wording is in VTI #2823 as N1, N2 and N4.

Conformance: HCP, the suite and VTI agree that the carriage cannot be claimed, and that a claim needs a full binding and a valid discovery document. But every spec makes a client check the provider's VID against the HCP discovery document and its JWKS. HCP's discovery schema requires at least one conformsTo entry and one binding. VTI plans no discovery document in V0 and one with no conformsTo in V1, so a client that follows the specs cannot talk to the V0 or V1 VTA.

Every governance task requires a Management Client accessToken, yet no task issues one, and VTI's V0 has Keyring send governance with no token.

HCP Core 5.4 also puts governance on HTTP only, so any Core claim depends on question 37.

Our plugin plus vta-mcp is an HCP Client bridge, not an MCP binding. Running hcp/* through vta_call as it is does not work, for three reasons:
- the token enters the model's context;
- vta_call cannot resubmit on a held thread;
- vta-mcp has no receive loop for the revocation notice.
vta-mcp's MCP version cap and loopback-only listener also conflict with VTI's plan to build Agent Interop in it. VTI forbids a Context Client to hold an ACL entry, which clashes with our memory agent's entry. VTI's design and the suite also give different error codes for a revoked grant.

tracks.title: Signing, canonicalization, digests, encodings, envelope vs Keyring and VTA
tracks.summary:
The signing details are compatible. I took the PR demo's Management Client revoke request, put back the token the printout hides, and checked it with Keyring's own recipe (canonicalize plus noble, as documentProof.ts does it). The proof verifies. Signing the same document with the same key and created time gives the PR's proofValue byte for byte. Two controls fail as they should: the printed copy with the token hidden, and a timestamp written as .000Z.

Every verifier involved (the PR's TS, Rust, Go and Dart libraries, and the VTA at f7b78e29d) accepts either authentication or assertionMethod, as long as the key is listed under that relationship. Keyring's VtaClient already signs hcp/* with authentication. The rule to verify over the document as received is already in the framework at our pin, and the VTA's network entry point already does it. Keyring's wireTimestamp is harmless but no longer needed there.

accessTokenDigest (base64url, prefix u) is a record the provider keeps for itself. It never goes on the wire, so it does not clash with Keyring's base58btc (prefix z) digests. Framework 0.6.0 is older than our pin's text, and nothing changed in the envelope or proof rules between the pin and the PR.

Things to raise with Brendan:
- All 47 example proofs in the hcp specs use assertionMethod. The framework says SHOULD authentication, and the PR's own libraries, demo and the VTA all sign with authentication.
- The regenerated Go and Dart types drop a required null (for example a persistent grant's expiresAt), so they produce documents the PR's own schemas refuse. Fix branches exist but are not in #1380.
- VTI V0 and our plan D2 have Keyring send governance tasks with no token, but every Management Client request schema requires accessToken and allows no other members.

Gaps on Keyring's side:
- VtaClient uses reply payloads without checking them against the schema, and only logs the proof result.
- verifyTrustTaskProof does not check that the key is authorized for the proof's purpose. It even accepts keyAgreement.
- verifyDocumentProof refuses anything not signed assertionMethod unless told otherwise.
- Keyring's Ajv ignores the date-time and uri formats.
- In JS, an undefined value silently becomes an absent member where the schema requires null.

tracks.title: Error handling and held-request handling vs Keyring and VTA
tracks.summary:
Errors are mostly compatible with Keyring. Every hcp/* spec uses trust-task-error/0.6. That version is byte-identical at our pin, and both Keyring and the VTA already speak it. The specs use five standard codes and four namespaced ones: hcp:invalidToken, hcp:versionConflict, hcp:credentialInvalid and hcp:exportTooLarge. They map HCP 5.5 the same way in all 28 specs. None of these codes collides with Keyring's colon splitting or exact-string matching, and none triggers the version step-down. Keyring already words refusals from codes, so the fixed "one text for every refusal" causes no conflict.

Keyring work, none of it needed for the V0 demo:
- VtiRefusal drops retryable and retryAfter, so HCP's `unavailable` gets no wait or retry.
- The VTA leg would read a trust-task-next-step as a success, and every resubmit starts a new thread.
- Keyring handles task-consent request 0.1 and decision 0.2 already, with verification and the owner check. But it shows only effects[].summary. The HCP checklist needs published effect kinds and detail shapes, and Keyring must still show each summary word for word.

Asks for Brendan:
- VTI #2823 says `scope-denied` where the PR uses hcp:invalidToken or permissionDenied. `scope-denied` is not a valid 0.6 code.
- grants/request reports a decline as permissionDenied. The SPEC on its own branch says a decision task should report a refusal in its success response.
- When the provider gives up on a hold, the next resubmit on the same thread asks the person again. With a 300 s hold and 5 s resubmits, that repeats the ask on Keyring.
- retryAfter is a date-time in errors but seconds in the next-step hint, and the hint has no schema.
- In the demo a 1 h token sits under a 4 h grant. When it expires, hcp:invalidToken reads as a revocation, and there is no way to refresh the token.
- hcp:exportTooLarge is specific to export but uses the family-wide namespace.
- task-consent/request has no place for the held request's threadId, so the scan match cannot work.
- decision/0.2 cannot carry a narrower approval or a chosen purpose.
- There is no next-step support anywhere in the VTA stack (service, sdk, mcp) at the pin.

tracks.title: Do hcp/* tasks work like ceremonies, and could they later
tracks.summary:
I read the PR as a whole (#1380 with #1381 and #1382) against the framework's ceremony layer: the SPEC.md ceremony and verdict sections, the definition schema, the three ceremonies already published, the design note and the ceremony verifier code. A ceremony is a published description laid over existing tasks, plus an optional `ceremony` field on each document; no task schema needs to change. Even so, every act and every way out of a waiting state has to be a document, retries need a fixed limit, and one sender can't fan out to many receivers.

No hcp/* spec is part of a ceremony in this PR, and no ceremony refers to hcp. The hcp tasks target framework 0.6.0, whose document schema already allows both `ceremony` and `parentThreadId`, so ceremonies can be added later without touching the specs. I wrote four draft ceremonies (connect, revoke, end delegation, move context between providers) and ran a copy of the registry's own checker on them. All four pass, and three deliberately broken versions are rejected.

Revoke and export→import already work with the tasks as written. Onward sharing isn't a multi-step flow and needs nothing. Connect only works by borrowing task-consent for the person's approval, which the PR leaves to "the provider's own modality". Three gaps there are cheap to close now:
- Nothing links the approval exchange to the held request's thread.
- A hold the provider gives up on is silently reopened on the same thread. Read as written, this also lets a client tell a real but silent account from an unknown one; that's my reading of the text, not tested.
- The next-step `retryAfter` hint has no schema.

Ending a delegation runs into a gap in the ceremony format itself: one provider sending notices to many clients can't be described. It also must not give those clients a shared ID, because HCP keeps their grants unlinkable.

Full notes: <review>/notes/ceremonies.md. The draft ceremonies and checker copy are in my scratchpad: <scratch>/ceremony-check.

tracks.title: JSON-to-JSON schema comparison and vector tests, HCP vs the proposed TT schemas
Verify the five points we said we would raise, and the TypeScript question
tracks.summary:
Four of the five points hold. One needs a correction, and checking P3 turned up the most serious issue.

P1 holds. In #1382 the person's approval is a function call inside the provider that always approves. No Management Client approves or declines. None of the four ports (TS, Rust, Go, Dart) has a declined state or a decline test. This matches the suite, which deliberately has no task for the person's decision ("The person's decision never travels through the client"). A decline is the same fixed permissionDenied as an unknown person. VTI #2823 puts Keyring in that role through task-consent, and its A3 task does require a decline test.

P2 holds, with one correction. HCP says governance goes over HTTP only (1.6 "HTTP only", 5.4, 9.1, 10.1). Question 37 is in 18 specs: revoke, audit, the disclosure summary Keyring polls, grants/list and others. But adding a memory (hcp/entries/create) is a context operation, not governance, so question 37 does not apply to it.

P3: all 28 hcp/* requests require a proof. Keyring already signs every document it sends to its VTA (eddsa-jcs-2022, authentication purpose), and I found no unsigned path. So signing is not new. What is new: every governance request also requires accessToken in its schema. VTI #2823 V0 says Keyring sends no token, and the VTA refuses a payload that fails its schema. As written, the two documents conflict. Smaller items: the spec examples all use assertionMethod, and Keyring only logs, never refuses, unsigned VTA replies.

P4 holds. #1374 to #1379 contain no TypeScript files (184 files read in full). Issue #1377's TypeScript row (TypeScript reads a missing field as undefined) is minor for Keyring if it validates replies and tests for null exactly.

P5 holds. hcp_entries is a new store, separate from the memory keyspace behind vta/memory/*. No document says whether or how the two merge.

There is no separate TypeScript PR. The generated TypeScript library is in #1380 (41 files under trust-tasks-ts/), and the TypeScript demo is in #1382 (examples/hcp-demo-ts).

findings.title: Every HCP context and governance operation has an hcp/* task
findings.claim: Every operation in HCP 5.2 has a task: query, get, create, revise, withdraw, read-own, relinquish and shares/report. Every operation in HCP 5.4 has one too: grants list and revoke, audit read, export, import, disclosure summary, hard delete, confirm, set-categories, restrict-purposes, rules set/remove/list and directives set/remove/list. So do delegations list and end (9.4.13) and the revocation notice (6.2.3, 9.9). That is 27 carried tasks plus grants/request, which carries no HCP operation.
findings.evidence: HCP spec:1121-1131 (5.1 table), spec:1298-1311 (5.4 table), spec:2060-2085 (9.2 endpoints); carries.operation front matter of the 28 specs/hcp/**/0.1/spec.md; grants/request/0.1/spec.md:65 "This task carries no HCP operation."
findings.keyringImpact: Keyring, as Management Client, has a task for every governance screen it plans.
findings.corrected:
The claim holds, and "ok" is the right severity for coverage. Three things need tightening:

(1) HCP 5.4's table says only "Set or remove a standing rule" and "Set or remove a directive" (spec:1310-1311). The list operations come from the 9.2 rows "List or set standing rules" and "List or set directives" (spec:2081, 2083). The PR splits those rows into separate tasks named "List standing rules", "Set standing rule", "List directives" and "Set directive". Those are not HCP's exact wording, while SPEC.md:1307 asks for "the protocol's own name for the operation". This is a naming note only.

(2) Two acts in Core have no HCP endpoint and no task: "Keeping both", which dismisses a conflict (spec:1054), and declining a proposal (spec:1084). This is a gap in HCP, not in the PR.

(3) The Keyring impact line holds only for HCP's governance screens. Keyring's authorization screens have no hcp/* task: Approve with the checklist, "Keep it connected", "Extend", and electing onward sharing when an agent is added to a room. The person decides "through the provider's own modality, never through the client" (grants/request spec.md:87). In our plan that is the VTA's task-consent request to Keyring (plan:1412). Also, every governance task depends on a reading of HCP that is still open, question 37. HCP 5.4 says governance operations "are carried only by the HTTP Binding" (spec:1296), and the PR carries them over Trust Tasks "pending HCP confirmation" (entries/confirm spec.md:99).
findings.reasons:
HOLDS: I opened every citation and each says what the claim says. HCP spec at b790561, 5.1 table, spec:1121-1131: eight context rows (query, get entry, create, revise, withdraw, read own grant, relinquish own grant, report onward sharing) plus the governance row. The 5.4 table, spec:1298-1311, has 12 rows. The 9.2 endpoint table, spec:2060-2085, adds "List delegations" and "Relinquish or end delegation" (9.4.13, spec:2342-2343). Revocation notification is in 6.2.3 (spec:1647-1657) and 9.9 (spec:2445-2486).

On PR branch pr1382 (e163cac1d) there are exactly 28 specs under specs/hcp. 27 of them declare carries (protocol HCP, version 2.0-draft-3, reference to blob/b790561), and their operation values match the 8 context operations, the 16 governance tasks, the 2 delegation operations and the revocation notification. grants/request has no carries member, and spec.md:65 says "**This task carries no HCP operation.**" The pr1380 worktree (94ed4200c) has the same 28 specs with the same operation values, and pr1381 also has 28.

I looked for any operation left out. The MCP tools in 10.3 are a subset of 5.2. Appointing a delegation happens at the Authorization Service, "not through this binding" (spec:2345). Client registration and discovery are not HCP operations. The only uncovered items are the Core conflict acts above, which have no HCP endpoint, so the PR could not carry them.

The refinements in correctedClaim are precision points and a narrower Keyring impact line, not a refutation.

findings.title: Some HCP acts have no task, two of them not even an HTTP endpoint
findings.claim: Some HCP acts have no task. Keeping both entries in a conflict (HCP 4.7.3) and declining a proposal (4.7.4) are acts of the Context Subject through a Management Client. Neither has an endpoint in HCP 9.2 or a task, and question 35 ('not carried') appears in the PR description only. HCP 18.4 still requires that the person can resolve conflicts. Also without a task: establishing a delegation (done by the Authorization Service, by design), client registration (Client Operator, notification endpoint, legal retention, directives claim), token refresh, issuing a Management Client credential, and the discovery document (question 36).
findings.evidence: spec:1054 "Keeping both. ... the Context Subject may close it"; spec:1084 "A proposal the Context Subject declines is removed"; spec:2345 "A delegation is established by the Authorization Service, not through this binding"; grants/request/0.1/spec.md:111 "Version 0.1 issues no refresh token"; grants/revoked/0.1/spec.md:120 "at registration, the client MUST give the provider the VID"; PR #1380 body: "Not carried: dismissing a conflict and declining a proposal (35) ... neither is HCP discovery (36)"
findings.keyringImpact: Keyring cannot offer 'keep both' or 'decline proposal' over hcp/* when memory conflicts arrive (V3, Memory Manager).
findings.askOfPR: Put the 'not carried' list (questions 35 and 36) into the family's text, and say how a client is registered (its notification VID, Client Operator and directives claim), since grants/revoked assumes registration exists.
findings.corrected:
The claim holds, but three parts of it go too far. Severity stays "note"; the documentation ask could be a small "raise".

What holds: "keeping both" (HCP 4.7.3) and declining a proposal (HCP 4.7.4) are acts of the Context Subject. Neither has an endpoint in HCP 9.2 or an MCP tool, and no hcp/* task carries them. Question 35 ("not carried") and question 36 (discovery) appear only in the PR #1380 body, not in any spec text on pr1380, pr1381 or pr1382.

What goes too far:
(1) HCP 18.4 (spec:3497) requires only "resolve a conflict by rejecting, accepting, or superseding an entry". hcp/entries/confirm carries reject and accept, and hcp/entries/revise (by a Management Client) carries supersede. So 18.4 does not require "keep both" or "decline", and the gap is not an 18.4 conformance problem. A provider may also offer 18.4 through any modality of its own.
(2) The Keyring impact puts "keep both" under Memory Manager conflicts, which is wrong. Keep both applies only "where the conflict changed no status" (spec:1054). Memory Manager's candidate pairs all include a `model-inferred` entry and are "the pairs whose conflicts change status" (spec:3213). Keep both matters instead for person-declared/issuer-attested pairs, which is exactly the person-declared-only demo lane (bam C6). Declining a proposal does apply to Memory Manager proposals.
(3) The title says "two of them not even an HTTP endpoint", but delegation establishment (spec:2345), client registration, token refresh (an OAuth matter, HCP 13.4) and the Management Client credential have no HCP 9.2 endpoint either. What sets the two apart is that they are HCP Core person-acts that HCP's own HTTP Binding leaves out. The others are outside HCP's bindings by design.

For the ask: the family already says outright that it does not define registration (grants/request/0.1/spec.md:85, "mapped to it by the provider's registration, which this specification does not define"). The PR body also lists "registering a client at first approval (52)", but that question appears in no spec text either. So the ask should be to put the "not carried" items (35, 36) and question 52 into the family text, rather than to define registration from scratch.
findings.reasons:
HOLDS: Every cited quote is accurate and on the right commit: HCP at b790561, PR family on pr1382, with pr1380 (94ed420, the PR head) as its ancestor. spec:1054 and spec:1084 say what the claim quotes. HCP 9.2 (spec:2060-2085) has no dismiss or decline endpoint, and the MCP tools (10.3) are context-plane only. spec:2345 says a delegation is established by the Authorization Service. grants/request:111 says no refresh token. grants/revoked:120 requires the client to give its VID at registration. The PR body (read with gh) lists 35 and 36 under "Not carried". A git grep on pr1380, pr1381 and pr1382 finds neither question in any spec text. So the core finding stands.

It is overstated in three ways. First, HCP 18.4 lists only reject, accept and supersede, and all three are carried (entries/confirm per its spec lines 276-277, entries/revise by a Management Client). Second, keep-both cannot happen in Memory Manager's status-changing pairs (spec:3213 together with spec:1054), so the Keyring impact points at the wrong kind of conflict. Third, the title's "two of them" ignores that the other uncarried items also have no HCP HTTP endpoint. On top of that, the family text already says it does not define registration (grants/request:85), and the PR body's question 52 on registration is also missing from the spec text.

findings.title: HCP's MCP binding, and its rule that the token must stay out of the model, is never cited
findings.claim: No hcp/* spec or schema cites HCP 10 beyond passing mentions, and none cites 10.5. The family moves the bearer token from the HTTP header into the payload (accessToken). Its token rules address a client that must not log the token, not an MCP host whose model builds the payload. HCP 10.5 says the token MUST NOT enter the model's context or be returned as tool content, that the host holds the grant, and that the host applies directives.
findings.evidence: grep -rn "10\.5" specs/hcp returns nothing on pr1380, pr1381 or pr1382; entries/query/0.1/spec.md:120 "`Authorization: Bearer` header (HCP 9.3) | `accessToken` | Moved from the transport into the payload"; HCP spec:2757 "The access token MUST NOT enter the model's context, and MUST NOT be returned as tool content"; spec:2760 "A local stdio bridge to a remote HCP Provider is an HCP Client in its own right"
findings.keyringImpact: Our plugin is an MCP host. Without this rule in the family, an implementer could pass tokens through a generic tool.
findings.askOfPR: Add a short section to the family (or to each task's 'access token' section) restating HCP 10.5 for an MCP host or agent runtime that carries hcp/* tasks: the token is held and injected by the host and never reaches the model or tool results, and directives are applied by the host.
findings.corrected:
The finding holds and should stay at "raise", with four corrections.

(1) The family's token rules are broader than "must not log". Every task says the token "MUST travel only to the provider" (entries/query/0.1/spec.md:329, repeated family-wide). grants/request/0.1/spec.md:339 says to "present [it] only to the provider that issued it". Read strictly, that already bars handing the token to a model hosted by another party. But no rule names a model, a host, tool results or a local model, and line 96 admits the carriage moves the token into the document, "where it can be stored or forwarded".

(2) The directive half is already partly covered. query:185, grants/read-own:160 and directives/remove:180 say a client that claims to follow directives MUST follow them. _shared/0.1/directive.schema.json:33 says a client presents a directive "to a model as data, never as instructions (HCP 7.4)". What is missing is HCP 10.5:2759 / 21.10:3780: the host applies directives, and "Placing a directive in the model's context is not following it."

(3) HCP 10.5 is scoped "Under the MCP Binding" (spec:2754), and hcp/* over TSP is not that binding. So the restatement should rest on Core as well: 3.11 invariants 6, 9 and 14 hold "in every binding and profile" (spec:561, 570-578). The informative 3.13 step 6 (spec:609) says "Credentials never enter the model's context". Citing these avoids the restatement reading as a new rule, which SPEC §9.4 item 6 forbids (SPEC.md:1631ff on pr1380).

(4) Keyring impact, stated precisely: the MCP host is the agent runtime (Claude Code), not our plugin. Under HCP 10.5:2760, a local stdio bridge such as vta-mcp is itself the HCP Client that holds the token. The risk is concrete: vta-mcp exposes a generic `vta_call` that invokes any Trust Task by URI (vta-mcp/src/server.rs:4 at f7b78e29d), so a model-built hcp/* payload would carry `accessToken`. VTI #2823's own design already applies 10.5 (hcp.md:77, :327 "never in a model's context", :513, :557). The gap is only in the trust-tasks hcp/* family text. | The claim holds but needs narrowing. Severity stays "raise", at low priority.

1. CONFIRMED: no hcp/* spec or schema cites HCP 10.5, on pr1380, pr1381 or pr1382. HCP 10 shows up only as 10.1 (36 times, "governance only over the HTTP Binding"), 10.3.6 once, and the phrase "HCP's own HTTP and MCP bindings" (entries/query:80). No spec tells a client that runs under a model or agent runtime to keep accessToken out of the model's context or out of tool results.

2. The family is not silent about models or directives:
- _shared/0.1/directive.schema.json:33 says "A client presents it to a model as data, never as instructions (HCP 7.4)".
- entries/query:315 says "following them is on a client that claims to".
- The family does not say that the host, not the model, applies directives, or that placing a directive in a model's context is not following it.

3. The token rules are not only about logging. "It MUST travel only to the provider" (entries/query:329) and "present only to the provider that issued it" (grants/request:339), read literally, already rule out sending the token to a remote model API or returning it as tool content. They just never say so.

4. The family's token binding limits the damage of a leak:
- Every token-bearing request needs a proof from the issuer VID (Q22 and Q53, entries/query:331).
- So a token that leaks into a model cannot be replayed over the Trust Task carriage from another VID.
- The remaining exposure is HCP's HTTP Binding, which accepts the token alone (HCP 9.3, quoted at query:331), if the same provider serves both paths. I did not check whether VTA tokens work on both.

5. HCP 10.5's MUST is scoped to the MCP Binding, and its bridge bullet assumes the HTTP Binding (spec:2760). The rules that hold in every binding are in Core: 3.11 invariants 6, 9 and 14 (spec:561, :570, :573, :578), and 3.13 step 6, which is informative: "Credentials never enter the model's context" (spec:609).

The ask should therefore cite Core 3.11 and 3.13, with 10.5 as the MCP precedent, and not "restate 10.5" as a rule for non-MCP carriage. Put it in each spec's "What HCP requires that a document cannot express" section. SPEC §9.4 item 6 (SPEC.md:1642) asks a family to list there the protocol requirements a document cannot express.

Keyring impact is smaller than stated. The VTI design already treats vta-mcp as a 10.5 bridge and applies directives "in code, never in a model's context" (vti2823 hcp.md:77, :327; editor question N1 at :604). Our companion does the same (2026-11-25-bam.md:121, :129, C9 at :176). This is a spec-clarity ask, not a blocker.
findings.reasons:
HOLDS: I checked every cited quote and it is accurate.
- `git grep '10\.5'` over specs/hcp finds nothing on pr1380, pr1381 or pr1382.
- The only HCP 10 / MCP mentions are passing ones, the same on all three branches: entries/query:80 (names HCP's MCP binding), grants/relinquish:68 (the MCP binding does not carry the operation) and shares/report:106 (HCP 10.3.6 tool name).
- query:120 is the quoted mapping row, the same on the pr1380 worktree.
- HCP spec:2757 and :2760 match word for word, inside 10.5 "Who Holds the Grant" (2752-2760). 2756 (the host holds the grant) and 2759 (the host applies directives) are also there.

Trying to disprove it, I found three things.
- The family's token rules do include "MUST travel only to the provider", not only "must not log".
- The family already requires clients to follow directives and to present them to a model as data.
- The same token-out-of-model principle also sits in Core (3.11 invariants, applied in every binding) and in the informative 3.13 step 6 (spec:609). 10.5 itself is scoped to HCP's MCP binding.

None of this refutes the claim. No hcp/* text restates the rule that the token must not enter the model's context or tool results, or that the host, not the model, applies directives. These only sharpen the ask and where it should be anchored. "Raise" is the right severity: it is not an interop blocker, just a clarification worth asking for, made concrete by vta-mcp's generic `vta_call`. || HOLDS: I looked for counter-evidence and found nothing that refutes the core claim. Grepping all three branches finds no 10.5 citation and no rule keeping the token away from a model or agent runtime.

What I did find narrows it:
- The family does address models once, for directives.
- Its "travel only to the provider" rule implicitly forbids passing the token into a model or tool result.
- Its proof-bound token rule limits replay of a leaked token over the Trust Task carriage.
- HCP 10.5's MUST applies by its own terms to the MCP Binding. The same rules for every binding sit in Core, at 3.11 (invariants 6, 9, 14) and 3.13 step 6, so those are the right citations for the ask.
- The VTI design and our own companion already handle this, so the Keyring risk is lower than the finding says.

findings.title: Questions 44, 45 and 47 (and 35, 36, 41, 43, 46, 48-52) are in no spec; the PR description has titles only
findings.claim: No spec.md or schema on pr1380, pr1381, pr1382 or the remote hcp branches contains questions 35, 36, 41, 43, 44, 45, 46, 47, 48, 49, 50, 51 or 52. The specs cite only 1-34, 37-40, 42 and 53. PR #1380's description lists 44, 45 and 47 by title only, yet says every spec's Pending section cites the questions by number. The full wording appears only in VTI #2823 hcp.md §12 as N1, N2 and N4; that mapping is inferred from the titles.

findings.title: Specs require the HCP discovery document and JWKS, but a carriage-only provider cannot publish a valid one
findings.claim: Every hcp/* spec says the provider MUST bind its VID to its HCP identity through its discovery document, and the client MUST check that binding before it sends a token. grants/revoked also requires the client to refuse a notice whose key is not in the provider's HCP JWKS. HCP's discovery schema requires conformsTo and bindings, each with at least one item. VTI V0 publishes no HCP discovery document, V1 plans one 'with no conformsTo', and VTI's docs never mention JWKS. The demo skips the check ('no DID resolution and no network'). So a client that follows the specs cannot send a token to the V0 or V1 VTA, or accept its notices.
findings.evidence: entries/query/0.1/spec.md:136 "its DID document lists the discovery document as a service, or its discovery document names the VID, or both. A client MUST check that binding before it sends a token to a VID."; grants/revoked/0.1/spec.md:82 "MUST refuse a notice whose key it cannot find in that provider's JWKS"; hcp-spec schemas/2.0-draft-3/discovery.json conformsTo minItems 1, bindings minItems 1 enum [http,mcp]; vti2823 hcp-plan.md:132 "discovery with no `conformsTo`"; grep of jwks in vti2823 hcp*.md: none
findings.keyringImpact: Keyring, as a Management Client sending tokens, and our agent plugin, receiving notices, must either skip a MUST or fail against the VTA V0/V1 VTA.
findings.askOfPR: Define a carriage-native binding that works without an HCP discovery document. For example, the provider's DID document carries the notice key (assertionMethod) and the family names it as the source. Or say what a carriage-only, non-claiming provider publishes.
findings.corrected:
The claim holds, with these corrections.

1. The rule appears in 27 of the 28 `hcp/*` specs, most of them by reference to `entries/query`'s Parties section. `grants/revoked` has its own version instead: the client checks that the `issuer` VID is bound to the provider, and refuses a notice whose key is not in the provider's JWKS (spec.md:82). The client-side words "before it sends a token" are explicit in 22 specs. `grants/request` says "before it relies on a token the response carries" (:120). `revise`, `withdraw`, `relinquish` and `shares/report` state only the provider half.

2. The schema point is right, and HCP's text says the same thing. `discovery.json` requires `conformsTo` (minItems 1), `bindings` (minItems 1, enum http/mcp) and `jwks_uri`. HCP 19.3 adds that each binding listed must have its identifier in `conformsTo`. A provider that serves only the Trust Task carriage and claims no conformance therefore has nothing valid to put in either list.

3. "VTI's docs never mention JWKS" is too broad. VTI's HCP design docs (`hcp.md`, `hcp-plan.md`, `hcp-tasks.md`, `tasks/hcp-demo-plan.md`) never mention it, but the pinned VTI clone does use JWKS in other areas (OID4VP, accounts).

4. For V0 the conclusion holds as planned. No V0 work package publishes an HCP discovery document; the only discovery in V0 is `trust-task-discovery`. Our companion agrees ("publishes no HCP discovery document listing an HCP identifier").

5. For V1, "cannot" is overstated; the right word is "not shown". `hcp-plan.md:132` plans a "discovery with no `conformsTo`", which breaks HCP's schema. But the suite's binding check does not say the document must pass that schema: the check passes if the provider's DID document lists the discovery document, or the discovery document names the VID. The V1 plan does not say whether its document will name the VTA's DID, appear in the DID document, or carry a `jwks_uri`.

6. A point that strengthens the ask: HCP Core 6.2.3 hands notice signing to the HTTP Binding ("How it is delivered — push delivery, signing, identifiers, and retry — is defined by the HTTP Binding (9.9)"). The `jwks_uri` rule is an HTTP Binding rule that the suite brought into the carriage.

Severity should be "raise", not "blocker". The suite requires a discovery document that HCP 19.1 requires only of implementations that claim conformance, and says nothing about what a provider that claims nothing and serves only the carriage publishes. That is worth asking the PR to fix. But it is not a wire incompatibility, and VTI could close it for our deployment without changing the PR: publish a document carrying `provider`, `jwks_uri` and the VTA's DID, and sign notices with a DID key that is also in that JWKS. It counts as a blocker only against the V0 plan as currently written. | The claim holds in substance, but it is overstated in three places. The right severity is "raise" (a strong one), not "blocker". Precise version:

(1) Scope. 27 of the 28 specs state the provider MUST. Four of them (entries/withdraw, entries/revise, grants/relinquish, shares/report) give only the provider MUST, "As for hcp/entries/query", and do not restate the client check. grants/revoked has its own, stricter rule at line 82: the notice key must be in both the DID document and the HCP JWKS, and the client MUST refuse a notice whose key is not in the JWKS. Line 120 points back to the query binding.

(2) The dependency comes from the suite, not from HCP. HCP requires a discovery document only of "Every implementation claiming HCP conformance" (spec:3535). HCP's JWKS rule for notices sits in the HTTP Binding (spec:2480, 9.9), and Core 6.2.3 hands signing to that binding (spec:1649). So a provider that carries HCP only as Trust Tasks and makes no claim has no HCP identity under HCP, yet the suite requires it to bind its VID to one and to publish a JWKS.

The schema point is correct. HCP's discovery.json requires conformsTo (minItems 1) and bindings (minItems 1, enum http/mcp). 19.3 (spec:3612) says each listed binding must also be claimed in conformsTo, and 18.1 forbids listing a Part the provider does not meet in full. So a schema-valid discovery document needs a real HTTP or MCP binding claim. One caveat: the suite never says the binding document must pass HCP's schema, and never names the member that "names the VID". A V1 document with no conformsTo could still name the VID and give a jwks_uri, and let a client's check pass. VTI's V1 plan (hcp-plan.md:132) does not say whether it will.

(3) Keyring impact is overstated for V0. In V0 Keyring sends no token: management is proven by the admin DID ("no token (§4.4)", hcp.md:158; also hcp.md:230-239 and decision 7 at :551). So "check that binding before it sends a token" does not apply to Keyring in V0. Keyring's V0 mismatch is a different one: the governance payload schemas require accessToken. Keyring is affected from V1, when management tokens arrive.

Those who are blocked now:
- The Context Client (our agent plugin) at V0. The grants/request spec says the client "MUST check that binding before it relies on a token the response carries", and query and the other context tasks say the same before a token is sent.
- Every notice receipt at V0 and V1. No VTI document mentions a JWKS.

VTI's divergence register (hcp.md:586-598) records neither gap. As designed, V0 and V1 do not meet the provider MUST of the suite VTI pins.

It is an interop break only for an independent client that follows the suite strictly. Keyring and our plugin can work. The ask stands as written: a binding that works through the carriage alone, or a statement of what a provider that serves only the carriage and makes no claim publishes. VTI should also record the gap as a divergence.
findings.reasons:
HOLDS: I read every cited quote at its location on the right branch: the PR branch pr1382, the HCP spec at b790561, and VTI PR #2823. Each quote says what the claim says.

What I confirmed:
- `entries/query`'s Parties rule (:136) and the JWKS refusal in `grants/revoked` (:82).
- The discovery schema requires `conformsTo` (minItems 1, line 26) and `bindings` (minItems 1, enum http/mcp, line 36). It also requires `jwks_uri` and does not forbid extra members.
- HCP 19.1 (:3535): "Every implementation claiming HCP conformance MUST publish a discovery document". HCP 19.3 (:3612): "Each binding listed here has its identifier in conformsTo".
- VTI `hcp-plan.md:132` plans "discovery with no `conformsTo`". VTI's HCP docs have no JWKS, no VID-binding step, and no HCP discovery document in V0's work packages.
- The demo's `SCENARIO.md:48` says "There is no DID resolution and no network".
- `grants/revoke`'s payload requires `accessToken` (schema `required: [grantId, accessToken]`). So Keyring does send a token, even though VTI V0 manages grants by DID-proven request; that does not get it out of the binding rule.

Why it is not refuted:
- The core argument stands. The suite requires an HCP discovery document that is listed in the provider's DID document or names the VID, plus a JWKS. HCP's schema and text cannot be satisfied by a provider that claims nothing and serves only the carriage. VTI V0 publishes no such document, and VTI's HCP docs never mention a JWKS.

What is overstated:
- "Every spec": it is 27 of 28 plus `grants/revoked`'s own version of the rule.
- "VTI's docs never mention JWKS": true of the HCP design docs only.
- "Cannot" for V1: the suite's check does not require the discovery document to pass HCP's schema, and the V1 plan does not say whether it will carry the needed members. So for V1 it is "not shown", not "cannot".
- Severity: VTI can close this on its side without changing the PR, so "raise" fits better than "blocker".

New context: HCP Core 6.2.3 (:1649) sends notice signing to the HTTP Binding's 9.9 (:2480). The JWKS rule is HTTP-Binding-level, which supports the finding's ask for a key rule native to the carriage. || HOLDS: I found no exception, later section or default in the suite, the framework, HCP, VTI or the demo that removes the dependency:
- The binding text is the same on pr1380, pr1381 and pr1382.
- trust-task-discovery 0.4 binds no identity. Framework SPEC §9.4 item 5 only says a family must state what supplies a party identifier.
- HCP's discovery schema does require conformsTo and bindings, each with at least one item, from {http, mcp}.
- The demo does skip the check (SCENARIO.md:48, "There is no DID resolution and no network.").
- VTI's V0 and V1 milestones are "aligned pilot (no conformsTo)". VTI's PR docs never mention a JWKS. Its divergence table does not list the VID binding or the notice key.

What I found that narrows the claim:
- HCP itself does not require a discovery document or a JWKS of a provider that makes no claim (19.1; 6.2.3 hands signing to 9.9 in the HTTP Binding). The gap is the suite's own. This supports the ask; it does not refute it.
- In V0 VTI sends Keyring no token, so the token-gated check does not reach Keyring until V1.
- The suite never requires the binding document to be schema-valid, so a document with no conformsTo that names the VID (V1) is not ruled out.

So the core claim stands, but "blocker" for Keyring is too strong. "Raise" fits: Keyring can work, and the failure is limited to clients that follow the suite strictly (our plugin at V0, and every notice).

findings.title: Claim posture is consistent across HCP, the suite and VTI
findings.claim: HCP 1.7 and 18.1 require a conformsTo list in a discovery document naming Core and every whole Part claimed, with mandatory profiles triggered by behaviour, and every package needs a binding. The suite says a provider MUST NOT claim the carriage and advertises it through trust-task-discovery. VTI makes no claim in V0 or V1, claims First-Party at V2 through the HTTP Binding, and plans Provider and Agent Interop in V3. Before any claim there must be a full HTTP or MCP binding, a valid discovery document and JWKS, an authorization profile, General Context, the 18.4 person-facing capabilities, the published suite (it does not exist yet) and the 20.2 test hook. Identifiers use the placeholder hcp.example and will change.
findings.evidence: HCP spec:100-102, 104-128, 3452-3460, 3466-3475, 3535-3540, 3667, 3685-3687; entries/query/0.1/spec.md:94 "a provider MUST NOT claim this carriage in its HCP `conformsTo`"; SPEC.md §9.4 item 7 "Conformance stays with the protocol"; vti2823 hcp.md:60-64, 82-86, 617-623

findings.corrected: The claim holds at severity ok, but two items in its list of things needed before a claim are wrong. HCP, the hcp/* suite and VTI agree. HCP 18.1 requires a conformsTo list in the discovery document that names Core and every binding and profile claimed, each claimed whole. Profiles become mandatory through behaviour (model-inferred entries, issuer-attested health or education entries, delegated grants). Every package names a binding, and General Context is required in every package (Part III table). All 28 hcp/* specs on pr1380/pr1382 say a provider MUST NOT list the carriage in conformsTo and advertises it through trust-task-discovery, but this is marked "pending HCP confirmation (question 1)": the suite plans to ask HCP's editors for a carriage identifier, so this position is provisional. VTI makes no claim in V0 or V1, plans the First-Party package at V2 through the HTTP Binding, and plans Provider Interop and Agent Interop in V3 (H4, H5). The HCP requirements for any claim are: a binding (19.3 `bindings` Required), a discovery document (19.1) with jwks_uri (19.3 Required), an authorization profile (6.1 'the authorization profile an implementation claims'), General Context (in every package) and the 18.4 person-facing capabilities. The published HCP conformance suite and the 20.2 test hook are NOT HCP preconditions for a claim. HCP 20 'places no requirement on implementations beyond those in the sections it cites'. The 20.2 hook concerns only the First-Party Authorization Profile, and the suite specification defines it. A deployment holding any real person's context cannot offer it without failing 6.1.6. Those two items are VTI's own V2 exit gate (hcp-plan.md:235-237, 'the conformance suite passes ... the HCP 20.2 test hook exists only on lab builds'). They are not HCP's. Identifiers use the placeholder hcp.example, and the permanent namespace is to be fixed before v2 is final. Keyring's wording 'HCP-aligned pilot' matches VTI hcp.md:82-86 and HCP G1.2 ('a pilot that tests one rung should not claim the next'). A small VTI-side tension (note): V2 would publish the claim on 'one lab or fleet instance'. If that is a fleet instance holding real context, it cannot carry the hook, so the conformance run cannot be made against that same deployment (HCP 20.2 / 6.1.6).

findings.title: HCP Core itself puts governance on HTTP only, so a Core claim depends on question 37
findings.claim: HCP Core 5.4, in Part I, says governance operations 'are carried only by the HTTP Binding', and the 1.6 table lists HTTP only for governance. The suite carries all governance as Trust Tasks, pending question 37. VTI's V2 First-Party claim is made on a deployment where Keyring still does governance over Trust Tasks. If the provider lists Core, and Core is claimed whole, that claim depends on the editors answering question 37 yes, unless governance over Trust Tasks is turned off on the claiming deployment.
findings.evidence: HCP spec:1296 "Governance operations are performed only by a Management Client acting for the Authorizing Principal ..., and are carried only by the HTTP Binding"; spec:89-92; spec:3453 "A binding or profile is claimed whole"; grants/revoke/0.1/spec.md:207 "Question 37 — governance over a carriage other than the HTTP Binding"; vti2823 hcp.md:620
findings.keyringImpact: On a claiming deployment, Keyring may have to call governance over the HTTP Binding instead of Trust Tasks.
findings.askOfPR: In question 37, note that the HTTP-only wording is in Core 5.4, not only in the binding, so the answer decides whether a provider that carries governance over Trust Tasks can claim Core.
findings.corrected:
Severity stays "raise". The finding holds in substance but goes too far in two places, and its ask is partly done already.

(1) What holds (CONFIRMED). Core 5.4, which is in Part I (Part I runs from spec:269 to spec:2046), says at spec:1296 that governance operations "are carried only by the HTTP Binding". The 1.6 table at spec:90 says "HTTP only". Note that 1.6 sits in §1, which is "Claimable: No" (spec:18). Under 18.1, an implementation "MUST list Core" (spec:3452) and "MUST NOT list an identifier unless it satisfies every requirement of that Part" (spec:3453). That second rule is what makes Core all-or-nothing; the quoted sentence "A binding or profile is claimed whole" does not name Core. Every package lists Core (spec:3468), so the whole V2 First-Party claim is at stake, not only the Core line.

The VTI design keeps Keyring on the Trust Task carriage on the claiming deployment:
- hcp.md:76: "used by: Keyring, the agent client"
- hcp-plan.md:72: only the plugin moves to HTTP ("plugin B10 over the HTTP Binding")
- bam.md:180, C13: Keyring does governance over Trust Tasks, pending question 37

hcp.md:620 by itself does not say any of this.

(2) What is too strong. Saying the claim "depends on question 37 being answered yes" overstates it; it is an open ambiguity in HCP, not a settled dependency:
- 5.4's "are carried only by" has no BCP 14 keyword. Core's MUST at 6.1.9 (spec:1618) limits who may call a governance operation, not how it is carried.
- The Part I preamble (spec:273) judges behavior "as observed across an HCP binding or in an export", and a Trust Task carriage is not an HCP binding.
- HCP itself lets governance be reached outside any binding: 10.1 at spec:2495 says "reached through the HTTP Binding ([9]) or the person-facing capabilities required by 18", and 18.4 at spec:3507 says a provider with the HTTP Binding "MAY" offer them through a Management Client over it.
- Against that, 1.6 at spec:96 and 18.5 at spec:3528 say: "Where that interface is an HCP Client, it reaches governance operations as a Management Client over the HTTP Binding". VTI names Keyring as exactly that HCP Client (hcp.md:112).

So the outcome turns on whether Keyring over Trust Tasks counts as an HCP Client using a non-HTTP carriage (not allowed, unless question 37 says yes) or as the provider's own person-facing route (allowed).

(3) The ask's premise is wrong. Question 37 already cites Core 5.4: grants/revoke/0.1/spec.md:207 says "HCP 1.6, 5.4, 9.1, 10.1", and the text is the same on pr1380, pr1381 and pr1382. What is missing is the consequence. Neither question 37 nor the Conformance section (spec.md:81) nor question 1 (spec.md:202) says that a "no" would stop a provider serving the governance tasks from listing Core at all, and so from making any HCP claim. That is more than the carriage simply having no identifier.

Corrected ask: in question 37, say that because 5.4 is Core and 18.1 is all-or-nothing, the answer decides whether a provider that also serves `hcp/*` governance tasks can list Core, and with it any package. Also ask whether a Management Client run by the provider's own operator over a non-HTTP carriage counts as the "person-facing capabilities" route of 10.1 and 18.4. | Severity stays raise. The claim holds, but two parts need narrowing.

(1) What Core restricts. Core 5.4 (spec:1296) and the 1.6 table (spec:90, "HTTP only") put governance operations on the HTTP Binding. HCP still lets governance capabilities be reached outside any HCP binding:
- Core 6.1.5 (spec:1544): the person "MUST still be able to enumerate and revoke grants through a supported modality".
- 10.1 (spec:2493): governance is "reached through the HTTP Binding (9) or the person-facing capabilities required by 18".
- 18.4 (spec:3507): an HTTP-exposing implementation "MAY" offer them through a Management Client over HTTP.

What HCP rules out is an HCP Client reaching governance any other way. 1.6:96 and 18.5:3528 say "Where that interface is an HCP Client, it reaches governance operations as a Management Client over the HTTP Binding". The 5.4 sentence carries no capitalized MUST. 1.6:92 also places the carriage limit in the MCP Binding: "the MCP Binding carries none of them". So whether 5.4 binds a provider is itself the open point.

The conclusion stands. Both the suite and VTI cast Keyring as an HCP Management Client presenting an access token (revoke spec:87; hcp.md:112). VTI's V2 First-Party claim is on a deployment where Keyring keeps governance on Trust Tasks (hcp.md:69-80, :620; companion C13/C14). On that deployment a Core claim relies on question 37 being answered yes. The other ways out are:
- move Keyring's governance to the HTTP Binding;
- turn governance over Trust Tasks off there;
- recast Keyring as the provider's own person-facing app (3.2.5:354), not an HCP Client. That reading is also unconfirmed, and it conflicts with how the suite and VTI cast Keyring.

(2) The ask is mostly already met. Question 37 in all 18 governance specs already cites "HCP 1.6, 5.4, 9.1, 10.1", so Core 5.4 is named. The real gap is elsewhere:
- Question 1 ties question 37 only to a conformance identifier for the carriage, and neither question says the answer decides whether a provider serving governance tasks may list Core (and so the First-Party package).
- VTI #2823's mitigation "The claim rests on the HTTP Binding" (hcp-plan.md:258) assumes the Trust Task path cannot affect the Core claim.

The ask should go to both the suite (questions 1 and 37) and VTI #2823.
findings.reasons:
HOLDS: Every quote cited is accurate and from the right commit (hcp-spec at b790561; the suite on pr1380, pr1381 and pr1382, all with the same question 37 text). Core 5.4 is in Part I and does say governance is "carried only by the HTTP Binding". 18.1 makes Core all-or-nothing and requires it in every claim. VTI's V2 First-Party deployment keeps Keyring's governance on Trust Tasks. So the finding's core concern holds, and I did not refute it.

It is overstated in two ways:
- The dependency is not settled. 5.4's wording has no BCP 14 keyword, Core's MUST (6.1.9) limits only the caller, and HCP itself lets governance be reached outside any binding through the person-facing capabilities (10.1, 18.4, and the Part I interface-boundary preamble). On the other side, 1.6 and 18.5 say an HCP Client reaches governance over the HTTP Binding. HCP leaves this unclear rather than settling it, which fits "raise" as an ask for clarification.
- The ask says question 37 should note the wording "is in Core 5.4, not only in the binding", but question 37 already cites 5.4. What it lacks is the consequence: a "no" means the provider cannot list Core, and so cannot claim any package.

A smaller point: the quoted sentence "A binding or profile is claimed whole" does not cover Core; the rule that does is the sentence before it on the same line, 3453. || HOLDS: I searched for counter-evidence and found none that defeats the claim. All cited lines check out (spec:1296, :90, :3453; grants/revoke spec:207; hcp.md:620).

What I found narrows two things.

First, HCP does allow governance outside the HTTP Binding, through the provider's own person-facing interface or "a supported modality" (Core 6.1.5:1544, 10.1:2493, 18.4:3493 and :3507, 1.6:96). That route is closed only to an HCP Client (1.6:96, 18.5:3528). The suite and VTI both cast Keyring as an HCP Management Client that presents an access token, so the finding's conclusion still applies to the planned deployment. The 5.4 sentence has no capitalized MUST, and 1.6:92 places the carriage limit in the MCP Binding. Neither makes the finding wrong: they show the point really is open, which is exactly what question 37 asks.

Second, the ask "note that the wording is in Core 5.4" is already done. Question 37 cites 5.4 by number in all 18 governance specs. What remains missing is the consequence for a Core or First-Party claim. Question 1 links question 37 only to a carriage identifier, and VTI's risk mitigation says "The claim rests on the HTTP Binding".

The Keyring impact holds. The companion's C13/C14 keep Keyring's governance on Trust Tasks through P2/V2, and B10 moves only the plugin to the HTTP Binding.

findings.title: Governance tasks require a Management Client token that no task issues; VTI V0 sends none
findings.claim: The payload schema of every governance task (revoke, list, audit, export, import, rules, directives, confirm, set-categories, restrict-purposes, hard-delete, delegations, disclosure summary) lists accessToken as required. No hcp/* task issues a Management Client token: grants/request is for a Context Client. The demo hard-codes 'hcp_mt_demo_management issued at setup'. VTI V0 has Keyring send governance tasks with no token, authenticated by the admin DID and ACL, and adds management tokens only in V1. Under the published schemas those V0 documents are invalid.
findings.evidence: specs/hcp/*/0.1/payload.schema.json required: grants/revoke [grantId, accessToken], audit/read [accessToken], ...; grants/revoke/0.1/spec.md:86 "evidenced by the Management Client's access token in `accessToken`"; examples/hcp-demo-ts/src/demo.ts:111 MANAGEMENT_TOKEN "DEMO ONLY: issued to the person's app at setup"; vti2823 hcp.md:230-239 "authenticate the admin DID ... V1 adds dedicated opaque management tokens"
findings.keyringImpact: Keyring is the Management Client. Built against the suite's generated types, it must send a token it has no way to obtain. Built against VTI V0, its documents fail the published schema.
findings.askOfPR: Either add a task by which a Management Client obtains its credential (for example, one bound to the person's authentication), or define a DID-proven Management Client form in which the issuer proof is the evidence and accessToken is optional. State which one VTI should implement.
findings.corrected:
Severity should be raise, not blocker. The facts are right, but the gap is framed as the suite's when it comes from HCP itself and from VTI V0's design.

(1) CONFIRMED: every governance payload schema on pr1382 lists accessToken as required: grants/list, grants/revoke, audit/read, export, import, rules/*, directives/*, entries/confirm, set-categories, restrict-purposes, hard-delete, delegations/*, disclosures/summary. So does every context task except grants/request and the grants/revoked notice. pr1381 does not change this.

(2) CONFIRMED: no hcp/* task issues a Management Client credential, and grants/request is Context-Client-only. But HCP 2.0-draft-3 has no such operation either. Its 9.2 endpoint table has none. Per 3.2.3, a Management Client acts "under credentials the Authorizing Principal obtained by authenticating for that purpose", and 12.2 "does not mandate a wire-level request format" for the channel. The suite's schema calls the token opaque and provider-issued. So the VTA can mint a management token by its own means, which VTI already plans for V1. Keyring lacks a suite-defined way to get one; it is not left with no way at all.

(3) CONFIRMED: the suite rules out the DID-proven form as written. revoke spec.md:91 says "It is not the authorization: the token is." VTI V0 (hcp.md §4.4, decision 7) has Keyring manage with "no token", yet V0 pins the suite's schemas (hcp-plan A1) and Keyring uses the suite's types (C0-C3). V0 Keyring documents therefore fail the pinned schemas, or would carry a meaningless value. This part is inferred: VTI never says it leaves out the member.

(4) Minor: VTI V0 lists hcp/entries/create as a governance task, but HCP 1.6 puts Create on the context plane.

The asks:
- Primary, to VTI: either mint an opaque management token for Keyring in V0, or first get the suite to accept issuer-proven management.
- Secondary, to the PR: state that the Management Client credential is obtained outside the carriage and is provider-defined, and say whether an issuer proof from a Management Client the ACL names may stand in for accessToken (pending HCP confirmation, like question 37).

A new task that issues management credentials would go beyond HCP. The suite says "where it differs from the HCP text, the HCP text governs", which weighs against it. | The facts hold, but two parts are overstated and the severity should be "raise", not "blocker". What holds: every governance payload schema lists accessToken as required, and so does hcp/entries/create, which VTI routes through Keyring. hcp/grants/request is for Context Clients only. No hcp/* task issues a Management Client token. The demo hard-codes "hcp_mt_demo_management", issued at setup. VTI V0 has Keyring send governance tasks with no token. The suite also says outright that the document proof "is not the authorization: the token is". So the V0 documents VTI describes fail the published schema, and VTI's own divergence table records this only as a divergence from HCP 1.6/5.4, never as a schema break.

What is overstated:
(1) The missing issuance task comes from HCP itself, not from this PR. HCP 3.2.3 leaves Management Client credentials to authentication outside the protocol ("under credentials the Authorizing Principal obtained by authenticating for that purpose"). The HTTP Binding has no endpoint for getting them either. Framework SPEC §9.4 item 1 forbids a carrying task for an operation HCP does not define. So any issuance task would have to be a non-carrying task like hcp/grants/request.
(2) Keyring is not left with no way to get a token. The VTA already has auth/authenticate/0.3 over DIDComm, which mints tokens for the signing DID, and VTI's V1 adds dedicated management tokens. Our plan (D2) chose not to build that path; it was not impossible.

The ask needs narrowing. Ask the PR to say where a Management Client's token comes from: either "provider-defined, per HCP 3.2.3" or a non-carrying issuance task. Making accessToken optional on a DID proof would change what HCP requires (SPEC §9.4 item 6; HCP 9.3 requires a Bearer token), so it can only go in as a new pending-HCP question. Ask VTI to either mint a management token in V0 (for example through auth/authenticate) or record the schema deviation openly.
findings.reasons:
HOLDS: I opened every citation, and each one says what the claim says. The schemas require accessToken. The revoke spec takes the Management Client's token as the authority and says the proof is not. The demo hard-codes a token "issued to the person's app at setup". VTI hcp.md 4.4 sends no token in V0 and adds management tokens in V1. The citations are from the right versions: suite on pr1382 at e163cac1d (pr1381 leaves the revoke schema alone), HCP at b790561, VTI from PR #2823's docs. So the claim is not refuted.

It is overstated in two ways:
- "No hcp/* task issues a Management Client token" is just as true of HCP itself. HCP has no HTTP endpoint or operation for it and leaves the credential to the provider's own authentication (3.2.3, 12.2, 20.2). The suite carries HCP faithfully here, and the VTA can issue an opaque token by its own means. So "Keyring must send a token it has no way to obtain" goes too far: it has no suite-defined way.
- Keyring and the VTA are the only two parties on this path, and VTI controls the fix: mint a management token in V0, or move up its planned V1 tokens. Nothing breaks interop with the suite as published, so raise fits better than blocker.

What does stand: VTI V0's tokenless, DID-proven management contradicts the suite it pins. The suite says the token, not the proof, is the authority, and its schemas require the field. That needs settling before V0 Keyring documents can validate. || HOLDS: I searched the HCP spec, the suite, the framework SPEC, and VTI's design and source for counter-evidence. Nothing contradicts the factual core.

The schemas require accessToken. I checked every specs/hcp/*/0.1/payload.schema.json; only grants/request and grants/revoked lack it. grants/request is Context Client only (spec.md:5, :11). The suite states that the proof is not the authority (grants/revoke spec.md:91: "It is not the authorization: the token is"). VTI V0 has Keyring send no token (hcp.md:158 "no token (§4.4)", :230-239; demo plan :171 "management tokens come in V1"). So the V0 documents would fail the published schema, and VTI's divergence table (hcp.md:591) does not mention that.

Two pieces of evidence narrow the claim:
- **HCP leaves this open itself.** HCP defines no mechanism for a Management Client to obtain its credential. Spec :337 says "under credentials the Authorizing Principal obtained by authenticating for that purpose". The endpoint table at :2058-2085 has no such endpoint. The suite therefore faithfully carries something HCP leaves to the provider.
- **The VTA already has a way.** It mints DID-bound tokens over DIDComm through auth/authenticate/0.3 (handlers.rs:65, auth.rs:227, :273). Our plan's D2 (bam.md:450) chose not to use it ("no auth/authenticate fallback is built").

So "Keyring cannot obtain a token" is not true. "Cannot obtain one through an hcp/* task" is true, and that gap comes from HCP. Nothing here breaks interop, since Keyring and the VTA can fix it on their side, so "raise" fits better than "blocker". Also, SPEC §9.4 items 1 and 6 limit the proposed fixes: an issuance task would have to be non-carrying, like grants/request, and a DID-proven optional-token form departs from HCP 9.3.

findings.title: Our plugin with vta-mcp is an HCP Client bridge that tunnels Trust Tasks, not an HCP MCP binding
findings.claim: In HCP's sense an MCP binding is exposed and claimed by an HCP Provider: server/discover with the example.hcp/hcp extension, the six hcp_* tools on Core schemas, the 10.4 error mapping, and MCP 2026-07-28 statelessness. Our plugin runs vta-mcp locally (stdio or loopback) as the agent identity. Its generic vta_call tool tunnels any Trust Task by URI. Under HCP 10.5 that makes it an HCP Client in its own right, a bridge with its own Client Operator, not a binding. To conform as a client it must hold the token, expose typed tools, run the hold and notice loops, enforce useUntil and directives in code, and have answers to questions 44, 45 and 46 (N1, N2, N3).
findings.evidence: HCP spec:2491, 2502-2519, 2525-2539, 2756-2760, 3460 "a claim is made for an HCP Provider"; vta-mcp/README.md:9 "Transport is stdio", :54 "vta_call | Invoke any operation by URI with a JSON payload"; agent-connect-plan.md:920 D40 "The plugin reuses `vta-mcp` for every operation on the VTA"
findings.keyringImpact: Plan D40 does not cover hcp/*. The plan's own fallback, the plugin calling the VTA directly through the TypeScript SDK, is where the HCP client belongs.
findings.corrected:
Severity stays "note". The core of the claim holds: our plugin running vta-mcp is an HCP Client, not an HCP MCP Binding. Four parts need correcting.

(1) HCP's MCP Binding is something an HCP Provider exposes and claims. The provider identifies itself through server/discover with the example.hcp/hcp extension (spec:2502), exposes the six hcp_* tools (10.3), maps errors as 10.4 says and targets MCP 2026-07-28 with no session state (spec:2491). The plugin plus vta-mcp is none of that. It is an HCP Client under 3.2.3, which says "The component that presents credentials holds the grant" and lists "an MCP host or its integration... a command-line tool". The 10.5 sentence (spec:2760) describes a "local stdio bridge" that "calls the provider over the HTTP Binding". vta-mcp instead sends signed Trust Tasks over DIDComm or TSP, and with --listen it serves loopback HTTP rather than stdio. So 10.5 applies only by analogy until question 44 (N1) is answered.

(2) "To conform as a client" is the wrong frame. Under 18.1 (spec:3460) the only claim a client can make in this draft is the directives claim. Client obligations apply whether or not a claim is made.

(3) Not every item listed is an HCP requirement:
- **Required:** the access token must never enter the model's context (10.5). As things stand, vta_call sends whatever payload the model wrote (server.rs:174-182, 886-907). hcp/entries/query requires accessToken in its payload (payload.schema.json:11). So a bridge-side change is needed: either inject the token in the bridge or expose typed tools. Typed tools are one way to meet the rule, not a requirement of their own.
- **Required:** honouring useUntil (7.6), and the onward-disclosure rules.
- **Conditional:** the notice loop is needed only if the client registers a notification endpoint. Without one, copies are capped at 1 hour (7.6 item 4; grants/revoked/0.1/spec.md:246).
- **Conditional:** directives must be applied in code only if the client makes the directives claim (6.4; 10.5).
- **Not HCP's:** the hold loop is a rule of the Trust Task carriage (grants/request), not of HCP.

(4) The Keyring impact needs a fix. The HCP companion already puts the Context Client in the plugin's own code: B7 reads "The plugin as Context Client in vti-agent-connect (entries/query, notices), the CLI's code as its library" (2026-11-25-bam.md:386, :411), and the row at :121 covers use-until and directives. The real gap is wording: D40's "reuses vta-mcp for every operation on the VTA" (agent-connect-plan.md:920) would send hcp/* through vta_call, which contradicts B7. D40 should exclude hcp/*.
findings.reasons:
HOLDS: All cited quotes are accurate and from the right versions: HCP spec at b790561, vta-mcp at the VTI pin f7b78e29d, and the plan. Questions 44, 45 and 46 do map to N1, N2 and N3. The description of PR #1380 at head 94ed420 lists "a local bridge over a non-HTTP carriage (44); the Client Operator of an agent plugin (45)", and under onward sharing "a model API run by another organization (46)". These match VTI hcp.md:604-606.

So the conclusion holds: the plugin is a client-side bridge and an HCP Client, not a binding. Three parts are overstated:
- **Citing 10.5:** its text assumes a stdio bridge calling over the HTTP Binding, and ours uses a different carriage. That is exactly what N1 asks, so 3.2.3 is the firmer basis for calling it an HCP Client.
- **The requirement list:** typed tools, the notice loop and directives are presented as unconditional. They are a design choice, conditional or claim-dependent, and the hold loop is a carriage rule, not HCP's.
- **The Keyring impact:** it misses that the companion's B7 already places the HCP Context Client in the plugin's own library. The real issue is that D40's "every operation" wording conflicts with B7.

findings.title: vta_call would put the HCP token into the model's context, both ways
findings.claim: VtaCallParams has only operation and payload, and the model supplies the payload. Every hcp/* request needs accessToken inside the payload, so the model would hold the token. vta_call returns the reply payload to the model unchanged, so the grants/request response's accessToken would come back as tool content. Both break HCP 10.5 and the suite's rule that the token travels only between client and provider.
findings.evidence: vta-mcp/src/server.rs:174-182 (VtaCallParams: operation, payload); :882-908 vta_call → dispatch_trust_task; :299-309 finish → ok_json(value) unchanged; grants/request/0.1/spec.md:221 "`accessToken` ... the client presents the token unchanged as `accessToken`"; HCP spec:2757
findings.keyringImpact: Our plugin cannot use vta_call for hcp/*. It needs a token-holding client of its own.
findings.corrected:
The mechanism holds at the VTI pin f7b78e29d, but the claim needs three corrections. (1) Not every hcp/* request carries the token. 26 of the 28 payload schemas on pr1382 list `accessToken` as required. The two that do not are hcp/grants/request, which only requires `access` because it is the call that obtains a token, and hcp/grants/revoked, the provider's notice to the client. (2) The rules that forbid it: HCP 10.5 (spec:2757) says "The access token MUST NOT enter the model's context, and MUST NOT be returned as tool content". 10.5 also says "A local stdio bridge to a remote HCP Provider is an HCP Client in its own right. It holds the token", which describes vta-mcp exactly. vta_call is a raw pass-through and holds nothing, so sending hcp/* through it would make the bridge break 10.5. The suite's own wording is grants/request/0.1/spec.md:345 ("MUST travel only to the client that asked for the grant") and entries/query/0.1/spec.md:329 ("MUST travel only to the provider"). HCP 3.13's "Credentials never enter the model's context" is marked Informative. (3) The severity is raise, not blocker. Neither PR #1380/#1382 nor VTI #2823 sends hcp/* through vta_call. In #2823, hcp.md:113 makes the Context Client "a CLI for the demo, then the agent plugin", with its own VID and no ACL entry. Decision 13 at hcp.md:557 is "MCP is not a shortcut", and MCP is deferred to H5 (MCP over Streamable HTTP, mapped onto OAuth). So nothing breaks interop with the PR. What it breaks is our own plan: agent-connect-plan.md:920, D40, says "The plugin reuses `vta-mcp` for every operation on the VTA". D40 needs an hcp/* exception: the plugin, or a token-holding HCP tool, must keep the token, sign hcp/* itself and give the model only the answers. A second reason vta_call cannot carry hcp/grants/request at the pin: VtaCallParams has no thread member, and build_task_document makes a fresh document with no `threadId`, so vta_call cannot "resubmit on the same thread" (grants/request spec:63). A possible ask to VTI, not to the suite PR: the "MCP guard risk class" in #2823's A8 should deny hcp/* in vta_call, or mask accessToken, rather than only set how risky the call is. | Severity should be raise, not blocker. The mechanism holds, but only once hcp/* can be sent through vta_call. At the pinned VTI commit f7b78e29d there are no hcp URIs at all (grep -c hcp vta-sdk/src/trust_tasks.rs = 0), so vta_call cannot reach any hcp/* task today. VTI #2823's A8 step (hcp-plan.md:106, hcp-tasks.md:173-179) would make them reachable. It adds a TASK_* constant per hcp URI to vta-sdk, and those constants feed ALL_URIS even when a feature is off (trust_tasks.rs:1589). ALL_URIS feeds dispatch_routed_uris and so vta_call's catalog (server.rs:852). A8 also adds hcp/* to the vta-mcp census and to an MCP guard risk class. Once that lands:
(a) The model writes the payload (VtaCallParams has only operation and payload, server.rs:174-182). So for the 26 hcp/* tasks whose schema requires accessToken, the model must hold the token. Two of the 28 need none: grants/request is how a client gets a token, and grants/revoked is sent by the VTA.
(b) The grants/request reply's accessToken comes back to the model as tool text, unchanged. dispatch_trust_task returns the payload, finish() hands it to ok_json, and ok_json writes it as text (server.rs:97-100, :299-309). Nothing in vta-mcp holds it back: the guard has no class that keeps a task out of vta_call (the Sensitive class only asks for confirmation, guard.rs:57-60, :1035-1066), and redact_call only cleans the logs.
This conflicts with HCP 10.5 (spec :2756-2757; :2760, which says a stdio bridge is an HCP Client that holds the token) and with the suite's rule at grants/request spec.md:345 ("MUST travel only to the client"). VTI's own decision 13 (hcp.md:557) says the same: "MCP is not a shortcut".
Why not a blocker:
- Interop and Keyring are not broken. Keyring is the Management Client.
- Our HCP plan does not send hcp/* through vta_call. The agent CLI, and later the plugin, is its own Context Client with its own VID and keeps the token (companion 2026-11-25-bam.md:239-242 B1-B4, :411 B7 "the CLI's code as its library"). So the "Keyring impact" is already planned.
- #1380 has nothing to change.
Asks: VTI #2823 A8 should keep hcp/* out of vta_call, or have vta-mcp hold the token and remove it from results. Our D40 (agent-connect-plan.md:920, "reuses vta-mcp for every operation on the VTA") needs a carve-out for hcp/*.
Two notes:
- The suite ties a token to the VID that asked for it, so a token the plugin's VID holds would be refused (permissionDenied) if sent through vta_call under the vta-mcp identity K_a, over TSP or DIDComm (hcp.md:157).
- A client of our own meets the letter of 10.5 but not isolation: plan :716 says the model's shell tool runs as the same OS user, so a token kept in a file is within the model's reach.
findings.reasons: HOLDS: CONFIRMED: every quote cited matches the VTI pin (git HEAD f7b78e29d) and pr1382 (e163cac1d). server.rs:174-182: VtaCallParams has only `operation: String` and `payload: Option<Value>`, with no token or thread member, so the model has to write accessToken into the payload. server.rs:882-908: vta_call hands the payload unchanged to `client.dispatch_trust_task(&p.operation, payload, 30)`. vta-sdk client/mod.rs:2052-2053 and 2510: the reply's payload comes back whole (`return Ok(payload.clone())`). server.rs:300-309 and 97-100: finish calls ok_json(value), which pretty-prints the value into a text content block. So a grants/request response's accessToken would come back as tool content. The only redaction is redact_call (observability.rs:173-213), and it applies to the call record and log only, never to what the model receives. grants/request/0.1/spec.md:221 and HCP spec:2757 say what the claim says. The overstatements: "every hcp/* request" is false for grants/request and grants/revoked. "blocker" does not fit the review's definition, because the PR and VTI's design never propose vta_call for hcp/*. The conflict is with our plan's D40, which reuses vta-mcp for every operation. That makes it a raise against our plan, with an optional ask to VTI about vta-mcp's guard. It does not block the PR. || HOLDS: I found no exception that undoes the mechanism. No later HCP section makes the token safe in the model's context: 10.5 is explicit, and VTI's own design agrees (decision 13). vta-mcp has no way to hold a token for the model or remove one from a result: the guard only allows, denies or asks, and the redaction covers the call record and logs, not what goes back to the model. Several things narrow the claim, though. hcp/* cannot reach vta_call at the pinned commit; it would only after VTI's A8 step. Two of the 28 tasks carry no token, so "every hcp/* request" is too broad. Most important for severity: our companion plan already gives the plugin its own token-holding Context Client (B1, B7), so Keyring's interop is not blocked. That makes this a raise against VTI #2823's A8 and against our own D40 wording, not a blocker. I also read HCP 10.5 as covering vta_call even though vta_call is not HCP's own MCP Binding, because of 10.5's final bullet and VTI decision 13.

findings.title: vta_call cannot resubmit a held grants/request on the same thread
findings.claim: build_task_document mints a fresh id and sets no threadId, and vta_call exposes no threadId. The grants/request hold requires every resubmission to carry the held request's threadId, issuer and payload, and a request on a new thread is a new request that is put to the person again. A next-step reply comes back from vta_call as a plain payload.
findings.evidence: vta-sdk/src/client/mod.rs:4203-4230 build_task_document (id, type, issuedAt, payload, issuer, recipient, idempotencyKey only); vta-mcp/src/server.rs:174-182; grants/request/0.1/spec.md:174 "The client resubmits on the same thread: a new document with a fresh `id`, the same `threadId`"; :305 "A request on a new thread is a new request"
findings.keyringImpact: Through vta_call, Keyring would receive a new consent request on every poll.
findings.corrected:
The technical claim holds. At the VTI pin f7b78e29d, `vta_call` takes only `operation` and `payload`. It goes through `dispatch_trust_task` → `signed_task_document` → `build_task_document`, which mints a fresh `urn:uuid` id and never sets `threadId`, and no vta-mcp tool takes one. Under the framework (SPEC §4.9), each `vta_call` therefore opens a new thread. A `trust-task-next-step` reply has no `code`/`message`, so `extract_trust_task_payload` hands it back as an ordinary payload. So `vta_call` cannot do the held `hcp/grants/request` resubmission (spec.md:174, :305 on pr1380 and pr1382; :190, :321 on pr1381).

The severity should be "raise", not "blocker", and the Keyring impact is overstated:
(1) Nothing reviewed sends `grants/request` through `vta_call`. The PR's own demo sets `threadId` itself. VTI #2823's V0 to V2 have the agent client send it over TSP with its own VID. MCP from vta-mcp is H5/V3, and decision 13 there says "MCP is not a shortcut". Our HCP lane also sends it over TSP: B2 "hold and resubmit over TSP", and B7 is the plugin using the CLI's code as its library.
(2) At the pin, `vta_call` cannot reach any `hcp/*` URI at all. vta-sdk, vta-mcp and vta-service contain no "hcp".
(3) Under VTI's design, Keyring accepts a `task-consent/request` only for the VID and `threadId` it scanned (hcp.md:159). A poll through `vta_call` would make the VTA hold a fresh request on each new thread, but the person would not be asked again each time. The grant would simply never complete through `vta_call`.

The real ask goes to VTI #2823 and to our own plan, not to PR #1380. VTI's A8 adds `hcp/*` to the vta-mcp guard risk classes and census, so `vta_call` would likely list `hcp/grants/request` once hcp lands. Either `vta_call` excludes held tasks, or it gains a `threadId` and returns a next-step as a next-step. Our D40 ("reuses `vta-mcp` for every operation on the VTA") should leave out `grants/request`. | Severity: note, not blocker. The mechanics are right. At f7b78e29d, vta-sdk's build_task_document mints a fresh `id`, sets no `threadId` (and the SDK has no thread-aware entry point). vta_call takes only `operation` and `payload`. A `trust-task-next-step` reply passes verify_reply and extract_trust_task_payload, so vta_call returns it as an ordinary payload. A client using vta_call therefore cannot continue a held `hcp/grants/request` the way the spec requires (spec.md:174, :305, SPEC §8.6).

But neither design sends `hcp/grants/request` through vta_call. In VTI #2823 the Context Client is a third party: its own VID, no ACL entry, the request sent over TSP with a proof by its issuer (hcp.md §4.3, §5.2). HCP over MCP is H5/V3 through OAuth (decision 13, "MCP is not a shortcut"). In our plan the CLI sends the request over TSP (companion B2), and the P1 plugin uses the CLI's code as its library (B7), not vta_call. So this blocks nothing in #1380-#1382 or in Keyring.

The Keyring impact is also overstated. By design, Keyring accepts a consent request only for the VID and `threadId` it scanned (hcp.md:159, :290). A request on a new thread would not prompt the person. What actually happens is that a vta_call client never gets its grant.
