The VTA's existing consent code also sends one push per question, not one per resubmission (policy_gate.rs:666-675; oob_sign_in.rs:1152). Whether A3 keeps that across threads is not yet decided.

Remaining ask (a raise to VTI, not to Brendan): once A8 adds `hcp/*` to the vta-mcp guard and census, either deny `hcp/grants/request` in vta_call or give vta_call a `threadId`. Otherwise a model could call it, get the next-step payload back, and resubmit on a new thread.
findings.reasons:
HOLDS: All cited evidence checks out on the right commits.

CONFIRMED in source:
- `build_task_document` sets only id, type, issuedAt, payload, issuer/recipient and an optional idempotencyKey, with no threadId.
- `VtaCallParams` has only `operation` and `payload`.
- `vta_call` calls `dispatch_trust_task`, which ends in `extract_trust_task_payload`. That returns any `payload` without `code`+`message` as success, so a next-step comes back as a plain payload. `verify_reply` does nothing special for next-step.
- No vta-mcp tool exposes a `threadId` or `dispatch_trust_task_document`.
- The grants/request spec quotes are exact on pr1382 and pr1380 at :174 and :305.
- SPEC §4.9 (:457-459) makes a document without `threadId` the start of its own thread, so each `vta_call` is a new request.

Overstated or mis-scoped: no reviewed design sends `grants/request` through `vta_call`. That covers the PR demo (demo.ts:211-214 sets `threadId`), VTI #2823 (hcp.md:283-294 agent client over TSP; hcp-plan.md:38/159 MCP is H5/V3; decision 13) and our plan (companion B2 over TSP, B7 'the CLI's code as its library'). At the pin there is no hcp code to reach. VTI's design has Keyring accept consent only for the scanned VID and `threadId`, so the person would not be asked again on every poll.

The gap is real but latent. VTI's A8 would add `hcp/*` to vta-mcp's guard and census, and our D40 says 'every operation'. So it is a 'raise' to VTI #2823 and to our plan, not a blocker for PR #1380. || HOLDS: The code-level part of the claim holds. vta-sdk/src/client/mod.rs:4203-4230 builds `id`, `type`, `issuedAt`, `payload`, `issuer`, `recipient` and an optional `idempotencyKey`, and no `threadId`. There is no thread-aware path anywhere in vta-sdk/src/client/mod.rs. vta-mcp/src/server.rs:174-182 VtaCallParams has only `operation` and `payload`. server.rs:882-906 calls dispatch_trust_task(&p.operation, payload, 30). mod.rs:2399-2426 (verify_reply) checks the next-step document, and mod.rs:2492-2511 (extract_trust_task_payload) returns its payload as Ok because it has no code/message pair. The grants/request spec (:174, :176, :305) and SPEC.md §8.6 (1536, "answers a resubmission in the same thread") require the same `threadId`.

What narrows the claim:
(1) VTI hcp.md:206-208 says "The agent client is a third party. It must not hold an ACL entry". vta-mcp, by contrast, logs in as an operator or as a dedicated agent identity with an ACL entry (agent_connect.rs:147-172). hcp.md:283-294 sends `hcp/grants/request` over TSP with a proof by its issuer. hcp.md:557, decision 13, says "MCP is not a shortcut". hcp-plan.md:38 puts MCP for HCP at H5/V3.
(2) Our companion, 2026-11-25-bam.md:28-33 and :240 (B2 "grants/request with hold and resubmit over TSP"), and :411 (B7 "the CLI's code as its library"). No route goes through vta_call.
(3) hcp.md:159: "Keyring accepts it only for the VID and `threadId` it scanned". :290: "checklist, if the VID and threadId match the scan". A request on a new thread would not reach the person.
(4) The existing VTA consent code dedupes pushes: policy_gate.rs:675, "So the push follows the *question*, not the submit". oob_sign_in.rs:1152, "A concurrent poll raised it first: answer with its request". That is the template A3 is modelled on. A3 itself is not built.

The gap is real only for a future vta_call path that no design uses. It becomes reachable once A8 lists `hcp/*` in the vta-mcp guard and census (hcp-tasks.md:173-179). So it is a note, or a raise to VTI. It is not a blocker and not an ask for Brendan's PRs.

findings.title: vta-mcp has no receive loop to acknowledge hcp/grants/revoked
findings.claim: vta-mcp serves MCP and never runs a loop for inbound requests: serve() does not call AgentSession::run, and AgentSession::run's handler has no way to reply. The notice requires the client to verify it, acknowledge with an empty #response, deduplicate on noticeId for at least 25 hours and stop using every copy. With vta-mcp alone, the provider would retry, abandon delivery, and tell the person the client was not notified.
findings.evidence: vta-mcp/src/main.rs:393-417 serve() (stdio or listen, then shutdown); vta-sdk/src/agent_session.rs:332-379 run(handler) returns AgentControl only; grants/revoked/0.1/spec.md:211 acknowledgement, :248 "MUST keep its record of a processed `noticeId` for at least 25 hours", :253 "MUST stop using every copy"; vti2823 hcp-plan.md:116 B4 "a mediator receive loop that acknowledges `hcp/grants/revoked`"
findings.keyringImpact: Keyring's revoke screen would show 'not told' for agents running through vta-mcp only.
findings.corrected:
Severity should be "note", not "blocker". What holds: at VTI pin f7b78e29d, vta-mcp has no inbound path. serve() only serves MCP (stdio or --listen) and then calls shutdown(), and nothing in vta-mcp/ or vti-mcp-common/ calls receive_next or AgentSession::run. So vta-mcp by itself cannot verify, acknowledge or deduplicate an hcp/grants/revoked notice. What is wrong: it is not true that AgentSession::run's handler has no way to reply. The handler does return only AgentControl, but the closure can capture the client and call VtaClient::send_message. That method is documented as "Safe to call concurrently with a receive_next loop", and InboundMessage keeps claimed_from "for routing a reply". What is overstated: no design relies on vta-mcp alone to receive the notice. In VTI's design the Context Client is the agent client, with "Its own VID with a mailbox on a mediator" and "No ACL entry" (hcp.md:113). The receive loop that acknowledges the notice is work package B4 in the agent client (hcp-plan.md:116). Our companion has the same split: B4 is "a mediator receive loop (TSP and DIDComm)" (:242), and B7 is "The plugin as Context Client in vti-agent-connect (entries/query, notices)" (:411). Our plugin design already has its own mediator/ pickup socket and inbound path, separate from vta-mcp (plan §3.12, :690, :700). HCP also allows a client to register no notification endpoint: it is then not notified and its copies are capped at 1 hour (HCP :1651, :2760 for a stdio bridge). Keyring's design already shows that case (companion C5 :172, "the revoke screen says no notice was sent"). Nothing breaks interop. The real follow-up is our own: the plugin's core (B4/B7) must do the acknowledgement, keep noticeIds for 25 hours, and stop using every copy. It must not be left to vta-mcp, and D40 ("reuses vta-mcp for every operation") should say that notices are an exception. | Severity: note, not blocker. It is true that vta-mcp at f7b78e29d only serves MCP and never runs an inbound loop (main.rs:393-417). It also has no HCP code at all: server.rs has 0 matches for "hcp". But neither VTI's design nor ours makes vta-mcp the HCP Context Client. The Context Client is "the agent client: a CLI for the demo, then the agent plugin", with "Its own VID with a mailbox on a mediator" and "No ACL entry" (hcp.md:113). The notice is "pushed over TSP" to that client (hcp.md:160). The receive loop that acknowledges hcp/grants/revoked is work package B4 in vti-agent-connect (hcp-plan.md:116, the line the claim itself cites). vta-mcp's HCP role comes only in H5/V3, MCP over Streamable HTTP (hcp-plan.md:38, :159).

HCP also sends a notice only to a client that registered a notification endpoint (HCP 6.2.2 :1638, 6.2.3 :1651, 7.6 :1866; revoked spec :120, :246). A client without one has its use-until capped at 1 hour and gets no notice, so there are no retries and no "not notified" abandonment. A refused request also counts as a notice (HCP :1643).

"AgentSession::run's handler has no way to reply" is also wrong. The handler can capture agent.client() and call VtaClient::send_message. That method is documented as "Safe to call concurrently with a receive_next loop" (client/mod.rs:2789-2790), and claimed_from is kept "for routing a reply" (agent_session.rs:177). It is only DIDComm, though, and there is no ready-made helper for a Trust Task response.

What is left is a note for our plugin. It must register for notices only a VID that its own receive loop serves: the CLI's own VID, which has no ACL entry. It must not register vta-mcp's ACL-scoped K_a, whose DIDComm socket holds the mediator's one-per-DID slot (main.rs, attach() comment). Only that misconfiguration leads to the retry, abandon and "couldn't tell" path the claim describes.
findings.reasons: HOLDS: I opened every citation. The quotes from the revoked spec are accurate on pr1382: line 211 is the acknowledgement, 248 is "MUST keep its record of a processed `noticeId` for at least 25 hours", and 253 is "MUST stop using every copy". vta-mcp/src/main.rs:393-417 serve() runs MCP and then calls shutdown(), and a grep of vta-mcp/src and vti-mcp-common/src finds no receive_next, run or inbound handling. The core fact holds: CONFIRMED. One part of the claim is wrong. The handler signature in agent_session.rs:332-379 is FnMut(InboundMessage) -> Fut<AgentControl>, but a closure can capture the client and send a reply with VtaClient::send_message (client/mod.rs:2796). The blocker conclusion is not supported by the claim's own evidence. The cited hcp-plan.md:116 B4 puts the receive loop in the agent client (vti-agent-connect), not in vta-mcp. hcp.md:113 gives the Context Client its own VID and mailbox and no ACL entry. vta-mcp, by contrast, runs as an agent scoped by an ACL entry. Our companion (B4 :242, B7 :411) and plan §3.12 (the mediator/ module, "receives chat and room offers") also put inbound handling in the plugin. Under HCP 6.2.3 a client with no notification endpoint is a legal configuration with a 1-hour cap, and Keyring already designs for showing that the client was not told. So this is a "note" (our plugin must own notice handling), not an interop blocker. || REFUTE: The finding's facts about vta-mcp's code are right, but its consequence and its blocker severity do not hold. (1) The HCP Context Client in both designs is the agent client, which has its own VID and its own receive loop (B4). It is not vta-mcp. vta-mcp has no hcp/* tools, so on its own it could never request or hold a grant, and no notice would ever be addressed to it. (2) HCP sends a notice only to a client with a registered notification endpoint. A client without one gets a 1-hour useUntil cap and no notice, so the claimed chain (provider retries, abandons, tells the person the client was not notified) does not follow. Our companion C5 (2026-11-25-bam.md:172) already handles this case: "Otherwise the 1 h cap applies, and the revoke screen says no notice was sent". (3) The handler can reply through client().send_message, so the "no way to reply" sub-claim is false.

findings.title: vta-mcp's MCP version cap and loopback-only listener conflict with HCP's MCP binding
findings.claim: HCP's MCP binding targets MCP 2026-07-28 with no session state, and Agent Interop needs Streamable HTTP with OAuth resource-server behaviour. vta-mcp serves up to 2025-11-25 and never 2026-07-28, because its confirmation gate uses elicitation. Its listener refuses non-loopback addresses with no flag to widen, and uses a local bearer token, not OAuth. VTI H5 nonetheless plans Agent Interop 'from vta-mcp'.
findings.evidence: HCP spec:2491 "It targets MCP version 2026-07-28 and relies on no session state"; spec:2498; spec:2937-2943; vti-mcp-common/src/listen.rs:125-139 "up to `2025-11-25`, never `2026-07-28`"; :141-144 check_loopback; vti2823 hcp-plan.md:159 "H5, Agent Interop | MCP over Streamable HTTP from `vta-mcp`"
findings.keyringImpact: None for Keyring. It affects whether 'any MCP host' can reach HCP without our plugin.
findings.askOfPR: For VTI #2823 rather than Brendan's suite: say how H5 resolves the elicitation and version cap and the loopback rule, or place the provider's MCP endpoint somewhere other than vta-mcp.
findings.corrected:
The claim holds and stays a "raise" aimed at VTI #2823, not at Brendan's suite. It needs two corrections.

(1) The version cap is a temporary choice, not a permanent "never". vti-mcp-common/src/listen.rs:135-136 says "Lift it only once confirmation is answered with an `InputRequiredResult` that the hosts in use are known to handle", and docs/05-design-notes/vtc-mcp.md:351-352 says "The cap lifts once confirmation is answered with an `InputRequiredResult`". In vta-mcp the cap is unconditional (server.rs:1070-1074): it applies whether or not --confirm is set, and over stdio too (docs/02-vta/vta-mcp.md:399). The cap also blocks HCP 10.2: a provider identifies itself through `server/discover` (spec:2502), which belongs to MCP 2026-07-28.

(2) The bigger gap is the role vta-mcp plays, not only its version, loopback and token settings. VTI's own hcp.md cites HCP 10.5 to make vta-mcp a client of the provider: hcp.md:513 "HCP 10.5 already makes a bridge a client of the provider", and :557. vta-mcp.md:8 calls it "a bridge, not an authority" whose authentication boundary is starting the process or holding the bearer token (:61-64). Agent Interop, by contrast, is a claim the provider makes: the provider's MCP server must be the OAuth resource server (spec:2498, 2937-2939, 3475). hcp-plan.md:38 plans H5 as "`vta-mcp` PRs; nothing in the VTA". So H5 is planned work that would have to change vta-mcp, not something that cannot be done. The ask should therefore also cover: in H5, is vta-mcp the provider's own MCP endpoint, running on the provider side as the OAuth resource server, or an HCP 10.5 client? The docs say both.
findings.reasons:
HOLDS: Every citation checks out, read at the right commits: the HCP spec at b790561, the VTI pin at f7b78e29d, and the copy of the VTI #2823 docs.

1. The HCP spec at line 2491 says "It targets MCP version 2026-07-28 and relies on no session state". Line 2498 says Streamable HTTP is "Required for the Agent Interop package" and that "the server is an OAuth resource server". Lines 2939-2943 (section 13.5) say "The HCP Provider, as MCP server, is the OAuth resource server" and that it "publishes OAuth 2.0 Protected Resource Metadata (RFC 9728)". Line 3475 adds "MCP over stdio does not qualify" for Agent Interop.

2. vta-mcp's version cap. listen.rs:125-139 says "up to `2025-11-25`, never `2026-07-28`" and explains that confirmation is "a server-to-client elicitation request, which `2026-07-28` forbids". vta-mcp applies this cap to its MCP handler in every mode, stdio included (server.rs:1070-1073), and a test asserts that 2026-07-28 is absent (server.rs:1185-1187). The cap is deliberate and comes with a stated way out: "Lift it only once confirmation is answered with an `InputRequiredResult` that the hosts in use are known to handle." So it can be lifted, but nothing in the plan says how H5 will do that.

3. Loopback only. check_loopback (listen.rs:143-151) refuses any non-loopback address, and from_listen calls it unconditionally (:105). The module documentation (:20-23) says "None of these can be turned off", and the `--listen` argument in main.rs:184-191 has no flag to widen it. rmcp's Host-header check also admits loopback hosts only (:293-297).

4. Authentication is a local shared secret, not OAuth. require_bearer (:323-338) compares the request's bearer token with a token from an environment variable or an owner-only file. A refusal sends a bare `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer` with no resource metadata. A search of vta-mcp/src and vti-mcp-common/src finds no oauth, resource_metadata or 9728 anywhere.

5. The VTI plan. hcp-plan.md:159 reads "H5, Agent Interop | MCP over Streamable HTTP from `vta-mcp`, MCP authorization onto HCP 13.5". Line 38 says "`vta-mcp` PRs; nothing in the VTA", and hcp.md:513 and :623 say the same. None of the four VTI docs mentions elicitation, the version cap or the loopback rule.

Two further points, not in the claim, that support it:
- HCP 10.2 (lines 2502-2509) has the provider identify itself in a `server/discover` response, which belongs to 2026-07-28. A host held to 2025-11-25 falls back to `initialize`, as listen.rs:132-134 itself notes. The listener also keeps a session per host (LocalSessionManager, :300), while the HCP binding relies on no session state.
- VTI hcp.md:513 justifies placing the endpoint in vta-mcp with "HCP 10.5 already makes a bridge a client of the provider". But HCP 10.5 (line 2763) is about "A local stdio bridge … is an HCP Client". Under 13.5 the Agent Interop endpoint must be the HCP Provider itself, acting as the OAuth resource server. That supports the ask to say how H5 works, or to put the endpoint somewhere else.

Severity "raise", aimed at VTI #2823, is reasonable: it asks the plan to clarify a phase-V3 step. Nothing breaks today, and the claim's statement of no Keyring impact is right. || HOLDS: I looked for counter-evidence and found nothing that overturns the claim.

- **No other MCP endpoint:** no VTI code outside vta-mcp, vtc-mcp and vti-mcp-common pulls in rmcp, so vta-service has no MCP endpoint of its own.
- **Listener rules:** vta-mcp serves HTTP only through Serving::from_listen, and that always runs check_loopback. listen.rs:20 says "None of these can be turned off". The only check is a single local bearer token (require_bearer). There is no OAuth or protected-resource metadata anywhere in vta-mcp or vti-mcp-common.
- **HCP spec:** only MCP 2026-07-28 is named, at spec:2491 and in the reference table at :3975. Nothing allows an earlier version.
- **The H5 plan:** confirmed at hcp-plan.md:38, hcp-plan.md:159 and hcp.md:623. No VTI doc explains how H5 would deal with the cap or the loopback rule.

What narrows the claim:
- The cap is documented as temporary. It lifts once confirmation moves to InputRequiredResult (listen.rs:135-136, vtc-mcp.md:351-352).
- H5 is explicitly planned as changes to vta-mcp, so it describes future changes, not an impossibility.

What strengthens it:
- HCP 10.2's `server/discover` also depends on 2026-07-28.
- VTI's own hcp.md treats vta-mcp as an HCP 10.5 client, while also planning to make it the provider's Agent Interop endpoint.

The listener also keeps per-session state (LocalSessionManager, listen.rs:300). That is a minor point: HCP's "relies on no session state" does not by itself forbid sessions.

Keyring impact: none, as the finding says.

Severity "raise" is right.

findings.title: VTI gives a client rule as the reason to build a provider binding in vta-mcp
findings.claim: VTI §9.4 recommends putting MCP over Streamable HTTP in vta-mcp because 'HCP 10.5 already makes a bridge a client of the provider'. Agent Interop and the MCP Binding are provider claims (HCP 18.1). A bridge that HCP 10.5 makes a client cannot also be the provider's claimed MCP binding, unless vta-mcp is run as a provider-operated, remote front end that enforces grants as the provider.
findings.evidence: vti2823 hcp.md:513 "MCP over Streamable HTTP | Extend the separate `vta-mcp` process; nothing in the VTA. HCP 10.5 already makes a bridge a client of the provider"; hcp.md:557 decision 13; HCP spec:3460 "a claim is made for an HCP Provider"; spec:2760
findings.keyringImpact: Low. It affects the V3 path to 'any MCP host without the plugin'.
findings.askOfPR: For VTI #2823: state whether H5's vta-mcp is a client bridge (then it gives no Agent Interop claim) or a provider front end (then it is remote, OAuth-protected and part of the provider).
findings.corrected: Holds; keep severity raise, with three precision points. (1) HCP 10.5 (spec:2760) is narrower than VTI §9.4 puts it: "A local stdio bridge to a remote HCP Provider is an HCP Client in its own right". VTI's own decision 13 (hcp.md:557) states it correctly ("makes a stdio bridge such as `vta-mcp` a client"). The faulty reasoning is only in the §9.4 row (hcp.md:513), which cites that client rule as the reason to build the Streamable HTTP surface in vta-mcp, and in the H5 end state that claims Agent Interop from vta-mcp (hcp.md:623, hcp-plan.md:38 and 159). (2) The spec never says "remote". What it requires is that "The HCP Provider, as MCP server, is the OAuth resource server" (spec:2939), with audience-restricted tokens and a grant-status check on every request (spec:2954), enforced by the provider "independently of any decision made by an intermediary" (spec:346). So the ask should be: is H5's vta-mcp a client bridge (then no Agent Interop claim comes from it), or part of the provider, run by the Provider Operator as the OAuth resource server and enforcing grants itself? (3) VTI marks §9.4 as "recommendations" with "the placements in §9.4" still open (hcp.md:507-508, 563-565), so this is a clarification for a V3 item, not a decided design. Keyring impact stays low. | Holds, severity raise. One sharpening. HCP 10.5 (spec:2760) makes only "a local stdio bridge to a remote HCP Provider" an HCP Client, so VTI §9.4's reason ("HCP 10.5 already makes a bridge a client") does not even cover the Streamable HTTP case it is given for. Which role a Streamable HTTP vta-mcp plays depends on 3.2.3, 3.2.4 and 13.5. If it holds and presents the grant to the VTA, it is a client, and its endpoint is not the provider's MCP Binding. If it is the provider's MCP server, it is the OAuth resource server (13.5) and part of the provider, which is a provider-operated remote front end. VTI's own plan already takes the second reading for H5: "MCP authorization onto HCP 13.5" and an Agent Interop claim. That contradicts decision 13, the reason in §9.4, and the hcp.md:77 diagram, which lists "an MCP bridge (HCP 10.5)" among HTTP-Binding clients. The pinned vta-mcp is a client by construction: it acts with its own VTA identity, `--listen` is loopback-only with no flag to widen it, and the MCP version is capped at 2025-11-25, while the HCP MCP Binding targets 2026-07-28. So "extend vta-mcp" for Agent Interop means reversing those standing rules, not adding a small extension. The ask to VTI #2823 stands: say which of the two roles H5's vta-mcp is.
findings.reasons:
HOLDS: I read every cited line in its context, on the right versions: hcp-spec at b790561, the VTI #2823 docs, and the VTI pin f7b78e29d.

- **The VTI quote is exact.** hcp.md:513 recommends "MCP over Streamable HTTP | Extend the separate `vta-mcp` process; nothing in the VTA. HCP 10.5 already makes a bridge a client of the provider". hcp.md:623 and hcp-plan.md:159 then make "Agent Interop" the conformance result of H5, "MCP over Streamable HTTP from `vta-mcp`".
- **HCP 10.5 is a client rule.** spec:2760 says the bridge "holds the token, calls the provider over the HTTP Binding, has its own Client Operator, and is bound by every rule for HCP Clients".
- **The claims Agent Interop needs belong to the provider.**
  - spec:3460: "a claim is made for an HCP Provider", and the only exception is the client directives claim.
  - spec:2502: "An HCP Provider exposing the MCP Binding identifies itself in its server/discover".
  - spec:3470/3475: Agent Interop requires the provider's MCP Binding over Streamable HTTP, with OAuth.
  - spec:2939: "The HCP Provider, as MCP server, is the OAuth resource server".

  So the rule VTI cites makes vta-mcp a client, and a client cannot be where the provider's MCP Binding is claimed. The reason given does not support the recommendation. If anything, it argues against it.
- **The VTI pin confirms vta-mcp is a client today.** It authenticates to the VTA as a scoped agent identity (main.rs:12-29: "the VTA is the authority — every call is gated there on the bridge identity's role"). Its HTTP mode already speaks MCP Streamable HTTP, but on loopback only with a static listen token, not OAuth (vti-mcp-common/src/listen.rs:2, 22, 143-148; main.rs:182-191).

The finding is only slightly overstated. "Remote" is not a spec requirement; the real requirements are provider-as-resource-server and the provider enforcing grants itself (spec:346, 2939, 2954). VTI also labels the §9.4 placements as open recommendations. The finding stands, and raise is the right severity. || HOLDS: I looked for something that contradicts or narrows the claim and found nothing that does.

1. The MCP Binding and Agent Interop are provider claims.
   - spec:3460: "a claim is made for an HCP Provider ... It is the only client claim in this draft"; the one exception is directives.
   - spec:2502: "An HCP Provider exposing the MCP Binding identifies itself".
   - spec:2939 (13.5): "The HCP Provider, as MCP server, is the OAuth resource server".
   - spec:3475: Agent Interop needs Streamable HTTP with MCP authorization mapped onto OAuth.

2. HCP 10.5's bridge rule is narrower than VTI's paraphrase.
   - spec:2760: "A local stdio bridge to a remote HCP Provider is an HCP Client in its own right."
   - Decision 13 (hcp.md:557) reads it correctly ("a stdio bridge such as `vta-mcp`"). The §9.4 row (hcp.md:513) widens it to "a bridge" and uses it as the reason for the Streamable HTTP placement. This makes the finding stronger.

3. No exception lets a client-side bridge serve as the provider's binding.
   - The HCP guides, the path-to-v2-final roadmap, the introduction and the tt hcp/* specs have nothing on it.
   - spec:285 lists "an MCP tool implementation" as a component, and 1.4 governs only the interface boundary. So a separate process can be part of the provider if the provider runs it. That is the finding's "unless" clause, not a refutation.

4. VTI's own plan is internally inconsistent.
   - hcp-plan.md:38 and :159, and hcp.md:623, plan H5 as "MCP over Streamable HTTP from `vta-mcp`, MCP authorization onto HCP 13.5" with an Agent Interop claim. That is the provider reading.
   - hcp.md:77 and decision 13 call vta-mcp a client or bridge.

5. The pinned vta-mcp (f7b78e29d) is a client by design.
   - vta-mcp/src/main.rs:31-32: "every call is gated there on the bridge identity's role, ACL and context scope".
   - vti-mcp-common/src/listen.rs:141-151: loopback only, "the endpoint speaks with this bridge's identity, so it is never offered to the network".
   - vti-mcp-common/CLAUDE.md: "listen is loopback, a token and no browsers — none of it optional".
   - listen.rs:125-139: versions "up to `2025-11-25`, never `2026-07-28`". HCP 10.1 (spec:2491) targets MCP 2026-07-28.

Severity raise fits: it is a design inconsistency in a docs-only PR that affects only V3 (H5), and Keyring's impact is low.

findings.title: VTI says a Context Client must not hold an ACL entry, but our memory agent does
findings.claim: VTI #2823 says the agent client must not hold an ACL entry, because an entry confers authority and the client's only authority is the grant. It admits the agent through a counterparty hook only after the ACL refuses the sender. Our plan's agent K_a holds an ACL entry (role application, memory contexts) and runs vta-mcp, which assumes one for --enroll and vta/memory. Either one agent uses two identities (an ACL DID for memory and an HCP VID for the grant), or VTI decides that an ACL-entry holder may also act under a grant.
findings.evidence: vti2823 hcp.md:206-208 "The agent client is a third party. It must not hold an ACL entry"; :216-220 "only after the ACL has refused the sender"; agent-connect-plan.md:496-510 (ACL entry for K_a); vta-mcp/README.md:19-31; 2026-11-25-bam.md:94 "The lane's agent has no ACL entry and no VDC in the demo"
findings.keyringImpact: P1's 'merge the two connect paths' (C12) must choose: Keyring shows one agent but may have to manage both an ACL entry and a grant, under two DIDs.
findings.askOfPR: For VTI #2823: say whether a DID that holds an ACL entry may also present an HCP grant, and what the per-request check does then.
findings.reasons:
HOLDS: I could not refute it. Every cited quote is accurate, is in context and comes from the right version.

**VTI #2823 (local copy of the PR docs).**
- hcp.md:206-208 reads "The agent client is a third party. It must not hold an ACL entry: an entry confers authority under VTI-ACL-001, and the client's authority is meant to be the grant and nothing else."
- hcp.md:216-220 reads "a new `hcp::is_context_client_task` admits only the agent-sent `hcp/*` URIs, and only after the ACL has refused the sender (`AppError::Forbidden`)", and the claim it yields is zero-authority.
- The same rule appears in four other places: the roles table (hcp.md:113 "**No ACL entry.** Its authority is the grant"), decision 10 (hcp.md:554 "keeps the agent out of the ACL"), hcp-tasks.md:163-164 (A8 acceptance) and tasks/hcp-demo-plan.md:168 ("The agent has no ACL entry.").

**Our plan.**
- agent-connect-plan.md §3.3 (around :496-510) gives K_a an ACL entry: role `application`, memory contexts, memory-read/write, and room capabilities added later.
- Step 9 (:480) runs device/register and acl/swap-key for K_a.
- :700 says the plugin "runs `vta-mcp` as `K_a`, as a dedicated agent".
- D40 (:920) says the plugin reuses vta-mcp for every VTA operation.

**The VTI pin (f7b78e29d).**
- vta-mcp/README.md:22-30 tells you to `pnm acl create --did <agent did:key> --role application ...` and then `--enroll`.
- vta-mcp/src/main.rs:325-333 refuses `--enroll` outside dedicated-agent mode, because enrolment "attaches to the agent's own ACL entry".
- vta-service/src/trust_tasks/memory.rs:71 and :120 gate memory on `require_capability` / `Capability::MemoryRead`.

**The companion.**
- 2026-11-25-bam.md:94 quote is exact.
- :179, :386 and :409 show that C12 (P1) merges the two connect paths without saying which identity results. Neither the companion nor the plan settles it.

**Extra evidence that supports the ask.**
- At the pin, vta-service/src/messaging/auth.rs:80-81 admits any DID that holds an ACL entry straight away as `Standing::Acl` (`Ok(auth) => return Ok((auth, Standing::Acl))`). Every counterparty hook is reached only on `Forbidden` (:86, :108-118).
- So if K_a keeps its entry and sends `hcp/*`, it is not refused. It arrives on its full ACL claim and is charged to the operation budget (:63-69), and the new hook never runs. VTI #2823's design does not describe this case, which is exactly the question the ask puts to it.
- P1's C10 (memories on HCP, `entries/*`) would not remove the need for the entry. Rooms (`room-present` / `room-open` and the `ai-agent` consumer kind) and vta-mcp's `--enroll` / device/register still need it.
- That leaves the claim's either/or standing: two identities, or a VTI ruling that one DID can hold an entry and also act under a grant.

**Severity.** "raise" is right. It does not block the demo, where the agent has no ACL entry (bam.md:94). It is an open design choice for C12 in P1 that VTI #2823 should state. || HOLDS: The claim holds and "raise" is the right severity. I looked for an exception, a later section, a different code path or a default that would let one DID hold both an ACL entry and an HCP grant, and found none. What I found narrows the claim in places and makes the conflict sharper.

1. VTI #2823 names our plugin directly, not only the demo CLI. hcp.md:113 lists the Context Client as "The agent client: a CLI for the demo, then the agent plugin … **No ACL entry.** Its authority is the grant". The plugin in our plan does hold an ACL entry. hcp-plan.md:157 also describes Delegated Authorization as "an HCP capability, not an ACL entry". Decision 10 (hcp.md:554) gives its reason as "keeps the agent out of the ACL".

2. In the pinned code (vta-service/src/messaging/auth.rs:80-88), the ACL is checked first, and a sender with an entry returns `Standing::Acl` at once. Only an `AppError::Forbidden` goes on to the counterparty hooks. So an ACL holder sending `hcp/*` would never reach the planned `hcp::is_context_client_task`, which runs only after the ACL refuses (hcp.md:216-220, hcp-tasks.md:163-164). The per-request check in §4.2 does not depend on standing ("Every context operation runs the per-request check … client VID equals the sender equals issuer"). Nothing in the design refuses an ACL holder, and nothing says what an ACL claim may confer inside the `hcp` handlers. The design is silent on this case, which is exactly what the ask raises.

3. Moving memory to HCP does not remove the need for an ACL entry. Agent-written entries are `model-inferred`, and the VTA refuses them until the Memory Manager Profile, which is V3 (hcp.md:555, hcp-tasks.md A4). C10 in P1 only moves Keyring's own list, delete and edit onto `entries/*`. So the plugin still needs `vta/memory/*` for its own writes, and memory.rs:193/225/260 gates those on the `MemoryWrite`/`MemoryRead` ACL capabilities. Rooms (`room-present`) and the VDC subject are also tied to the ACL entry K_a (plan §3.3, :505, :510).

4. vta-mcp at the pinned commit f7b78e29d does not mention HCP anywhere. Its README says "All access is bounded by the bridge identity's VTA role / ACL" (README:70) and shows `pnm acl create` and `--enroll` (README:23, :30). Our plan runs it as K_a (plan:700, D40). The only HCP path for vta-mcp in the VTI plan is H5 (V3), MCP over Streamable HTTP with OAuth (hcp-plan.md:38, :159; hcp.md:513, :557). That is after P1's C12.

5. The P0 demo has no conflict: the CLI has no ACL entry (companion :94; hcp-demo-plan.md:168). C12 (plan 7.29, :1428; companion :409) merges "the HCP grant over §3.2's pairing carriage" in P1. That carriage creates the ACL entry at step 7 and enrols at step 9 (plan :478-480). Neither our plan nor the companion (Q-H4, B7) says which DID is the Context Client's VID. VTI's design does not say either.

Every citation in the claim checks out as quoted. This is not a blocker: running two identities is a workable option. It is a real P1 design question, and the right ask is a clarification from #2823.

findings.title: VTI and the suite answer a revoked grant with different codes
findings.claim: The suite answers a request under a revoked grant with hcp:invalidToken (question 2), and maps HCP scope-denied to permissionDenied. VTI #2823 says revoked, expired, wrong-purpose and unknown tokens all answer 'scope-denied', and its revoke diagram ends 'V-->>C: scope-denied'. HCP 6.2.2 makes such a failure a notice the client must act on, so a client that follows the suite would not recognise VTI's answer as a revocation.
findings.evidence: entries/query/0.1/spec.md:64-70 (hcp:invalidToken for a revoked grant), :258, :284; vti2823 hcp.md:197-199 "Revoked, expired, wrong purpose and unknown token all answer the same `scope-denied`"; hcp.md:416; HCP spec:1643
findings.keyringImpact: Our plugin's revocation handling must follow one of the two. Keyring is not affected directly.
findings.askOfPR: Ask that the VTI design adopt the suite's codes on the wire (hcp:invalidToken for a revoked or expired grant, permissionDenied for scope), or that both state one mapping.
findings.reasons:
HOLDS: I opened every citation and each one says what the claim says. All are on the right versions: the PR branch pr1382, whose query spec matches pr1380 byte for byte; the VTI #2823 worktree; and HCP at b790561.

What the suite says (entries/query/0.1/spec.md):
- :64-69 declares `hcp:invalidToken` and says "A request under a revoked grant also fails here ... pending HCP confirmation (question 2) ... Such a failure is itself a notice of revocation to the client (HCP 6.2.2)".
- :258 says "The token's grant was revoked, so the provider refuses the query with `hcp:invalidToken`".
- :284 maps HCP `scope-denied` to `permissionDenied`, "with one fixed `message` whatever the reason".
- :303 is question 2.
- The demo does the same. SCENARIO.md:143 says "The grant is not `active` → `hcp:invalidToken`", and transcript.golden.txt:365/398 show step 5 failing with hcp:invalidToken.
- 26 hcp/* specs declare hcp:invalidToken, so this reading holds across the whole suite.

What VTI says (hcp.md):
- :197-200 says "Revoked, expired, wrong purpose and unknown token all answer the same `scope-denied`".
- The revoke diagram ends at :416 with "V-->>C: scope-denied".
- hcp-tasks.md:96-97 (A2) repeats it as an acceptance criterion.

What HCP says:
- specification.md:1643 says "A request that fails because its grant has been revoked is itself a notice. The client MUST treat it exactly as a notification."

So a client built to the suite would see VTI's answer as an ordinary scope refusal, not as a revocation. The codes really do differ.

Precisions, none of which overturn the claim:
1. VTI uses HCP's own error names and never states the Trust Task code it puts on the wire. Two things point to `permissionDenied`. A2 sends errors through `reject_declared`, which only emits codes the task's spec declares (pinned VTI vta-service/src/trust_tasks/helpers.rs:457-467), and hcp/entries/query declares only hcp:invalidToken. The suite's own table maps scope-denied to permissionDenied. That is still not hcp:invalidToken. Even in HCP's own names the two disagree: VTI says scope-denied, the suite reads it as invalid-token. Separately, VTI's N6 / §12 (hcp.md:595, :609) treats `permissionDenied` and `scope-denied` as different answers, while the suite's table makes them one wire code. That is a second inconsistency for the same ask.
2. The ask is stronger than written. VTI puts "expired" under scope-denied, which contradicts HCP Core itself, not just the suite: HCP 5.5 (specification.md:1399) gives `invalid-token` for "Missing, malformed, or expired authorization evidence". The divergence register (hcp.md:586-598) does not list this.
3. What softens it: VTI also pushes `hcp/grants/revoked` with at least 5 attempts over at least an hour (hcp.md:372-386). So treating the failure as a notice is a fallback for when that notice is not delivered, and the harm is a client that keeps using copies until their useUntil. Under the suite, hcp:invalidToken does not tell revoked apart from expired either, but either way the client stops.

Severity "raise" is right: VTI #2823 is a design doc, so it is easy to change, and a client loses only that fallback path. || HOLDS: The claim holds, and I found nothing that undercuts it. The suite gives one answer for a revoked grant everywhere: hcp:invalidToken. That holds in every hcp/* spec that takes a token (query, get, create, revise, withdraw, read-own, relinquish, shares/report, revoke Q2), in pr1381 as well, and in the demo, whose SCENARIO.md:140-143 says "No grant has the token → hcp:invalidToken ... The grant is not active → hcp:invalidToken". Wrong purpose or category gets permissionDenied (SCENARIO.md:144-145). VTI #2823 never mentions hcp:invalidToken at all (grep finds nothing in hcp.md, hcp-plan.md, hcp-tasks.md or hcp-demo-plan.md). Instead it puts revoked, expired, unknown token and wrong purpose under one answer, scope-denied (hcp.md:197-198, hcp-tasks.md:96-97, diagram hcp.md:416).

Things I checked that sharpen the claim without refuting it (all CONFIRMED):
(1) A bare `scope-denied` cannot be a Trust Task wire code. SPEC.md:1471 says "Extended codes MUST be namespaced", and the suite carries HCP scope-denied as `permissionDenied` (query spec.md:284). So VTI's revoked answer is either the suite's permissionDenied or an undeclared code. Neither is hcp:invalidToken. VTI's N6 (hcp.md:609) treats `scope-denied` and `permissionDenied` as two different answers on the wire, which suggests VTI did not take its codes from the suite's Errors table.
(2) VTI's grouping also conflicts with HCP itself, not only with the suite:
- HCP 5.5 (spec:1399): "invalid-token | Missing, malformed, or expired authorization evidence", so an expired or unknown token is unauthenticated in HCP, not not-authorized.
- HCP 10.4 (spec:2732): "a request with missing, invalid, or expired authorization is rejected at the HTTP layer with status 401 ... This is how the binding reports unauthenticated". This bears on VTI's later MCP rung (V3).
- HCP's "MUST NOT disclose which" (spec:1400) only applies within scope-denied, so it does not justify the grouping.
- HCP 6.2.2 (spec:1636) says evidence under a revoked grant is "invalidated", which fits the suite's reading.
(3) VTI groups revoked with wrong purpose, so no client can follow HCP 6.2.2 (spec:1643, "A request that fails because its grant has been revoked is itself a notice") against VTI's answer without also purging its copies on an ordinary scope miss. That makes the problem VTI's whatever the suite does.
(4) Mitigation, which is why this is raise and not blocker: VTI still pushes hcp/grants/revoked and retries until it is acknowledged (hcp.md:405-410). Revocation therefore reaches the client by the notice. The failure-as-notice is the fallback when a query races ahead of the notice, which is the suite demo's step 5 (SCENARIO.md:199).
(5) Keyring side: our own HCP companion copies VTI's wording (2026-11-25-bam.md:226, "`scope-denied` without detail"), so our plan needs the same fix as the ask.
(6) UNVERIFIED nuance: VTI's plan says "error_code_census witnesses" and "No census allowlist grows" (hcp-plan.md:106). The census at the pinned VTI commit (vta-service/src/trust_tasks/error_code_census.rs, UNWITNESSED_CEILING at :434) requires a witness for every code a bound spec declares. hcp:invalidToken is the only code the query spec declares, but VTI's refusal list names no condition that produces it, apart from possibly a missing or malformed token. I did not confirm how hcp/* would be bound.

Severity raise is right. Keyring is not directly affected because it acts as the Management Client.

findings.title: vta-mcp's guard would class hcp/shares/report and hcp/entries/query as read-only
findings.claim: The shared guard classifies by the final verb. 'report' and 'query' are in READ_VERBS, so hcp/shares/report (declared sideEffects mutating, it appends context.shared) and hcp/entries/query (discloses secret context) would be ReadOnly and pass --read-only. The crate's own rule says a read that discloses standing or secrets is Sensitive. VTI A8 plans an MCP guard risk class for hcp/*.
findings.evidence: vti-mcp-common/src/guard.rs:414-430 READ_VERBS includes "query", "report"; :919-937 classify; shares/report/0.1/spec.md:34-35 "sideEffects: level: mutating"; entries/query/0.1/spec.md:41-42 "discloses: secret"; vti2823 hcp-plan.md:106 "the MCP guard risk class and the `vta-mcp` census"
findings.keyringImpact: None directly.
findings.corrected:
Severity stays "note". Part of the claim is overstated. Confirmed: at the VTI pin f7b78e29d, nothing classifies hcp/* explicitly. There is no hcp override, no vti-specs-hcp crate and no hcp pin. So `classify` would fall to the last-segment verb, and READ_VERBS contains "query" (guard.rs:427) and "report" (guard.rs:430). `--read-only` refuses only `risk != Risk::ReadOnly` (guard.rs:1051), so both tasks would pass a read-only bridge. Neither census would catch this, because both verbs are already known (`unclassified_verbs`, guard.rs:865-867). The fix therefore has to be an explicit SLUG_OVERRIDES entry made in VTI's A8 (hcp-plan.md:106; hcp-tasks.md:179 names vti-mcp-common/src/guard.rs). A green census will not show that the entry was made.

(1) hcp/shares/report is a real misfit. Its spec declares `sideEffects: level: mutating` (spec.md:34-35): it appends a durable `context.shared` event. ReadOnly means "Reads state" (guard.rs:52-54). It should be at least Mutating. However, VTI's plan places it in V1/H1 (hcp-plan.md:138), not among the six tasks V0 serves. It only matters once VTI pins and serves it.

(2) hcp/entries/query is a judgement call, not a clear misclassification. Its spec declares `sideEffects: none` and `discloses: secret` (spec.md:36-37, 42). The crate's actual rule is narrower than the claim says: "a read that returns key material or discloses the principal's standing is `Sensitive`" (vti-mcp-common/CLAUDE.md). The guard also keeps reads of the principal's own data ReadOnly: `persona/attribute/list`, "which returns the values themselves", stays ReadOnly (guard.rs:455). `vault/credentials/get` and `vta/memory/get`/`list` are also ReadOnly through their verbs. Against that, `rooms/keys/open` is Sensitive for returning plaintext (guard.rs:193-196). Whether HCP context is "secret material" in the guard's sense is VTI's A8 decision. The point is worth raising, but the defect is not established.

Keyring's wallet is not affected, but our planned vti-agent-connect plugin would be, because it calls through vta-mcp.
findings.reasons:
HOLDS: Every citation checks out on the right versions. guard.rs is from the VTI pin f7b78e29d. The two spec.md files are on the pr1382 branch, and their Type URIs are https://trusttasks.org/spec/hcp/..., so `slug_of` resolves them and the verb rule applies. The cited VTI plan line is real. The mechanism is confirmed. An exact slug override is checked first and the hcp tasks have none. "report" and "query" are not in DESTRUCTIVE_VERBS, so the tasks reach READ_VERBS and come out ReadOnly, which `--read-only` permits. The censuses only flag unknown verbs, so they would stay green.

Two parts are overstated. First, the claim paraphrases the crate rule as "discloses standing or secrets". The rule actually says key material or the principal's standing, and the guard's own precedents keep reads of personal data ReadOnly (persona/attribute/list, vault/credentials/get, vta/memory/*). So entries/query being ReadOnly is debatable, not plainly wrong. Second, shares/report is out of VTI's V0 scope. The claim says "would", which is accurate because no hcp task is pinned at the VTI pin. Severity "note" is appropriate.

findings.title: At the f7b78e29d pin, memory and ACL carry no purposes; the plan cites a later VTI
findings.claim: At f7b78e29d, vta/memory is pinned at put/list/delete 0.1 and 0.2 and get 0.1, and memory.rs never mentions a purpose. acl/grant is pinned at 0.2, whose bundle names no purpose, and AclEntry has no purposes field. The plan says vta/memory 0.3 with a request purpose and ACL purposes exist 'at the pinned VTA'; those are from a later VTI commit, not this pin. HCP needs a purpose (an absolute URI) on every query and get.
findings.evidence: vti-specs-vta/trust-tasks.toml:48-51; grep -c purpose vta-service/src/trust_tasks/memory.rs → 0; vti-specs-core/trust-tasks.toml:7 "acl/grant" = "0.2"; vti-common/src/acl/mod.rs:893-960 (AclEntry fields); agent-connect-plan.md:811 "0.3 adds the purpose a request names"; HCP spec:1585
findings.keyringImpact: The plan's purpose rows on the ACL entry need the VTI version they were read at, not f7b78e29d.
findings.corrected:
Severity: note. The finding holds for memory but is overstated for the ACL.

The memory part is right. The external clone is at f7b78e29d, the PINS.json pin. There, vti-specs-vta/trust-tasks.toml:48-51 pins memory put/list/delete at ["0.1","0.2"] and get at "0.1". memory.rs has 0 mentions of "purpose", and so do operations/memory.rs, the sdk and cli memory files and every memory bundle. Yet agent-connect-plan.md:811 says put/delete/list 0.3 and get 0.2 are "the highest the pinned VTA serves of each", with "0.3 adds the purpose a request names". Those versions first appear at afc06a431 (2026-11-10, "feat(acl)!: purpose of use on ACL entries and memory reads (VTI-ACL-100 – 110) (#2539)"), one day after the pin. They are still there at 71d524572 and 4e5861d95, where memory.rs has 118 mentions of "purpose".

The ACL part is right about the pin but wrong about the plan. At f7b78e29d, acl/grant is "0.2" only, its bundle has 0 mentions of "purpose", and AclEntry has no purposes field (`pub purposes: PurposeScope` appears at 71d524572 and 4e5861d95). But the plan never says ACL purposes exist at the pinned VTA:
- Its §2.1 header (line 299) says the facts were read at VTI origin/main 71d524572, and that f7b78e29d "is not used as ground truth". That covers the acl/grant/0.3 `purposes` row at line 328.
- Line 352 says outright "a VTA from `afc06a431` serves only `acl/grant/0.3` ... and 0.3 **requires** `purposes`".
- The §3.3 table (line 498/507) says only "newest served acl/grant (0.3 shape...)".

So the ACL purpose rows already name the version they were read at. The fix is one line: line 811 should name afc06a431 or later (for example "at 4e5861d95", matching line 807 just above it) instead of "the pinned VTA". Or the PINS.json pin moves past afc06a431. HCP spec:1580/1585 is quoted correctly: a purpose is an absolute URI, and every query and get entry names one.
findings.reasons: HOLDS: Every cited source checks out. On the pinned clone (HEAD f7b78e29dfa0fc79d125eba5970cce66d82b53d5) the toml pins match the claim, no memory file mentions a purpose, acl/grant is 0.2 only, and AclEntry (mod.rs:892-991) has no purposes field. `git log -S` finds the memory 0.3 pins and the ACL purposes field first added at afc06a431 (#2539), a descendant of f7b78e29d. Plan line 811 really does say "the highest the pinned VTA serves", and PINS.json in both the plan worktree and origin/main pins f7b78e29d, so that line is wrong for the pin. The overstatement is the ACL half. The plan's §2.1 header (line 299) says its VTI facts come from 71d524572 and that f7b78e29d is not ground truth, and line 352 credits ACL purposes to "a VTA from afc06a431". The ACL rows already name their version; only the memory sentence at line 811 mislabels its commit. That is a citation slip with no effect on interop, so the severity stays at note.

findings.title: Whether sending disclosures to a model API is onward disclosure (question 46) decides a Claude Code plugin
findings.claim: HCP 3.12 forbids passing disclosed context to a party operated by another organisation. A plugin inside Claude Code sends whatever it reads to Anthropic's model API. That question is 46 in PR #1380's description, by title only, and N3 in VTI. VTI's demo avoids it by answering deterministically. Until it is answered, our plugin cannot give HCP disclosures to Claude. Who the Client Operator is (question 45 / N2) also decides whether 3.12 even allows the plugin's own components.
findings.evidence: HCP spec:585 "An HCP Client MUST NOT pass context disclosed to it under a grant to a party operated by a different organization"; PR #1380 body "a model API run by another organization (46)"; vti2823 hcp.md:606 N3; hcp.md:559 decision 15 "The demo's client answers deterministically"
findings.keyringImpact: It decides whether P1 'memories on HCP' can feed a Claude Code session at all.
findings.askOfPR: Give the full wording of question 46 in the PR, and rank it high: it decides whether any agent plugin in a commercial host can be an HCP Context Client.
findings.corrected:
The finding holds, and "raise" is the right severity. Four parts are overstated or misplaced.

(1) HCP draft 3 does not clearly forbid this; it leaves it open. Spec 3.1 (:285-287) calls a language model "a component", never an actor or party. Spec 3.12 (:585) forbids passing context to "a party operated by a different organization", and its MAY covers only "components and services operated by its own Client Operator". A model hosted by another organisation fits neither sentence cleanly. That is why question 46 and VTI's N3 exist. So the accurate statement is: on the strict reading the plugin may not put HCP disclosures into a hosted model's context, and the conservative course is not to until the editors answer. It is not settled that it cannot.

(2) The model API is not always Anthropic's. It is whatever provider the host is set up to use (Anthropic or a cloud reseller), and in each case it is an organisation other than our Client Operator. Also, a plugin does not have to send everything it reads. Spec 3.13 step 6 (:607) says "The HCP Client decides what reaches any model". It can use disclosures in its own code, as VTI's deterministic demo does, or with a model its operator runs or one on the device (guides G1.3). What it cannot do without a ruling is feed disclosures to the hosted model, which is the only useful case.

(3) The wrong package is named. C10 "memories on HCP" is Keyring's Management Client screens (entries/get, withdraw, revise). Those are not disclosures under a grant, so 3.12 does not touch them. The affected package is B7 in the companion: the plugin as Context Client using entries/query inside a Claude Code session, in P1. The P0 demo avoids the question, as VTI decision 15 does.

(4) The ask should be narrower than "whether any plugin can be a Context Client". It is whether a Context Client in a commercial host may put disclosures into that host's hosted model. The full wording already exists as VTI N3 (hcp.md:606). Question 46 is cited only by title in the PR #1380 body and in no spec's "Pending HCP confirmation" section on pr1380, pr1381 or pr1382. So the ask is that the PR include or link the editor question list. Question 45 / N2 (the Client Operator of a plugin in a commercial host) is confirmed. It matters because 3.12's MAY depends on the Client Operator, and spec 10.5 (:2760) gives a stdio bridge its own Client Operator, bound by 3.12. | The finding mostly holds; it needs narrowing, and "raise" is the right severity. HCP 3.12 bars an HCP Client from passing disclosed context to anyone not operated by its own Client Operator (spec:585). The onwardSharing exception does not help here: it covers only Low-sensitivity context, the client must use its own words, it may not pass entries or copies, and it must report each share (spec:589-594).

HCP already answers one case without question 46. A model is a component (spec:285-287), and 3.12 allows "components and services operated by its own Client Operator" (spec:585). Under the MCP Binding the grant sits with "the MCP host or its HCP integration" (spec:2756). So when the HCP Client's operator also runs the model, for example a host vendor's own integration on its own model, sending context to the model is already allowed.

Question 46 / N3 only matters when the model is run by a different organization from the Client Operator. That is our case. Our plugin is a 10.5 stdio bridge, "an HCP Client in its own right… has its own Client Operator… bound by… onward disclosure" (spec:2760). And the First-Party rung needs the Client Operator to be the Provider Operator, the lab (spec:2872; bam C1). So questions 45/N2 and 46/N3 decide it together, not 46 alone.

"Sends whatever it reads" is overstated. The client decides what reaches the model (spec:609). A plugin can use disclosures in its own code and keep them out of tool results, which is what VTI's deterministic demo does (hcp.md:559).

Scope of the impact:
- P0's base path (VTA memory through vta-mcp, no HCP grant) is not bound by 3.12.
- P0's HCP demo uses a deterministic CLI.
- The question bites at P1's HCP increment (plan:278), where disclosures would go into Claude's context.

Reword the ask: give question 46's full wording in PR #1380, rank it high, and pair it with 45. Together they decide whether a plugin whose Client Operator is not the model's operator may put HCP disclosures into the model's context. That is narrower than "whether any agent plugin in a commercial host can be an HCP Context Client".
findings.reasons:
HOLDS: Every cited quote is accurate and from the right versions: HCP spec at b790561, PR #1380 head 94ed4200c, and VTI PR #2823's docs. Spec :585 is word for word. The PR body (fetched read-only) lists "a model API run by another organization (46)" and "the Client Operator of an agent plugin (45)", by title only. git grep finds no "question 46" or "question 45" text on pr1380, pr1381 or pr1382, even though the PR body says every spec cites its questions by number. VTI hcp.md:606 is N3, :605 is N2, and :559 is decision 15 ("Repeatable, and no disclosure to a model provider"). hcp.md:163 and tasks/hcp-demo-plan.md:181-182 say the same.

The central claim, that HCP disclosures cannot go to Claude until the question is answered, holds only as the strict reading. The spec itself is ambiguous: 3.1 says a model is a component, never an actor, and 3.12 forbids passing to a "party" while permitting the operator's own "components". The spec has no text on a hosted model API (I searched the spec, guides and introduction). 21.10 "Intermediaries" is informative only. The plan mapping is off: C10 is Management Client work, which 3.12 does not cover; the plugin-as-Context-Client work is B7. The severity and the existence of the gap both stand. || HOLDS: I looked for anything that contradicts the claim and found no exception to 3.12 for model processors (outside providers that process data on the client's behalf). I checked the spec's 3.1, 3.2.10, 3.11, 3.12, 3.13, 10.5 and 21.1/21.4/21.10, guides G5.4/G5.5, and path-to-v2-final.md. The spec's only carve-outs are the Client Operator's own components and services, and onwardSharing for Low-sensitivity context, which forbids passing entries or copies. So under the literal text a model API run by another organization is not allowed, and the question is a real one that the spec leaves open.

- git grep over pr1380, pr1381 and pr1382 finds no spec text for 45 or 46.

What narrows the claim:

So 46 only bites when the model's operator differs from the Client Operator, and which case we are in turns on 45/N2. The claim notes this link, but overstates 46 as deciding "any agent plugin".

findings.title: vta_call's signing, reply check and transport already meet the suite's rules
findings.claim: vta_call builds and signs a document with the agent key (issuer = agent DID, recipient = VTA DID), which meets the REQUIRED request proof of question 53. It verifies the reply's proof against the VTA DID. It rides DIDComm or TSP, whereas the VTA refuses hcp/* over REST. Payloads for unpinned URIs are not schema-checked on the client; once vti-specs-hcp is pinned they will be.
findings.evidence: vta-sdk/src/client/mod.rs:4159-4185 signed_task_document; :4203-4230 build_task_document; :2380-2420 verify_reply ("its proven signer must be the agent"); :1855-1866 check_payload_conforms (None → Ok); vti2823 hcp.md:201-202 "Sender binding holds on TSP and DIDComm only"
findings.keyringImpact: An HCP client in the plugin can reuse the same SDK signing and transport.
findings.corrected:
Severity ok for the signing, the reply check and the schema check, with the transport sentence and the Keyring impact narrowed (a note):

(1) Signing. `vta_call` (vta-mcp/src/server.rs:900-904) calls `dispatch_trust_task`. That goes through `exchange_trust_task` to `signed_task_document` (vta-sdk/src/client/mod.rs:2123), which signs every document unconditionally. `issuer` is `identity.client_did` and `recipient` is `identity.vta_did`, both set from one `ClientIdentity` (:4219-4224). The proof key comes from that same identity (`holder_key`, :108-117), and `issuedAt` is always set (:4211). This meets the hcp/* `proofRequirement.request: REQUIRED` and `issuedAtRequirement: REQUIRED` (question 53, and the `issuer` binding of question 22). A client with no identity is refused locally and never sends an unsigned document (:4166-4184). In the dedicated-agent rungs `issuer` is the agent DID; in session mode it is the operator's DID.

(2) Reply check. Every non-error reply is verified, and its signer must equal `identity.vta_did` (:2445-2472). That meets `proofRequirement.response: REQUIRED`. A `trust-task-error` reply is exempt and is returned unverified (:2412-2414), as the framework allows (RECOMMENDED). `require_signed_replies` defaults to true, and vta-mcp never calls `trusting_unsigned_replies`.

(3) Transport, narrowed. `vta_call` rides whatever transport the connect ladder chose. The did:key and did:webvh-bundle rungs (the ones our plan uses, `--agent-did`/`--agent-key`) build a DIDComm client with `tsp: None` (:707-708), and vta-mcp never adds a TSP leg. So in our setup it is DIDComm only. TSP, or REST against a VTA that advertises only REST, happens only in session mode (`TransportChoice::Auto`, agent_connect.rs:22-24), which uses the operator's credential. Token mode is REST with no identity, so it fails locally before sending. "The VTA refuses hcp/* over REST" is the #2823 design (hcp.md:161, 201-202; hcp-plan.md A8). The pinned VTA (f7b78e29d) has no hcp code at all. That design does accept DIDComm ("TSP and DIDComm"), although its agent client is drawn over TSP (hcp.md:157; hcp-plan.md:116).

(4) Schema check. Confirmed: `schema_for` answering None means no check (:1856-1858), and no hcp/* task is pinned at f7b78e29d. `vti-specs-hcp` is planned (hcp.md:545), not present.

Keyring impact, narrowed. Only the `vta_call` path reuses vta-sdk's signing and transport. The plugin itself is TypeScript, built on @openvtc/trust-tasks (agent-connect-plan.md:675), so a direct HCP client in it would not use this SDK. The review's own notes/coverage-mcp.md §4.4 lists why `vta_call` alone does not make a working HCP client: no threadId, the token passes through the model, no receive loop, and the identity has an ACL entry.
findings.reasons:
HOLDS: Every cited line says what the claim says, at the right commit (VTI pin f7b78e29d; vti2823 for the design quote).

- `vta_call` calls `dispatch_trust_task` (server.rs:900-904).
- `dispatch_trust_task` calls `check_payload_conforms` (mod.rs:2043) and then `exchange_trust_task`.
- `exchange_trust_task` calls `signed_task_document` (:2123) and runs `verified_reply` on the REST, TSP and DIDComm arms (:2188, :2224, :2280, :2289).
- `build_task_document` sets `issuer` and `recipient` from one identity (:4219-4224).
- `verify_reply` compares the proven signer with `vta_did` (:2465).
- The hcp specs declare a REQUIRED proof on both request and response (entries/query/0.1/spec.md:21-29), and the 'Question 53' text is at grants/revoke/0.1/spec.md:208. So the 'ok' on signing and the reply check holds.

Two parts are overstated, but neither is wrong enough to refute:

1. 'It rides DIDComm or TSP'. vta-mcp's dedicated-agent rungs give DIDComm only (`tsp: None`, mod.rs:707-708; no TSP leg is enabled anywhere in vta-mcp). TSP, or REST against a REST-only VTA, comes only through session mode's Auto choice.
2. 'The VTA refuses hcp/* over REST'. That is the #2823 design only. `git grep -i hcp` finds nothing in the pinned vta-service, vta-sdk or vta-mcp.

The quote 'its proven signer must be the agent' is correct: in context, 'agent' means the VTA the client talks to (mod.rs:2382-2385). The Keyring-impact line overreaches, because the plugin is TypeScript and reaches vta-sdk only through vta-mcp, and the review's own notes list gaps beyond signing and transport.

findings.title: Keyring's eddsa-jcs-2022 recipe reproduces the PR demo proof byte for byte
findings.claim: I ran Keyring's signing recipe (canonicalize@1.0.8 JCS, sha256(JCS(proof config)) || sha256(JCS(doc minus proof)), Ed25519, z+base58btc) on the demo's Management Client revoke request, with accessToken restored to MANAGEMENT_TOKEN. It verifies the PR's proof. Signing the same document with the demo key (0x31 repeated) and the same created gives the identical proofValue. Two controls fail: the transcript as printed (token redacted), and issuedAt rewritten to .000Z.
findings.evidence: examples/hcp-demo-ts/transcript.golden.txt:325-345 (proofValue "z2Q3HYiNtXPb…8MrQa", "proofPurpose": "authentication"); src/demo.ts:111 MANAGEMENT_TOKEN = "hcp_mt_demo_management"; demo.ts:162 party("Management Client", 0x31, 0x32); Keyring packages/trust-tasks/src/documentProof.ts:285-303; script scratchpad/sf/crosscheck.mjs output: "2. Keyring recipe, authentication, reproduces PR proofValue byte-for-byte: true", "4. Control: transcript as printed (token redacted) verifies: false"
findings.keyringImpact: No canonicalization or hashing change needed for Keyring to sign or verify hcp/* documents.
findings.reasons:
HOLDS: The claim holds and the severity "ok" is right. I checked each citation on branch pr1382 (HEAD e163cac1d) and on Keyring's d3-fast-send tree.

What I confirmed:
- **Transcript.** transcript.golden.txt:325-345 is the Management Client revoke request. It has the quoted proofValue `"z2Q3HYiNtXPbSn3kPPYD2WUd2s9GmmgXpDRwG1fD7cYdUe7ft8LHePqKhSfSXjqD5NwZmAwmibDF4fp7Eb8m8MrQa"` (line 338), `"proofPurpose": "authentication"`, and the redacted `"accessToken": "hcp_mt…"`.
- **Why the token shows redacted.** The transcript prints `redact(doc)` (demo.ts:452). That function cuts accessToken to 6 characters (demo.ts:496). So restoring the token from demo.ts:111 (`MANAGEMENT_TOKEN = "hcp_mt_demo_management"`) is legitimate, and the demo sends that full token at demo.ts:585.
- **Key.** demo.ts:162 is `party("Management Client", 0x31, 0x32)`, and demo.ts:95 fills 32 bytes with the seed.
- **Same recipe on both sides.** The PR's signer (trust-tasks-ts-proof/src/sign.ts:66-111) hashes sha256(JCS(config)) followed by sha256(JCS(body)). It builds the proof config with the same members as Keyring's documentProof.ts:267-279, and both write timestamps the same way (`.000Z` becomes `Z`). Keyring's code at documentProof.ts:285-303 does what the claim says: canonicalize, sha256 of the config then of the document, and `z` plus base58.
- **Canonicalize version.** Keyring's node_modules has canonicalize 1.0.8.
- **Script run.** I ran scratchpad/sf/crosscheck.mjs myself and got: did:key matches the issuer; check 1 (verifies) true; check 2 (reproduces the proofValue byte for byte) true; check 4 (token left redacted) false; check 5 (issuedAt as `.000Z`) false. That is exactly what the claim reports.
- **Purpose.** Keyring's `purposeForDocumentType` (proofPurpose.ts) returns `authentication` for any hcp/* type, so the purpose used in check 2 is the one Keyring would actually pick.
- **No `@context` difference here.** The transcript has no `@context` anywhere (count 0). So the PR putting `@context` into the proof and Keyring only doing that with `carryContext` makes no difference for these documents.

Precision notes. None of these refutes the claim:
- **The script copies the recipe; it does not call Keyring's function.** It uses Keyring's own canonicalize and noble libraries plus @scure/base. It does not call `signDocumentProof`, which signs through credo's KMS. Ed25519 signatures are deterministic, so the KMS path should give the same bytes.
- **Only one document was tested.**
- **Verifying needs the right call.** Keyring's `verifyDocumentProof` assumes `assertionMethod` unless told otherwise (documentProof.ts:453), so it would reject these `authentication` proofs. Verifying hcp/* documents needs `verifyTrustTaskProof`, or `proofPurpose: 'authentication'` passed in. That is a choice of which call to make, not a change to canonicalization or hashing, so the impact sentence stands as written.

findings.title: All hcp spec example proofs use assertionMethod, against SPEC 4.7.3 and the PR's own libraries
findings.claim: No hcp spec states a proofPurpose requirement, and none declares its proof an attestation under SPEC 7.3 item 8. Yet all 47 example proofs in the 28 spec.md files carry assertionMethod, and none carries authentication. The framework says a producer SHOULD sign with authentication and SHOULD NOT use assertionMethod unless the spec defines the proof as an attestation. The PR's TS and Go signers default to authentication, every proof in the demo transcript is authentication, and the VTA signs hcp responses with authentication (they are not in ATTESTATION_SLUGS).
findings.evidence: specs/hcp/grants/revoke/0.1/spec.md:139 "proofPurpose": "assertionMethod"; specs/hcp/entries/query/0.1/spec.md:171,250 same; tt/SPEC.md:374 "A producer SHOULD sign a Trust Task document with proofPurpose authentication … SHOULD NOT sign … with assertionMethod unless"; trust-tasks-ts-proof/src/sign.ts:79 options.proofPurpose ?? "authentication"; trust-tasks-go/proof/sign.go:148; vta-sdk/src/trust_task_sign.rs:254 purpose_for_document_type; vta-sdk/src/trust_task_proof/purpose.rs:122-150
findings.keyringImpact: Keyring's purposeForDocumentType signs hcp/* as authentication, matching the libraries and the VTA. Anyone copying the spec examples would sign assertionMethod instead. That still verifies, but it is the wrong signal, and if a response is later declared an attestation, Keyring's mirror of ATTESTATION_SLUGS must follow.
findings.askOfPR: Change the example proofs to authentication per SPEC 4.7.3. Or, where a response is meant as evidence a third party relies on (query, export, the provider's disclosures), say so in proofRequirement and name the required purpose, so the VTA and Keyring can classify it.
findings.corrected:
Holds; severity raise is right. Three points need tightening. (1) It is true that no hcp spec states a proofPurpose requirement, names assertionMethod outside its example JSON, or declares outcomeEvidence. But seven specs (entries/query, entries/get, export, audit/read, entries/set-categories, entries/confirm, entries/restrict-purposes) cite SPEC §7.3 item 8 and call their REQUIRED response proof "a signed assertion that any third party can verify". The query and export rationales also point to later disputes and to reliance by the importing provider. For those responses, assertionMethod may be what the author meant without saying so, which supports the second option of the ask. For request examples (grants/revoke:139, the wallet's request; entries/query:171, the Context Client's request) nothing in the spec supports assertionMethod. (2) "The VTA signs hcp responses with authentication" is a projection. The VTI pin f7b78e29d has no hcp code. Its classifier would sign any hcp/* document with authentication, and it never treats a #response as an attestation, even for an attestation slug (purpose.rs:133-135). So declaring an hcp response an attestation would mean changing the rule in both the VTA classifier and Keyring's, not just adding a slug. (3) "That still verifies" holds only if the signer's controller document lists the key under assertionMethod, since the VTA and the framework check the relationship the proof names. A side note for another finding: Keyring's ATTESTATION_SLUGS (proofPurpose.ts:10) has 3 entries, while the VTI pin has 4 (auth/oob/grant). | The claim holds and "raise" is the right severity. Three narrowings.

(1) The VTA mechanism is misattributed. The pinned VTA (f7b78e29d) has no hcp code at all. It signs every response it sends with authentication through sign_response, then attach_proof_in_place, then sign_as_authentication, whatever the slug. ATTESTATION_SLUGS only affects request documents: purpose_for_document_type returns authentication for any #response. Keyring's purposeForDocumentType does the same. So if HCP later declares a response (query, export, a disclosure) to be an attestation, adding the slug to Keyring's ATTESTATION_SLUGS mirror would change nothing. Both classifiers, and the VTA's sign_response, would need a rule for responses. The "so the VTA and Keyring can classify it" part of the ask should say this.

(2) Keyring has no hcp code yet. Its low-level documentProof.ts signs with assertionMethod by default (line 265). Its verifyDocumentProof, by default, rejects any proof whose purpose is not assertionMethod (line 453). Some callers pin authentication instead. So a future Keyring hcp verifier that pins one purpose would refuse either providers that copy the spec examples or the VTA. That supports the raise. The claim that an assertionMethod proof "still verifies" is true for the VTA's verifier and for Keyring's verifyTrustTaskProof, but only when the signer lists the key under assertionMethod.

(3) The 47 proofs split into 32 request examples, 14 response examples and 1 other. Every one is a top-level eddsa-jcs-2022 proof on the document itself, not a credential proof inside a payload. Several response rationales do describe reliance by third parties. entries/query, for example, says the client "can show which provider released which context ... which is what ... any later dispute turn on". That is the kind of reliance SPEC 7.3 item 8 has in mind. None of them names an attestation or a purpose, so the claim stands as worded.

Minor points. The TS, Go, Rust and Dart signers that default to authentication are the repo's existing proof libraries; PR #1380/#1382 does not change them. SPEC 4.7.3's rule on which purpose a producer signs with arrived in Working Draft 0.7.0, while the hcp specs target 0.6.0. In practice it still applies: no spec targets 0.7.0, the hcp specs already cite 0.7.0's §4.7.1, and our pinned framework (2a66a0351) has the rule at SPEC.md:373.

HOLDS: I checked every citation on pr1382 and on pr1380 (tt-drift). The 28 hcp spec.md files carry 47 proofPurpose values, all "assertionMethod", and none is authentication. The cited lines match exactly: grants/revoke:139 and entries/query:171,250. pr1381 keeps assertionMethod at query:205,284. SPEC.md:374 on the PR branch reads "A producer SHOULD sign a Trust Task document with proofPurpose authentication … SHOULD NOT sign … with assertionMethod unless the governing Trust Task specification defines the document's proof as such an attestation (… item 8)". The same rule sits at SPEC.md:373 on our pin 2a66a0351. It came in at b2ad67c8b (2026-09-27), well before the HCP PR, so the version is not in question. SPEC.md:375 lets a spec require a purpose "stating it with its proof requirement". The hcp proofRequirement blocks (query:22-29, export:22-30) do not do this. The libraries match the claim. The TS signer at sign.ts:79 has `options.proofPurpose ?? "authentication"`. The Go signer at sign.go:146-149 sets `if purpose == "" { purpose = "authentication" }`. The Dart signer at sign.dart:67 defaults to `'authentication'`. The demo transcript (examples/hcp-demo-ts/transcript.golden.txt) has 14 proofs, all "authentication", and the demo source sets no purpose. In the VTA, sign_in_place_with at trust_task_sign.rs:254 calls purpose_for_document_type. Keyring's proofPurpose.ts:25-29 copies that rule. I found no misquote and no wrong-branch problem. The overstatements are the ones listed in correctedClaim: the "signed assertion any third party can verify" wording in seven specs, and the VTA statement, which describes what its classifier would do, since the pin has no hcp code. || HOLDS: I searched for evidence against the claim and found none that overturns it.

- **The 47 example proofs:** all 47 in the 28 spec.md files use assertionMethod, the same on pr1380, pr1381 and pr1382. All are top-level eddsa-jcs-2022 proofs on the document, none an embedded credential proof. findings.title: No verifier in play would refuse a Keyring assertionMethod or authentication proof
findings.claim: The PR's TS, Go and Rust verifiers accept all four signing purposes. The VTA at f7b78e29d verifies whatever purpose the proof declares, bound to that relationship in the signer's DID document, and refuses keyAgreement. VTA-minted DIDs list #key-0 under both authentication and assertionMethod, and a did:key has all four implicitly. So neither purpose Keyring might use is refused. Only VTA approval decisions (task-consent/decision and similar) must be assertionMethod.
findings.evidence: trust-tasks-ts-proof/src/verifier.ts:47-52 SIGNING_PURPOSES; trust-tasks-go/proof/verifier.go:322; vta-sdk/src/trust_task_proof/verify.rs:313-316 "PurposeBound::for_proof(resolver, di)"; purpose.rs:81-94; verify.rs:336-391 APPROVAL_PROOF_PURPOSE = "assertionMethod"; vta-service/src/operations/did_webvh/document.rs:335-369; Keyring VtaClient.ts:1919-1933 { proofPurpose: purposeForDocumentType(type) }
findings.keyringImpact: Keyring's VtaClient path already sends hcp/* with authentication and needs no change. The bare signDocumentProof default (assertionMethod, documentProof.ts:265) also verifies at the VTA for VTA-minted DIDs.
findings.corrected:
Severity stays ok, but four points need to be said precisely.

(1) Proof purpose. The PR's TS, Go, Rust and Dart verifiers accept all four signing purposes and refuse keyAgreement. But the TS and Go verifiers handle did:key only (verifier.ts:68-69 "did:key only — no network, no resolver"; verifier.go:68-69). They would refuse a Keyring did:peer:2 or did:webvh proof as "not a did:key this verifier supports". That is a refusal over the DID method, not the purpose. So "no verifier would refuse" holds only for the purpose check.

(2) The DID that signs. Keyring's VtaClient does not sign with a VTA-minted DID. It signs with a did:peer:2 manager identity (VtiMediatorTransport.ts:433-434, createPeerDidNamingUri), and credo encodes its Ed25519 key as V (authentication). The VTA still accepts both purposes from it: its no-I/O did:peer resolver puts a V key under both authentication and assertionMethod (vm_resolver.rs:779-783 test "V key for {purpose}"). So the conclusion holds, for a reason the claim leaves out.

(3) The VTA rule has exceptions both ways. It does verify whatever purpose the proof declares, bound to the DID document, at the spine (trust_tasks/mod.rs:2051) and at verify.rs:315. But:
- the attestation slugs need assertionMethod (purpose.rs:122-127: step-up approve-response, task-consent/decision, confirm/response, auth/oob/grant; enforced by verify_approval_proof in step_up, task_consent and oob_sign_in.rs:869);
- attestation/mnemonic-export needs authentication (attestation.rs:337 `if proof.proof_purpose != "authentication"`).
So the bare signDocumentProof default (assertionMethod) is not accepted everywhere. Neither exception concerns hcp/*.

(4) Keyring does not send hcp/* today; there is no spec/hcp in its packages. What is true is that purposeForDocumentType would sign any hcp/* request for authentication, because hcp slugs are not attestation slugs, and the VTA would accept that. HCP consent itself goes through task-consent/decision (VTI hcp.md §5), which Keyring already signs for assertionMethod.

Side note, no ask in this finding: every hcp/* spec example uses "proofPurpose": "assertionMethod". The PR's own SPEC.md:374 says a producer SHOULD sign authentication, and the demo transcript uses authentication. No hcp spec requires a purpose in its normative text.
findings.reasons:
HOLDS: Every citation checks out at the right commit: the PR branch pr1382, the VTI pin f7b78e29d and Keyring d3-fast-send.
- verifier.ts:47-52 lists SIGNING_PURPOSES.
- verifier.go:322 lists SigningPurposes.
- verify.rs:315 has "PurposeBound::for_proof(resolver, di)".
- purpose.rs:81-94 parses the purpose and refuses keyAgreement.
- verify.rs:338 has APPROVAL_PROOF_PURPOSE = "assertionMethod".
- document.rs:335-369 puts #key-0 under both authentication and assertionMethod.
- VtaClient.ts:1933 has purposeForDocumentType.
- documentProof.ts:265 defaults to assertionMethod.

The core conclusion holds: nothing in play refuses either purpose Keyring would use for hcp/*. The claim overstates in four places, each set out in the corrected claim above:
- the TS and Go verifiers are did:key-only, so they refuse Keyring's real DIDs for a reason other than purpose;
- Keyring signs with a did:peer:2 manager identity, which the claim never names;
- the VTA rule has exceptions both ways (attestation slugs need assertionMethod, mnemonic-export needs authentication);
- Keyring does not send hcp/* today.

None of these makes the finding wrong, and none touches hcp/* interop, so ok stays the right severity.

findings.title: The as-received rule is already in our pinned framework and in the VTA ingress; Keyring's wireTimestamp comment is out of date
findings.claim: SPEC 4.7 'What a consumer verifies … as received' is the same text at our pin and the PR.
