The pinned framework at 2a66a0351 has the same text at SPEC.md:1355. SPEC §9.4 (carried protocols) has no carve-out that would let a protocol family put a carriage-only code under the family name.

2. **There is no shared definition.** specs/hcp/_shared/0.1/ holds only schemas, with no CONVENTIONS.md. Elsewhere in the registry, every family that uses a family-namespace code for a single spec defines it in a `_shared/<v>/CONVENTIONS.md` table:
   - provision/vta CONVENTIONS.md:98, `provision/vta:notClaimant`
   - external CONVENTIONS.md:44, `external:alreadyExists`
   - auth/oob and vta/dids do the same.
   
   The HCP family breaks that pattern for this code.

3. **No other spec uses it.** Only hcp/export declares `hcp:exportTooLarge`. hcp/import declares only `hcp:invalidToken`. The one other mention, the _shared/0.1/export.schema.json description, credits the code to "(hcp/export)".

4. **Its meaning is tied to this one task.** It is defined against "this task's declared maxDocumentBytes", and the spec calls it "Not an HCP error". So unlike `hcp:invalidToken`, `hcp:versionConflict` and `hcp:credentialInvalid`, no shared definition of it exists: those three map errors that HCP 5.5 defines once for the whole protocol.

5. **The build doesn't catch it.** checkErrorCodeNamespaces only builds the set of the slug and its prefixes, plus a check that the local part doesn't copy a standard code. DEVELOPMENT.md:397 says this check does not cover "whether the code is the right one to emit".

6. **It isn't a blocker.** The code is resolved against the Type URI (§8.5), and unknown codes fall back to taskFailed. Keyring reads only the part after the colon (vtiAgent.ts:443 and plainError.ts:106 use `split(':').pop()`), so Keyring is not affected. The spec is still a draft, so renaming the code to `hcp/export:tooLarge` is cheap, and the new name copies no standard code.

findings.title: hcp:invalidToken is declared 26 times with two wordings and has no shared family convention document
findings.claim: SPEC §8.5 rule 2 expects a family code to be 'defined once ... in a shared convention that the family's specifications reference'. Each hcp spec declares hcp:invalidToken (26 times, with two distinct meaning texts) and hcp:versionConflict and hcp:credentialInvalid in its own front matter. There is no hcp/_shared spec.md. They all cite HCP 5.5, and retryable is false everywhere.
findings.evidence: script over specs/hcp/**/spec.md front matter: ('hcp:invalidToken','false') 26 declarations, 2 distinct meanings; ls specs/hcp/_shared/0.1 → schemas only; tt/SPEC.md:1474
findings.keyringImpact: None.
findings.askOfPR: Optional: state the hcp:* family codes once (e.g. an hcp/_shared note) and have each spec reference it.
findings.corrected: The finding holds in substance, with two corrections. (1) There are four distinct meaning texts for hcp:invalidToken, not two. They fall into two groups: 18 specs say "...authorization evidence", here the Management Client's access token.", and 8 specs add the revoked-grant reading in three different wordings (6 share one text; entries/query and grants/relinquish each have their own). (2) The finding misses a fourth hcp:-namespaced code, hcp:exportTooLarge. Only hcp/export declares it, it is retryable false, and its own text says "Not an HCP error: HCP sets no size limit on an export". So "they all cite HCP 5.5" is true only of the three HCP-derived codes. The rest is confirmed on pr1380, pr1381 and pr1382: 26 hcp:invalidToken declarations across 28 specs (grants/request and grants/revoked declare no errorCodes), hcp:versionConflict 4 times, hcp:credentialInvalid 2 times, retryable false everywhere, and specs/hcp/_shared/0.1 holds only schemas. Other families in the same registry each keep a _shared/0.1/CONVENTIONS.md, among them did-management, acl, vault, persona, external, policy and voting; for example did-management:unknownDomain is defined there and referenced from each spec. Severity: 'note' fits the three HCP-derived codes. Each spec cites HCP 5.5, which defines their meaning once, so the gap there is mostly formal. hcp:exportTooLarge deserves 'raise'. SPEC §8.5 rule 2 says a family namespace MUST "never ... give a specification-specific code a broader name than it has earned", so the code should be hcp/export:<local> (e.g. hcp/export:tooLarge). The registry build does not catch this: checkErrorCodeNamespaces only checks the prefix. Keyring impact: none.
findings.reasons: HOLDS: SPEC.md:1474 says what the claim quotes. I parsed the front matter of all 28 specs/hcp/**/spec.md files with js-yaml. hcp:invalidToken appears 26 times, all retryable false, but after collapsing whitespace there are 4 distinct meaning texts (18/6/1/1). "Two wordings" is right only if you count the two groups. versionConflict (4) and credentialInvalid (2) are confirmed and both cite HCP 5.5. HCP 5.5 at b790561 does define invalid-token, version-conflict and credential-invalid, so the meaning of those three is defined once upstream and each spec references it. That softens the point to formal. Nothing in specs/hcp gives the hcp: family codes a shared definition the way did-management/_shared/0.1/CONVENTIONS.md defines did-management:unknownDomain. The claim leaves out hcp:exportTooLarge. It is a code for hcp/export alone, under the family namespace, which is a direct case of what rule 2 forbids. That part deserves 'raise'. The results are the same on pr1380 (tt-drift), and pr1381 adds no shared convention file.

findings.title: Refusals on a held thread leave the hold open, against 'an error closes the exchange' and next-step producer rule 5
findings.claim: grants/request refuses an interloper (permissionDenied) or a resubmission with a different payload (malformedRequest) on a held thread and says 'the held request is unaffected', then keeps sending next steps on that thread. SPEC §8.6 says an error closes the exchange. trust-task-next-step 0.1 producer rule 5 forbids a next step 'for a task it has already answered with a #response or a trust-task-error on the same thread'. A client that follows those rules strictly may give up after seeing its own malformedRequest.
findings.evidence: tt/specs/hcp/grants/request/0.1/spec.md:175-176 "the held request is unaffected"; tt/SPEC.md:1533 "an error closes the exchange"; tt/specs/trust-task-next-step/0.1/spec.md:85 "**MUST NOT** emit a next step for a task it has already answered with a `#response` or a `trust-task-error` on the same thread"
findings.keyringImpact: None for the app; plugin behaviour.
findings.askOfPR: Say that a refusal of a resubmission that does not match the held request does not close the held exchange, and reconcile that with next-step 0.1 rule 5.
findings.corrected: Severity should be note, not raise. All three quotes are accurate on pr1382, and pr1380 has the same text. SPEC.md is unchanged by the PR; the line is 1414 at our pin 2a66a0351. But the framework scopes an error to the document it answers, not to the thread. On a held thread, grants/request refuses a different document: the interloper's, or the mismatched resubmission. The held document is never answered with an error and stays `accepted`. The next steps that follow answer later resubmissions and cite them in `inResponseTo`. So the PR does not go against SPEC §8.6 or next-step producer rule 5. The interloper's permissionDenied goes to the interloper, so the legitimate client never sees it. The malformedRequest case reaches only a client that already broke rule 2 ("the same payload"). The first half of the ask is already in the spec, word for word: "the held request is unaffected". What is left is loose wording. The §4.4.1 table (SPEC.md:200) says a Failure "Closes the exchange? Yes", and §4.9 ties an exchange to threadId. One optional line in grants/request would remove the doubt, for example "a refusal answers only the refused document; the held document stays accepted". No Keyring impact. | There is no real conflict. Under the framework's own model, error responses and lifecycle states belong to one document, not to a whole thread. The held request in hcp/grants/request is never answered with an error. Each refusal reports on a different document: the interloper's document, or a resubmission whose payload differs. That ends that document and leaves the held exchange open, which is what the spec already says ("the held request is unaffected", spec.md:175-176). The quote from SPEC §8.6 (SPEC.md:1533) is the reason a consumer must not answer the HELD task itself with an error. It is not a general rule that any error on a threadId closes the exchange. All that remains is a wording point in the framework, not in PR #1380. In trust-task-next-step 0.1, producer rule 5 says "on the same thread", which could be read as thread-wide. The framework could say "for a document it has already answered", matching SPEC §8.2 and §8.4. Severity: note (framework editorial), not raise against the HCP suite. The first half of the proposed ask is already in the text. No Keyring impact.
findings.reasons:
REFUTE: The claim's conclusion is not supported once the cited lines are read in context.

(1) SPEC.md:1533 is a MUST NOT about answering a held task with an error "whose extended code or `details` says the task is held". The clause "an error closes the exchange" is only the reason for that rule. grants/request does not do this: its permissionDenied and malformedRequest are real refusals of other documents, not a hold dressed up as an error.

(2) The framework scopes an error to one document. SPEC.md:1467 says "A `false` value of `retryable` represents a hard failure for that specific document. It does not prohibit the *producer* from issuing a *new* *Trust Task document* ... (which **SHOULD** carry the same `threadId` ...)". SPEC.md:492 (Example 4, after an error) says "any subsequent document in this exchange — for example, a retry with a fresh `id` ... would carry the same `threadId`". The §4.12 lifecycle (SPEC.md:673ff) is per document, and a next step leaves "the document ... `accepted`". SPEC.md:1536 says the consumer "answers a resubmission in the same thread", so each resubmission is a separate document with its own answer.

(3) The next-step spec reads the same way. Line 73 says "An error terminates the document under SPEC.md §8.4". Line 68 says that on trust-task-error "The originating task is ... closed, unsuccessfully". So rule 5 at line 85 ("a task it has already answered ... on the same thread") refers to the answered task document. The held document is never answered with an error. The next steps after a refusal answer later resubmissions: SCENARIO.md:131 has "`inResponseTo` the resubmission" and demo.ts:409 has "inResponseTo: { typeUri: doc.type, id: doc.id }".

(4) The interloper's error goes to the interloper. demo.ts:355 calls refuse(), which is rejectWith(doc, ...), and that sets recipient to request.issuer (trust-tasks-ts/src/_runtime/document.ts:479). The legitimate client never receives it.

(5) The "client gives up after its own malformedRequest" scenario needs a client that resubmitted a different payload. That breaks grants/request rule 2 at spec.md:174, "the same `issuer` and the same payload".

(6) The ask "say that a refusal ... does not close the held exchange" is already in the spec at spec.md:175-176: "the held request is unaffected", stated for both cases.

The only thing left is the loose word "exchange" in the §4.4.1 table at SPEC.md:200, which makes this a note at most. || REFUTE: Counter-evidence, all read in the source (CONFIRMED):
(1) Errors and states are per document. SPEC.md:687: `errored` is terminal for the document, in the per-document lifecycle table. SPEC.md:1350: inResponseTo "names one instance where `threadId` names an exchange". SPEC.md:1467: "A `false` value of `retryable` represents a hard failure for that specific document… a new document… SHOULD carry the same `threadId`". next-step spec.md:73: "An error terminates the document under SPEC §8.4".
(2) The framework expects a thread to go on after an error. SPEC.md:492 (Example 4): after a proofRequired error, "any subsequent document in this exchange — for example, a retry with a fresh `id` and a valid `proof` — would carry the same `threadId`". If rule 5 were read thread-wide, a consumer could never hold that corrected document with a next step (for example, for consent). That would be absurd, so per-document is the reading the framework uses.
(3) The §8.6 sentence is narrow. At SPEC.md:1533, "an error closes the exchange" is the reason a consumer holding a task "MUST NOT answer [the held task] with … an error response whose … details says the task is held". grants/request never does that: it answers the held request and each matching resubmission with a next step.
(4) The interloper case is a separate exchange in the framework's terms. SPEC.md:780 (§4.13.3 rule 3): "Two producers whose exchanges share a `threadId` therefore hold two different exchanges". Also, SPEC.md:1338 sends the interloper's permissionDenied to the rejected document's own issuer, the interloper. The real client never sees it, so it has no reason to give up.
(5) The only error the real client can see is malformedRequest. It gets that only when it breaks step 2 itself by sending a different payload (spec.md:174, "the same payload"). It answers that client's new document, not the held request.
(6) The demo uses the same per-document model. examples/hcp-demo-ts/SCENARIO.md:131: "a further next step (same shape, `inResponseTo` the resubmission)". SCENARIO.md tests 9-10 (lines ~258-260): a malformedRequest on thread #3 is followed by a grant response on the same thread.
(7) The pinned framework 2a66a0351 has the same text: next-step 0.1 spec.md:85, SPEC.md:1348 and SPEC.md:1414.
What remains is only the wording "on the same thread" in rule 5. Read strictly, it suggests the whole thread. The fix belongs in the framework, not in the HCP suite.

findings.title: One fixed refusal text is compatible with how Keyring words failures
findings.claim: Keyring builds its sentences from codes and keeps the message behind Details, so a fixed permissionDenied text takes away nothing it relies on. The exception: refusedAsNotOnAcl reads the VTA's ACL wording ('DID not in ACL', 'ACL entry expired') from the message. On hcp/* refusals with a fixed text that test never fires, so 'this agent no longer accepts this phone' is detected only from Keyring's other tasks. At the pin, the VTA passes AppError text through as the message. Acting for the person, Keyring can re-read its own state (grants/list) to give a specific sentence.
findings.evidence: keyring vtiAgent.ts:384-389 "`code` ... belongs behind a Details control rather than in the sentence a person reads"; VtaClient.ts:859-862 NOT_ON_ACL regex on error.message; vti-common/src/acl/mod.rs:1370-1373 "DID not in ACL: {did}"; vta-service helpers.rs:153-158 message = err.to_string(); tt/specs/hcp/grants/request/0.1/spec.md:293 "Every `permissionDenied` carries the same fixed `message`"; demo.ts:112 NEUTRAL_DENIAL
findings.keyringImpact: Compatible as is. Keyring's hcp screens should not parse the message.
findings.corrected:
The claim holds with three corrections, and severity stays "ok" (or "note" because of the advice in point 2).

1. The suite does require one fixed text. Every hcp/* not-authorized refusal is a permissionDenied with one fixed message. That includes the tasks Keyring would send as Management Client, for example grants/revoke spec.md:171 and grants/list spec.md:228, not only grants/request:293, which is a Context Client task.

2. "The exception" is wrong. refusedAsNotOnAcl is not the only place Keyring reads the VTA's wording. deviceRefusalOf (vtaOwner.ts:173-245) picks its reason from the message: SELF_DELETE, ALREADY_EXISTS, 'auth:step_up_required' sent as the message, and, on permissionDenied, VTI-ACL-053 and VTI-ACL-107. ownExpiryFromRefusal (vtaOwner.ts:193-197) reads an expiry time out of a permissionDenied message. oobSignInAgent.ts:230 and 680 and vtaDevices.ts:279 also match codes inside the message. All of these are on acl/*, device/* and vault/* tasks, so a fixed hcp/* text takes away nothing Keyring relies on today. But Keyring's own pattern is to read the VTA's wording to tell permissionDenied cases apart. Its hcp/* screens must not copy that pattern; they should re-read state instead. Also, the cited vtiAgent.ts:384-389 says the CODE belongs behind Details. The support for "the agent's words are kept in Details" is vtaOwner.ts:142.

3. The detection gap only exists if the VTA scrubs its ACL refusal. At the VTI pin, the ACL refusal happens before the task is dispatched, for every task type: trust_tasks/mod.rs:1171-1177 sends `reason: e.to_string()`, which reads "forbidden: DID not in ACL: <did>". VTI's design (hcp.md:158 and §4.4) authenticates Keyring's hcp/* governance tasks through the ACL admin role. So "on hcp/* the test never fires" is true only if the VTA scrubs that early refusal for hcp/* types. The suite's "a caller that is not a Management Client" rule requires it, but the VTI design docs do not say they will. Until then, a phone dropped from the ACL would still get the ACL wording on hcp/* tasks.

Also, "passes AppError text through" is true for Forbidden and the other caller-fault cases (helpers.rs:154-157). It is not true of every error: internal errors and 502/504 are replaced with fixed text.
findings.reasons:
HOLDS: Every cited line exists and says what the claim says, on the right versions: the PR branch pr1382 at e163cac1d, the VTI pin f7b78e29d, and the Keyring d3-fast-send worktree.

- grants/request spec.md:293: "Every `permissionDenied` carries the same fixed `message`".
- demo.ts:112: NEUTRAL_DENIAL = "The request is not authorized."
- VtaClient.ts:859-860: the NOT_ON_ACL regex tested against error.message.
- acl/mod.rs:1370-1373: "ACL entry expired: {did}" and "DID not in ACL: {did}".
- helpers.rs:154-157: `let message = err.to_string()` becomes PermissionDenied { reason: message }.

The conclusion also holds. Keyring sends no hcp/* tasks today, so a fixed hcp/* text takes away nothing it relies on. Its device-action refusals do show plain words and keep the agent's own text in `detail` (vtaOwner.ts:142, 245).

Three parts are overstated or need a condition:

1. "The exception: refusedAsNotOnAcl" is false. Keyring reads the VTA's wording in several other places, including on permissionDenied (VTI-ACL-053, VTI-ACL-107, "your entry expires at", "cannot delete your own ACL entry"). Those are all on non-hcp tasks.
2. The vtiAgent.ts:384-389 quote is about the code going behind Details, not the message.
3. At the VTI pin, the "not in ACL" refusal is sent before dispatch for every task type (mod.rs:1171-1177). VTI hcp.md §4.4 routes Keyring's hcp/* governance tasks through the ACL, so refusedAsNotOnAcl would still fire on hcp/* unless the VTA scrubs that early refusal. The suite's not-authorized rule implies it must, but the VTI design does not say so.

None of this makes the "ok, compatible" verdict wrong, so the claim is not refuted. It needs the precise wording above.

findings.title: Nothing in the VTA stack at the pin emits or reads trust-task-next-step; the plugin's path needs it
findings.claim: At f7b78e29d there is no trust-task-next-step in vta-service, vta-sdk, vta-mcp or vti-common. vta-sdk's names_a_reply counts only #response and errors as replies, so a late next step would be dispatched as a request. vta-sdk's trust_task_error ignores an error with no message. vta-mcp maps every VtaError to an MCP internal_error with its text. HCP's hold needs a new emission path in the VTA and new handling in whatever our plugin uses.
findings.evidence: grep 'trust-task-next-step|NextStep|next_step' over vta-sdk/src vta-service/src vti-common/src vta-mcp/src → empty; vta-sdk/src/inbound.rs:131-140 names_a_reply; vta-sdk/src/client/mod.rs:2526-2528 "let message = payload.get(\"message\")?.as_str()?;"; vta-mcp/src/server.rs:87-90 "McpError::internal_error(e.to_string(), None)"
findings.keyringImpact: No effect on the Keyring app. Our plugin (vti-agent-connect over vta-mcp) cannot follow a hold until vta-sdk/vta-mcp handle next steps, or until the plugin handles them itself.
findings.askOfPR: VTI #2823: list next-step support in vta-sdk (reply classification, a resubmit helper on the same threadId, honouring hint.retryAfter) and in vta-mcp (how a hold reaches the host, not the model) as work items, or say the plugin does it without the sdk.
findings.corrected:
Severity should be "note", not "raise". The main fact holds: at f7b78e29d, nothing in the source of vta-service, vta-sdk, vta-mcp or vti-common emits or reads trust-task-next-step. Three of the supporting points need correcting.

(1) names_a_reply (vta-sdk/src/inbound.rs:135-140) is called by the servers that receive documents: vta-service/src/trust_tasks/mod.rs:1125-1127, vtc-service/src/messaging.rs:1341 and vti-witness. The vta-sdk client never calls it. So the point that a late next step would be dispatched as a request applies only when the VTA receives a next step. In HCP the VTA sends next steps and never receives one, so this is not on the plugin's path.

(2) A next step would not become a VtaError in vta-sdk. Its payload has `expects` and an optional `message`, and no `code`. trust_task_error (client/mod.rs:2527-2528) needs both `code` and `message`, so it returns None. extract_trust_task_payload then returns the next-step payload as a success, and nothing checks the reply's type. Over REST a 202 also counts as success. So through vta_call (vta-mcp/src/server.rs:882-906) a hold would reach the model as a successful tool result, not as internal_error. Separately, `message` is optional in every trust-task-error schema (only `code` and `retryable` are required). An error that leaves out `message` and arrives over TSP or DIDComm would therefore also be read as a success. That is a vta-sdk gap of its own, unrelated to holds.

(3) VTI #2823 already answers the ask. hcp-plan.md:116 gives "the hold and resubmit over TSP" to the TypeScript agent client (vti-agent-connect, B1-B4). A3 (hcp-tasks.md:110-119) is the VTA's emission work item. vta-mcp is changed only in H5/V3 (hcp.md:513, decision 13). Our companion (2026-11-25-bam.md:186) and plan line 675 (the plugin is built on @openvtc/trust-tasks in TypeScript) agree: the CLI/plugin sends grants/request over TSP itself, and vta-mcp is used only for vta/memory etc. At the pin those calls never hold, because the VTA's gates refuse (ApprovalRequired, auth:consent_required). VTI also already has a next-step emitter that A3 can follow: vtc-service helpers.rs:94-114 next_step_response, answered 202. It has a reader in vtc-client lib.rs:458 parked_from_next_step, and vti-trust-task-server's TrustTaskOutcome already carries a next-step body.

The only remaining ask is narrow, for V3: when H5 makes vta-mcp an HCP client, list next-step handling there. That means vta-sdk checking the reply type and resubmitting on the same threadId after hint.retryAfter, and vta-mcp passing a hold to the host rather than to the model as an ok result. | Severity should be note, not raise. The core fact holds at f7b78e29d: no source in vta-service, vta-sdk, vta-mcp or vti-common emits trust-task-next-step or classifies it. The impact and the ask are overstated, and one mechanism is misdescribed.

(1) The ask is already in VTI #2823.
- A3 lists the VTA's hold emission as a work item: hcp-tasks.md:110-112, "a held request answers `trust-task-next-step` with `continuation: resubmit`, never an error"; also hcp-plan.md:102.
- hcp-plan.md:116 puts "the hold and resubmit over TSP" in the TypeScript client `berkmancenter/vti-agent-connect` itself, not in vta-sdk or vta-mcp.
- Our own companion says the same: 2026-11-25-bam.md:240, "B2 | `grants/request` with hold and resubmit over TSP"; and :186, "The CLI sends the request over TSP".
- vta-mcp becomes an HCP client only at H5 (V3): hcp-plan.md:38, "H5: Agent Interop, MCP over Streamable HTTP from `vta-mcp`".
- So the V0 plugin's HCP path never goes through vta-sdk or vta-mcp.

(2) "A late next step would be dispatched as a request" does not apply to the plugin's path.
- `names_a_reply` is called only by server-side inbound dispatchers: vta-service/src/trust_tasks/mod.rs:1127, vtc-service/src/messaging.rs:1341 and vti-witness/src/dispatch.rs:268. The SDK client's receive path does not call it.
- On the client, an unmatched TSP frame is set aside as uncorrelated, not dispatched: vta-sdk/src/tsp_demux.rs:124-133.
- HCP's next step is the direct reply to each request or resubmission (grants/request spec.md:173), not a late message.

(3) What vta-sdk and vta-mcp actually do with an on-time next step: they pass it through as a success.
- `extract_trust_task_payload` returns `Ok(payload)`, because a next-step payload has no `code` (client/mod.rs:2492-2511).
- vtc-client already relies on this: vtc-client/src/lib.rs:1106-1107, "The session hands back the payload alone; a parked operation's is the next step's".
- So vta-mcp's `vta_call` would hand a hold to the model as a successful tool result (`ok_json`), not as an `internal_error`. `to_mcp` (server.rs:89-90) does map every VtaError to `internal_error`, but a next step is not a VtaError.

(4) A real SDK gap the claim misses.
- `build_task_document` never sets `threadId` (client/mod.rs:4203-4213).
- The TSP reply matcher accepts a reply only when its `threadId` equals the request's `id`: tsp_demux.rs:211, `doc.get("threadId")... == Some(request_id)`.
- Under SPEC §4.9 (SPEC.md:457), the reply to a resubmission carries the original thread's id, which is not the resubmission's own `id`.
- So vta-sdk can neither send a same-thread resubmission nor match its reply over TSP. This matters only for a Rust client or vta-mcp at H5.

(5) There is a working precedent to reuse.
- The VTC emits a 202 next step: vtc-service/src/trust_tasks/helpers.rs:99-110.
- vtc-client reads it: `parked_from_next_step`, lib.rs:458.
- The shared spine already expects next-step bodies: vti-trust-task-server/src/outcome.rs:24 and reject.rs:52-54.
- vti-specs/src/lib.rs:47 re-exports `trust_task_next_step` to vta-service and vta-sdk.

(6) The no-message sub-point holds and is slightly worse than stated.
- `message` is optional in trust-task-error 0.1-0.6 (required is only `code` and `retryable`).
- An error without a `message` is not just ignored: it is returned as a success payload.

Remaining ask, if any, for #2823's H5 row: next-step support in vta-sdk and vta-mcp, meaning reply classification, same-thread resubmission and TSP matching by thread.
findings.reasons:
HOLDS: The quotes are accurate and come from the right commit. The grep over the four crates' src is empty; the only mention is vti-common/CHANGELOG.md:2594, which is about the VTC. The conclusion that the plugin's hold path needs vta-sdk/vta-mcp support goes further than the evidence. names_a_reply sits on the VTA's inbound path, not the client's. A next step would come out of vta-sdk as an Ok payload, not as a VtaError, so to_mcp's internal_error is never reached. And both #2823 and our own plan put the hold and resubmit in the TypeScript agent client over TSP; vta-mcp changes only in V3. So the finding stands as a note about a gap that matters only in V3, plus a separate vta-sdk gap: an error document with no `message` is read as success. || HOLDS: The factual core is CONFIRMED: grepping the pinned clone (HEAD f7b78e29d) finds trust-task-next-step only in vtc-service, vtc-client, vti-specs (a re-export), vti-trust-task-server (comments only), docs and changelogs. Nothing turns up in the source of vta-service, vta-sdk, vta-mcp or vti-common.

Counter-evidence narrows the rest:
- VTI #2823 already lists the VTA's hold emission (A3).
- #2823 already gives hold and resubmit to the TypeScript agent client over TSP (hcp-plan.md:116, B1-B4), so the claim's alternative, "the plugin handles them itself", is already the design. Our own companion matches (B2).
- vta-mcp is an HCP client only at V3/H5.
- `names_a_reply` sits on server-side inbound paths, not the SDK client's receive path.
- An on-time next step passes through vta-sdk as a success payload, which vtc-client already depends on. Through vta-mcp it would therefore reach the model as success, not as an `internal_error`.

The claim also misses the sharper gap: the SDK cannot set `threadId`, and its TSP reply matching keys on the request's `id`, so a same-thread resubmission cannot work through vta-sdk. No ask to Brendan is needed for V0, so the severity drops from raise to note. The H5 work is the only place an ask remains.

findings.title: Keyring already answers task-consent request 0.1 with decision 0.2, after verification and an owner check
findings.claim: Keyring keeps task-consent/request/0.1 from its manager session. It shows a request only after checkConsentRequest passes: proof, authentication purpose, signer = issuer = the linked VTA, addressed to this phone, not expired. Approve requires the owner's biometric or passcode. The decision is sent as decision/0.2 with a step-down to 0.1. These are the versions VTI #2823 names. The vtaAgent comment calling requestCheck 'log-only' is out of date: the code does gate display.
findings.evidence: keyring VtaClient.ts:175-178 consentRequest 0.1, consentDecision02; :260 consentDecision ladder; :2165-2183 decideConsent; vtaAgent.ts:576-585 keepManagerMessage; :3886-3955 listIfChecked/passesCheck "A request that does not pass is not shown"; :3978 confirmOwner(APPROVE_REASON); consentCheck.ts:82-104; vti2823 hcp.md:26-27, 547
findings.keyringImpact: Compatible as is for the approve-as-asked V0 flow.
findings.corrected:
Mostly holds, and severity "ok" stands for the consent wire path. Keyring keeps task-consent/request/0.1 messages from its manager session (vtaAgent.ts:576). It lists one only after checkConsentRequest passes, which checks the type, the proof, the 'authentication' purpose, that the signer is the issuer, the expected issuer, that the recipient is this phone's managerDid, and that it has not expired (consentCheck.ts:82-104; vtaAgent.ts:3895-3896 "if (!ok || ...) return"). The comment at vtaAgent.ts:155-156 that calls requestCheck log-only is out of date.

Two corrections:

findings.title: Keyring shows effects[].summary only; an HCP checklist from detail needs published kinds and must keep summary verbatim
findings.claim: consentOutcome turns each effect into its summary (or its kind), and nothing reads detail. VTI writes 'one effect per item' for the HCP 6.1.6 checklist, with an open kind and a free detail, but no document names those kinds or detail shapes. The shared Effect schema requires a surface to render summary verbatim and never substitute its own prose. Our plan's C1 renders rows 'from the effects' detail' with Keyring copy, which is allowed only beside the summaries.
findings.evidence: keyring consentCheck.ts:47-62 "text((e as Record<string, unknown>).summary) || text(...kind)"; tt/specs/task-consent/_shared/0.1/task-consent.schema.json:12 required [kind, summary], :19-23 "A surface MUST render it verbatim; it MUST NOT substitute its own prose."; vti2823 hcp.md:263-270; agent-connect-plan/2026-11-25-bam.md:251 C1
findings.keyringImpact: Needs work in Keyring (C1): render the checklist from detail while still showing each summary verbatim.
findings.askOfPR: VTI #2823: publish the effect kind values and detail shapes for the HCP 6.1.6 items (categories with descriptions, actions, purposes, longest useUntil, temporary or persistent, expiry, client and operator, directives claim, provenance, onward sharing).
findings.corrected: The claim holds, severity raise, but it needs three corrections. (1) It is not an interop gap. HCP 6.1.6 only requires that the person "MUST be told" each item. If the VTA writes one effect per item, each with its own executor-written summary, today's Keyring already tells the person every item: consentOutcome keeps each summary, and ApprovalDetails shows each one as a bullet under "would do". Published kinds and detail shapes are needed only because plan C1 chose to build a structured checklist from detail. The detail is already kept on the approval record (keepManagerMessage spreads ...body.payload), so C1 is rendering work only. (2) The rule should be stated more exactly. Every effects[].summary must be shown verbatim, including for kinds Keyring does not know (request spec consumer rule 3). Keyring MAY add structured rows for kinds it knows, so C1's Keyring-worded rows (companion :199) must sit beside the summaries, never replace them. Companion :447 says C1 "adds" the display, which fits that, but the :199 copy lists no summaries. (3) The ask's item list is incomplete. HCP 6.1.6 and hcp/grants/request:87 also require: the Requesting Party where it differs from the person, any declared legal-retention record, and any standing rule that excludes a requested category. VTI hcp.md:265-268 is missing those three, and provenance and onward sharing too. Further support for the ask: VTI's own phone approver (vta-mobile-core consent.rs parse_effect) drops detail entirely. The template producer (remote_approval) uses a kind, signIn, and a detail shape {origin, device, notAfter} that exist only in code. The schema says well-known kinds are "registered in the prose", but task-consent/request has no such list, only examples. So the ask should also say that every item must be fully stated in its summary.
findings.reasons:
HOLDS: I could not refute it. Every cited source says what the claim says.

No code in trust-tasks reads an effect's `detail`. vtaAgent.ts:579 does keep the raw payload in the stored approval through `...body.payload`, but nothing renders `detail` from it. The only change Keyring makes to a summary is `.trim()`, which does not matter here.

2. The schema: task-consent.schema.json:12 requires `["kind","summary"]`. Lines 19-23 say "A surface MUST render it verbatim; it MUST NOT substitute its own prose." This text is the same on pr1382 and at our pin 2a66a0351.

3. The task-consent request spec supports the claim more directly than the schema does. It is not cited in the claim. specs/task-consent/request/0.1/spec.md:151 (consumer rule 3) says: "Render every `effects[].summary` verbatim, including for a `kind` it does not recognise. 4. VTI #2823: hcp.md:264-270 says "the shared `Effect` has an open `kind`, a `summary` and a free `detail`, so the VTA writes one effect per item". The text starts at :264; :263 is blank. Grepping hcp.md, hcp-plan.md, hcp-tasks.md and tasks/hcp-demo-plan.md finds no kind values and no detail shapes. The HCP specs in the suite define none either. At the VTI pin, vti-common/src/task_consent/effects.rs:31-41 keeps `kind` as an open string and `detail` as a free map.

5. Our plan: companion :251 C1 says "the C4 checklist rendered row by row from the effects' `detail`". The Keyring wording comes from finding 6's approve copy at about :198 ("Run by <Client Operator>.", "It can read <categories> to <purpose descriptions>."), not from C1 itself. Nowhere does the plan say the verbatim summaries are still shown. Companion :447 already says "Keyring today renders `effects[].summary` only, so C1 adds the structured checklist display over `detail`". So the work is already planned; what the plan is missing is the verbatim-summary rule and the dependency on published kinds.

6. The ask can be completed. HCP 6.1.6 (specification.md:1597) also lists the Requesting Party where it differs from the Context Subject, the record kept under a legal obligation, and standing-rule exclusions. The proposed list leaves out all three, and VTI's own list in hcp.md also leaves out provenance and onward sharing.

"raise" is the right severity: this is a clarification to ask of VTI #2823, and nothing here breaks interop. || HOLDS: Each part of the claim checks out in source. consentOutcome maps each effect to summary || kind, and nothing in Keyring reads detail. The only caller is vtaAgent.ts:584, and ApprovalDetails.tsx:88-92 shows only outcome.lines. VTI's design writes one effect per item but names no kinds and no detail shapes. findings.title: task-consent/request 0.1 has no place for the held request's threadId, so the scan match cannot be done
findings.claim: VTI #2823 says Keyring shows the checklist only if the client VID and the threadId match what it scanned. task-consent/request 0.1 carries requester (the client VID) but no member for the held hcp/grants/request's threadId. Keyring also keeps only body.payload, not the document's threadId or parentThreadId. The design does not say where the threadId travels.
findings.evidence: vti2823 hcp.md:159 "Keyring accepts it only for the VID and `threadId` it scanned", :290; hcp-plan.md:257; tt/specs/task-consent/request/0.1/payload.schema.json required [challenge, taskType, payloadDigest, sideEffects, exposure, effects, requester, approverSet, minApprovals, excludeRequester, expiresAt]; keyring vtaAgent.ts:576-585 "...body.payload"
findings.keyringImpact: Needs work in Keyring: keep the field once it is defined, and match it against the scan.
findings.askOfPR: VTI #2823: say where the held request's threadId goes in the consent request. parentThreadId (SPEC §4.9.2) set to the held thread is one option, a named effect detail another. Say also whether requester is always the client VID.
findings.corrected:
Holds, at severity "raise". One wording fix: the title says the request "has no place" for the held threadId, which is too strong. The accurate version: task-consent/request 0.1 has no payload member for it. Its payload sets additionalProperties:false and lists no thread member. It leaves the framework's document-level parentThreadId (SPEC §4.9.2, present at both our pin 2a66a0351 and the PR) and an Effect's free `detail` as carriers, but neither the task-consent spec nor VTI #2823 says which one carries the held hcp/grants/request's threadId. The framework narrows the choice. SPEC §13.1 item 2 says "A producer MUST NOT carry a threadId across exchanges that are not one exchange", so the VTA cannot reuse the held threadId as the consent request's own threadId. parentThreadId is the framework's sanctioned option. At the VTI pin f7b78e29d, the consent request document carries no threadId or parentThreadId at all, and PendingTaskConsent has no field for one, so the VTA needs a new field as well as a spec or design statement. VTI hcp-plan.md:189 lists "the approval document layout (A3 with C1)" as an interface contract still to agree. That makes this an open item the plan already names, not an oversight. The ask should be "settle it in that contract". Keyring's keepManagerMessage keeps body.payload plus the document id and drops threadId and parentThreadId. At the VTA pin, requester is the submitting party's DID (requester_did), so in the HCP case it would be the issuer of hcp/grants/request, which is the client VID. The design does not say this in so many words. | The core of the claim holds, but two parts go too far. Severity stays "raise", aimed at the approval document layout that VTI A3 and Keyring C1 still have to agree (hcp-plan.md:189).

What holds: VTI #2823 has Keyring show the checklist only when the client VID and the threadId match the scan (hcp.md:159, :290; hcp-plan.md:257). It never says how the held hcp/grants/request's threadId reaches Keyring. task-consent/request 0.1 has no named member for it. Today's VTA producer sets neither threadId nor parentThreadId on the request (consent_request.rs:111-118). The remote_approval pattern that A3 copies mints a fresh, unrelated correlator (oob_sign_in.rs:1135). So reusing that producer will not carry the held thread by default.

What goes too far, part 1: "has no place for it" is wrong. Three existing places work with no schema change:
- the document-level parentThreadId. Framework SPEC §4.9.2 (SPEC.md:512) says a producer working inside an enclosing exchange SHOULD set it to that exchange's threadId.
- the payload's `ext` (payload.schema.json:99).
- an Effect's open `detail` (task-consent.schema.json:35).

The consent request's own threadId cannot be the held thread: SPEC §13.1 item 2 (SPEC.md:1886) says a producer MUST NOT carry a threadId across exchanges that are not one exchange. Also, the plan already lists "the approval document layout (A3 with C1)" as an open contract between VTI and Keyring (hcp-plan.md:189). Our own companion already suggests "the threadId in an effect or `ext`" (2026-11-25-bam.md:186). So this is an open joint decision, not a gap nobody has noticed.

What goes too far, part 2: the Keyring impact. keepManagerMessage spreads all of body.payload (vtaAgent.ts:579), and VtaConsentRequest has a `[key: string]: unknown` index signature (VtaClient.ts:381-396). So if the threadId goes in payload `ext` or an effect's `detail`, Keyring already keeps it. Only the parentThreadId option means also keeping a document-level member, which Keyring drops today. Matching against the scan is new Keyring work whichever option is chosen.

The ask should be: VTI #2823 names the carriage in the A3/C1 layout. parentThreadId is the framework's own route; `ext` is the payload-level alternative. It should also say that requester is always the client VID (issuer), which the design implies but never states.
findings.reasons:
HOLDS: Every cited quote reads as the claim says, on the right branch.

**VTI #2823 design docs**
- hcp.md:159 says Keyring "accepts it only for the VID and `threadId` it scanned".
- hcp.md:290 says "checklist, if the VID and threadId match the scan".
- hcp-plan.md:257 says "for the VID and `threadId` it scanned".
- hcp.md:264-269 says the HCP 6.1.6 items go in effects. It never says where the held threadId goes.

**task-consent/request schema**
- On pr1382 the schema has the required list as quoted, with additionalProperties:false and no thread member.
- It is unchanged between pin 2a66a0351, pr1382 and pr1381.
- Neither the request spec.md nor the specs/hcp files mention parentThreadId or the link to task-consent.

**VTA source at f7b78e29d**
- consent_request.rs:111-118 builds the signed request document with only id, type, issuer, recipient, issuedAt and payload: no threadId or parentThreadId.
- oob_sign_in.rs:1132-1150 shows PendingTaskConsent has only a VTA-minted `correlator` and requester_did = the submitting device. There is no field for an enclosing thread.

**Keyring**

- VtaConsentRequest (VtaClient.ts:381-396) has no thread field.

**What tempers the claim**
- "No place" is too strong, because the framework's parentThreadId (SPEC.md:508-514) and the Effect `detail` exist.
- SPEC.md §13.1 item 2 rules out reusing the held threadId as the consent request's own threadId, which points to parentThreadId.
- hcp-plan.md:189 already defers "the approval document layout (A3 with C1)" to an interface contract, so the gap is acknowledged as open.

Severity "raise" is right: interop is not broken yet, but the stated anti-spoofing check cannot be built until the field is defined. || HOLDS: I looked for counter-evidence and found nothing that defeats the main claim. The VTI design docs never say where the held threadId travels. The only threadId lines are hcp.md:159, :283, :290, :294, :304, :312, :529, plus hcp-plan.md:102 and :257. hcp-tasks.md A3 (lines 110-118) is silent too. The task-consent/request 0.1 payload has no threadId member. The pinned VTA producer sets no thread link: mint_signed_requests builds the document with only id, type, issuer, recipient, issuedAt and payload. The remote_approval producer gives the pending consent a fresh `correlator: format!("urn:uuid:{}", ...)`, which by design (vti-common task_consent mod.rs:188-206) is never derived from anything outside. The hcp/grants/request spec in the PR leaves how the person is asked to the provider and defines no carriage. Keyring's keepManagerMessage does drop the document-level members.

Two things narrow the claim.
1. "No place" is overstated. The framework (at our pin 2a66a0351 and on the PR branch) defines parentThreadId with a SHOULD for documents inside an enclosing exchange. The consent payload allows `ext`, and an Effect allows an open `detail`. findings.title: decision/0.2 cannot carry a narrower approval or a chosen purpose
findings.claim: task-consent/decision/0.2 is {challenge, payloadDigest, decision, reason?, actionId?, evidence?, ext?} with additionalProperties false, and the digest binds the payload as asked. HCP 6.1.5.2 says the provider MUST ask the person to choose purposes when the request names none. grants/request's own example has the person approve fewer categories than asked. Neither can come back through a decision. VTI A3 mentions 'a purpose choice where none was named' but gives no wire form. V0 works, because the client names its purposes and the person approves as asked.
findings.evidence: tt/specs/task-consent/decision/0.2/payload.schema.json required [challenge, payloadDigest, decision], additionalProperties false; hcp-spec specification.md:1584 "Where a grant request names no purpose, the Authorization Service MUST ask the Authorizing Principal to choose one or more"; tt/specs/hcp/grants/request/0.1/spec.md:126, :279 "the person approved `travel_preferences` and not `general_preferences`"; vti2823 hcp-tasks.md:113-115
findings.keyringImpact: Keyring cannot send a narrowed or purpose-choosing approval through decision 0.2. That needs a spec change, then Keyring work. It blocks only requests that name no purpose, or a person who wants to narrow.
findings.askOfPR: VTI #2823 / Brendan: how does the person's choice (purposes, fewer categories, shorter duration, later persistence) reach the VTA? Options: an ext namespace on decision, a new decision version, or a consent request per option set. Until then, refuse grant requests that name no purpose.
findings.corrected:
The claim holds and "raise" is the right severity. Three points need sharpening. (1) "Cannot carry" is slightly too strong. decision/0.2 has no defined member for a choice: `decision` is only `approve` or `deny`, and the spec says "most of the payload is not the approver's to choose". But the schema does allow an open `ext` member with reverse-DNS namespaces. So a namespace agreed between the VTA and Keyring could carry the choice without changing the task-consent spec. The catch is that decision/0.2 does not allow `extCritical`, so its schema rejects that member. A VTA that does not recognise the namespace must therefore ignore it, and could silently issue the wider grant as asked. That is only safe if the VTA, as local policy, requires the namespace (SPEC.md:1188). A defined member or a new decision version is the safer fix. (2) The gap comes from VTI #2823's choice of task-consent as the consent channel (hcp.md decision 3, §5.1; and hcp.md:177-178, "A request may name none; the person is then asked to choose", with no wire form given). It does not come from PR #1380. That PR's grants/request leaves the method of asking the person to the provider ("through the provider's own modality … a management app, a web page, a message", spec.md:87). The ask belongs with VTI #2823 / Brendan, which the claim already says. (3) The payloadDigest is not itself the obstacle. It binds the grants/request payload that the client resubmits unchanged, so a narrowed grant does not break it. What is missing is a way back for the person's choice. Keyring today sends only {challenge, payloadDigest, decision, reason?}. | Severity stays "raise", but the claim needs narrowing. decision/0.2 has no typed member for the person's choice. Its schema allows only challenge, payloadDigest, decision, reason, actionId, evidence and ext, with additionalProperties false. VTI A3 also gives no wire form for "a purpose choice where none was named". That much holds.

Three parts are overstated:

(1) "Neither can come back through a decision" is too strong. decision/0.2 allows `ext`, which SPEC §4.5.1 makes the framework's sanctioned extension point. The proof covers it, and a consumer MAY require its own namespace. VTI already moves ecosystem-local narrowing in an ext namespace (`org.openvtc.capabilities` on acl/*). So a VTI-defined namespace could carry the chosen purposes, categories or duration today, with no trust-tasks spec change.

The real defect is that this fails open. decision/0.2 does not allow `extCritical`, so Keyring cannot mark the namespace critical. Under rule 5 a VTA that does not know the namespace ignores it, and it would then issue the full grant as asked. The pinned VTA's decision handler (task_consent.rs at f7b78e29d) never reads `payload.ext`. An ext route therefore needs discovery or version gating first. A safe, interoperable form needs decision 0.3 or extCritical on decision.

(2) "Needs a spec change" is too strong for the same reason, and there is a second route with no spec change. The VTA's remote_approval template binds a consent to a payload the VTA builds itself (oob_sign_in.rs:1085), not only to the request as asked. So the VTA can mint one binary consent per option. VTI configures exactly two purposes, so one consent per purpose meets HCP 6.1.5.2 with decision/0.2 unchanged.

Persistence and onward sharing are not choices to carry in the first decision at all. HCP 6.1.4 says "A single act MUST NOT both authorize access and elect persistence" (spec:1464), and onward sharing must also be its own later act (spec:1473). Each is naturally a second binary consent. Only onward sharing's `domains` limit and category or duration narrowing truly need data. Narrowing is a MAY (grants/request:128, :222), not an HCP requirement.

(3) The interim "refuse grant requests that name no purpose" conflicts with grants/request/0.1:126: "A detail that names no `purposes` is allowed: the provider MUST then ask the person to choose." Two conformant interims exist: one consent per configured purpose, or a declared VTA deviation.

The ask to VTI #2823 stands: say which route carries the person's choice.
findings.reasons:
HOLDS: All four cited sources say what the claim says, on the right versions.
- decision/0.2 is the same on pr1382, pr1380 and our pin 2a66a0351: additionalProperties false, required [challenge, payloadDigest, decision]. Decision is "enum": ["approve", "deny"] (task-consent/_shared/0.1). decision/0.2/spec.md:298 says "most of the payload is not the approver's to choose … `decision` is a two-valued enum".
- HCP b790561 specification.md:1584 reads exactly "Where a grant request names no purpose, the Authorization Service MUST ask the Authorizing Principal to choose one or more before approving."
- In hcp/grants/request/0.1/spec.md, :126 allows a detail with no purposes. :128 says "the person MAY choose less" on duration. :127 makes persistence a separate act. :222 says "its `access` may be narrower than asked". :279 says "the person approved `travel_preferences` and not `general_preferences`".
- VTI hcp-tasks.md:113-115 (A3) binds the pending task-consent/request "with the HCP 6.1.6 items as effects (or a purpose choice where none was named)", with no wire form. hcp.md:177-178 commits to "the person is then asked to choose". hcp.md §5.1/§5.2 and decision 3 route every approval through task-consent/decision.
- V0 works as claimed: the demo plan step 4 has the person approve the checklist with a biometric, and the demo client names its purposes.
I tried to refute it and could not. The two ways out I checked are the open `ext` slot on decision/0.2 (SPEC.md §4.5.1) and the open `detail` on Effect. `detail` can show options, but `ext` is the only way back. It is ignorable and cannot be marked critical at that level, so it is not a safe channel for a narrowing unless the VTA requires the namespace. That supports the raise rather than refuting it, and only softens "needs a spec change". || HOLDS: I tried to disprove it. The core holds: decision/0.2 has no member for the choice; additionalProperties is false. HCP 6.1.5.2 MUST is real (spec:1584). The grants/request example narrows (:279). VTI A3 says nothing on the wire form (hcp-tasks.md:113-115). The trust-tasks HCP suite leaves the consent channel to the provider ("The person reaches the decision through the provider's own modality", grants/request:87), so the gap is in VTI's design, as the claim says.

Counter-evidence that narrows the claim:
- decision/0.2 has `ext` (schema:36-38). SPEC.md:247 says a consumer MUST ignore namespaces it does not recognize. SPEC.md:252 says "A `proof` covers `ext`". So ext is a working carrier, but it fails open. There is no `extCritical` in decision/0.2. The pinned VTA's task_consent.rs never reads ext (grep empty).
- The precedent is VtaClient.ts:484-491: "The narrowing rides `ext` because the published `acl/*` schemas are `additionalProperties: false`".
- The VTA's remote_approval binds a consent to its own task_payload (oob_sign_in.rs:1085), so per-option consents are possible with no spec change.
- HCP 6.1.4 requires persistence and onward sharing as separate acts (spec:1464, :1473), so a later binary consent fits them.
- grants/request:126 says a request with no purposes "is allowed", which makes the proposed "refuse" interim non-conformant.

None of this makes the finding wrong. It is overstated on "cannot", "needs a spec change", "later persistence" and the interim. Severity "raise" is right.

findings.title: Management tasks' schemas require accessToken, but VTI #2823 has Keyring hold no token
findings.claim: The payload schemas of hcp/grants/revoke, audit/read, disclosures/summary, entries/create and grants/list list accessToken as required. VTI #2823 §4.4 has Keyring authenticate as the admin DID with no token in V0. A token-less request from Keyring would fail the schema with malformedRequest, which the TS pipeline sends unsigned and the VTA signed. This overlaps with the auth track.
findings.evidence: tt/specs/hcp/grants/revoke/0.1/payload.schema.json required ['grantId','accessToken'] (and the same for audit/read, disclosures/summary, entries/create, grants/list); vti2823 hcp.md:158 "no token (§4.4)", :229-239
findings.keyringImpact: Keyring must send some accessToken, or the VTA must take a token-less V0 form.
findings.askOfPR: VTI #2823: say what Keyring puts in accessToken in V0 (for example a placeholder the VTA ignores for an admin-DID sender), or relax the schemas.
findings.corrected: The claim holds, but the severity should be "raise", not "note", and the list of tasks is one too long. On all three branches (pr1380, pr1381, pr1382), the payload schemas of hcp/grants/revoke, audit/read, disclosures/summary and entries/create require accessToken. Each has additionalProperties:false and an accessToken of minLength 1. VTI #2823 §4.4 (hcp.md:230-239) says Keyring sends those four V0 governance tasks as the admin DID, with no token. A request without a token fails payload validation, and SPEC §8.3 answers that with malformedRequest. The TS library builds that error unsigned. The VTA signs every response, errors included. #2823 never says what Keyring puts in accessToken. Its §12 divergence row ("Management by DID-proven request, not an HCP token (V0)") names only HCP 1.6 and 5.4. It does not name the suite's own required accessToken. hcp/grants/list should come off the list of affected tasks: its schema does require accessToken, but VTI plans it for V2 (hcp-plan.md:145), after V1's management tokens (hcp-plan.md:132), so it has no V0 conflict. The placeholder idea in the ask conflicts with the suite spec. The spec says the provider "validates it exactly as over HCP's HTTP binding". It also refuses a token issued to a client other than the issuer VID with permissionDenied (revoke spec.md:87, :227). So a placeholder that the VTA ignores would also have to be recorded as a divergence from the suite spec. Severity is "raise": the finding asks something of #2823, and the V0 design cannot work as written. It is not a blocker, because the design is docs-only and V1 brings real management tokens.
findings.reasons: HOLDS: Every quote cited says what the claim says, on the right branch. tt is on pr1382; tt-drift (pr1380) and git show pr1381 return the same required lists. The supporting points also hold. SPEC.md:1417 maps a payload-schema failure to malformedRequest. The TS demo lists malformedRequest among the errors the library builds unsigned (SCENARIO.md:176-179, demo.ts:465-468: "The library builds those error responses itself, unsigned"). The VTA pin f7b78e29d signs error responses too (vta-service/src/trust_tasks/mod.rs:694: "Every response document — success **and** `trust-task-error` — is signed"). The only searches of #2823 for accessToken find the accessTokenDigest line (hcp.md:162). Nothing says what Keyring sends. Two points are overstated. First, grants/list is not one of the four V0 tasks in §4.4 (hcp.md:232-233). It is V2 in hcp-plan.md:145, by which time management tokens exist. Second, the severity: a "note" carries no ask, but this finding has one, and the V0 path fails as designed, so "raise" fits. One more point the finding misses: the spec says the provider validates the token exactly as over HCP's HTTP binding, so the placeholder option needs its own recorded divergence from the suite spec.

findings.title: hcp:credentialInvalid puts 'which check failed' in free-text message
findings.claim: HCP 5.5 has the detail name which check failed (proof, securing mechanism, verification method or status). The suite puts that in message with no details schema. A client then has to parse prose. Framework §8.2.1 item 3 bars 'the reason a signature failed beyond the fact that it did', which naming a public category arguably still meets. A details member would carry it cleanly.
findings.evidence: tt/specs/hcp/entries/create/0.1/spec.md:65-69 "The `message` says which, and reveals no status-list internals."; tt/SPEC.md:1397 item 3; hcp-spec specification.md:1405 credential-invalid row
findings.keyringImpact: None in V0: Keyring creates person-declared entries with no credential content.
findings.askOfPR: Optional: declare a detailsSchema for hcp:credentialInvalid, e.g. {check: proof|securingMechanism|verificationMethod|status}, and keep the message fixed.
findings.corrected: The finding holds, at severity note, but it needs to be stated more precisely. (1) The free-text problem comes from HCP, not from the suite. HCP's Core error object has only two members, `type` and a human-readable `detail` (specification.md:1394). Both bindings carry "which check" in that prose: the HTTP problem `detail` (:2421) and the MCP `structuredContent.detail` (:2731-2745). So `hcp:credentialInvalid` putting it in `message` is a faithful mapping, and a `details` member would add structure that HCP itself does not have. (2) Citation fixes: the HCP row is at specification.md:1403, not :1405. The more specific rule is at HCP 14.6, specification.md:3133: "The error's detail names which, and does not reveal the credential's position in a status list." The suite's own error-table row is at entries/create spec.md:241. The same pattern is in entries/revise spec.md:74 and :256, which the finding does not mention. (3) The tension with SPEC §8.2.1 is uneven across the four checks. Naming proof, mechanism or status as a public category fits :1399 ("derived from the code identifier and from the ... public vocabulary"). But HCP's verification-method case is "the verification method cannot be obtained" (:3133), which is a resolver outcome. §8.2.1's rationale (:1401) names "which identifiers it can resolve, and which of its dependencies are currently reachable" as exactly the oracle it guards against. HCP limits who can trigger this: a credential write is accepted only from a client authenticated as the issuer or authorized by it (:1224, :3139). Neither HCP nor the suite says that check runs before credential verification. (4) If a details schema is added, §8.5 requires naming the code and giving a JSON Schema fragment, and §8.2.2 (tt/SPEC.md:1407) requires declaring a bound. No `hcp/*` spec on pr1382 defines a `details` shape for any code; grep found none.
findings.reasons: HOLDS: The cited quotes say what the finding says, on the right branch. tt is on pr1382, and pr1381 has the same text at create spec.md:65-69 and :302. The quote at entries/create spec.md:65-69 is exact. The quote at SPEC.md:1397 item 3 is exact, and the same text is on our pin 2a66a0351 at SPEC.md:1278. HCP 5.5 does say the detail names which check failed. The suite defines no details schema, so a client has to read prose to tell which check failed. Severity note fits: V0 Keyring writes only person-declared entries, and the ask is optional. What the finding leaves out: HCP itself carries this only as free text, so the suite inherits the problem rather than creating it. Also, one of the four HCP checks, verification method not obtainable, sits closer to §8.2.1's resolver and reachability concern than "arguably still meets" suggests. The HCP line number is off by two.

findings.title: Connect: the person's approval is not a Trust Task in the suite
findings.claim: hcp/grants/request names only the Context Client and the Provider; the person's decision happens through 'the provider's own modality' and is never a document in the hcp/* family. A ceremony built from hcp/* tasks alone therefore has no step for the person's affirmative act (HCP 6.1.6), and must borrow task-consent/request + decision from outside the family.
findings.evidence: specs/hcp/grants/request/0.1/spec.md:87 "The person reaches the decision through the provider's own modality, never through the client: a management app, a web page, a message"; :180 "The person's decision never travels through the client"; :10-16 parties = Context Client, HCP Provider only; examples/hcp-demo-ts/SCENARIO.md:195 and transcript.golden.txt:123 "[person] approves the grant request on thread <#3> in the provider's app"; design note docs/design-notes/trust-ceremonies.md:520-525 (each step's issuer must know its turn 'from a document it received')
findings.keyringImpact: Keyring is the approver. VTI #2823 and our plan already use task-consent/request/0.1 + decision/0.2 for this leg, so the leg exists in practice, but the HCP suite says nothing about it, so nothing ties that choice to the grant request.
findings.askOfPR: Add a short paragraph to hcp/grants/request: where the provider asks the person through a Trust Task exchange (task-consent/request and decision being one way, not a requirement), say how that exchange relates to the hold (see the next finding).
findings.corrected:
The facts hold, but two parts are overstated, and the severity should be "note" (at most an optional, informative ask folded into the hold finding). What holds: on pr1382, hcp/grants/request names only two parties, the Context Client as issuer and the Provider as recipient (spec.md:10-16, :113-118). The person decides "through the provider's own modality, never through the client: a management app, a web page, a message" (:87). "The person's decision never travels through the client" (:180). No hcp/* spec mentions task-consent. The demo's approval is a printed line with no document (SCENARIO.md:195, transcript.golden.txt:123). The silence is deliberate and follows HCP: HCP 6.1.7 and 12.2 say "This specification does not mandate a wire-level request format", and the spec lists "The person's affirmative act" under "What HCP requires that a document cannot express" (:328-330). An hcp/* approval task would define an operation HCP does not define, which is the same reason grants/request declares no `carries` (:65).

Overstated (1): "must borrow task-consent". A ceremony built only from hcp/grants/request, with roles Context Client and Provider, passes design note §6.4 (trust-ceremonies.md:520-525). Each issuer learns its turn from a document it received: request, then next step, then resubmit, then response. The person's decision is the provider's own state and only decides which reply it sends. The person's act becomes a step only when the provider's modality is itself a Trust Task exchange with a separate party, as with VTA and Keyring. Even then task-consent is one choice, not a requirement. Mixing task families in one ceremony is normal: identity-vetting uses vetting/* together with credential-exchange/issue.

Overstated (2): the Keyring impact says "nothing ties that choice to the grant request". VTI #2823 does tie it on the provider side. hcp-tasks.md:110-116 (A3) says "the pending task-consent/request is bound to the request's digest and to the admin DID". hcp.md:159 says "Keyring accepts it only for the VID and threadId it scanned". What is missing is only a public, suite-level description of that pairing.

Interop does not break: the Context Client never sees this leg. | The facts hold, but two parts of the claim go too far, and the severity should drop from raise to note. Holds: hcp/grants/request names only the Context Client and the Provider, and no hcp/* task carries the person's approval. The spec says this outright at specs/hcp/grants/request/0.1/spec.md:328-330 ("What HCP requires that a document cannot express ... The person's affirmative act"). This matches HCP itself. HCP defines no approve operation: 6.1.7 and 12.2 say HCP "does not mandate a wire-level request format" and require only the outcome. The 9.2 endpoint table has no approval endpoint either. So a carried approval task could not exist. Overstated (1): a ceremony built from hcp/* tasks alone does not have to borrow task-consent. The framework lets the person's act happen outside any task: SPEC.md:1536, a third party's act with continuation: resubmit when the provider offers no task for it. That ceremony is still well-formed, because the client learns its turn from the next step it received (trust-ceremonies.md:520). The person can be declared an evidentiary role with no step (trust-ceremonies.md:421). Composing tasks across families is how ceremonies are meant to work (trust-ceremonies.md:92). task-consent is needed only if the act should be a signed document, which is what Keyring and VTI want. HCP 6.1.6 does not require it. Overstated (2): "nothing ties that choice to the grant request" is wrong. The framework ties any decision to a held exchange: SPEC.md:779, §4.13.3 rule 2 (normative, framework 0.6.0, already on upstream main, not added by this PR). It says a consumer "MUST NOT accept a decision as the answer to a referral unless the decision identifies the held exchange and its verified issuer is a party the referral named", on the terms of rule 3 (SPEC.md:780): carry the held threadId, or run a nested exchange whose parentThreadId names the held thread. task-consent/request also binds to the pending task through taskType, payloadDigest and requester (task-consent/request/0.1/spec.md:185-192). Because resubmissions repeat the same payload (grants/request:174), the digest still matches. A short paragraph in hcp/grants/request would still be welcome, but nothing breaks without it, so it is a note. What is left is a check on our side, not on the PR: VTI #2823 and our companion plan (2026-11-25-bam.md:186) put the held threadId "in an effect or ext". Under framework 0.6.0 rules 2 and 3, the task-consent exchange should instead carry parentThreadId naming the held grants/request thread. Our pinned framework 2a66a0351 does not have rule 2 yet.
findings.reasons: HOLDS: Every quote checks out on pr1382: parties at :10-16 and :113-118, "provider's own modality" at :87, "never travels through the client" at :180, SCENARIO.md:195, transcript.golden.txt:123, and design note :520-525. The suite (pr1381 included) never mentions task-consent, so the core observation stands. It is overstated in two places. First, the ceremony meta-schema allows only step kinds task and ceremony, but a ceremony over grants/request alone is still well-formed under §6.4, so borrowing task-consent is needed only for the VTA-to-Keyring design, not for every ceremony. Second, VTI #2823 already binds the consent request to the held request's digest and threadId. HCP itself leaves the approval channel to the provider with no wire format, and the PR says on purpose that a document cannot express the affirmative act. So asking for a new task would conflict with HCP, an informative paragraph is the most to ask for, and interop does not break. Severity "note" fits better than "raise". || HOLDS: I did not find a task in the suite, or a later section, that carries the person's decision. I also found no HCP operation the suite left out: HCP defines none, so the core claim stands (CONFIRMED). Searching independently turned up three things that narrow it. (a) SPEC §8.6's third-party case lets the act happen with no task at all. (b) The ceremony design note's evidentiary-role and composition rules mean an hcp/*-only ceremony is well-formed without a person step. (c) SPEC §4.13.3 rules 2-3 (framework 0.6.0, upstream main) already require any approver's decision to identify the held exchange, by threadId or parentThreadId, and to come from a party the referral named. task-consent/request binds to the held task by taskType, payloadDigest and requester. So "must borrow" and "nothing ties" are both overstated, and the ask is a clarity improvement, not an interop problem: severity note. What is left points at VTI #2823 and our plan, which carry the held threadId in an effect or ext rather than in parentThreadId.

findings.title: Nothing on the envelope ties the approval exchange to the held grant request
findings.claim: SPEC §4.13.3 rule 3 (normative) says evidence for a held exchange identifies it by carrying its threadId, or by a nested exchange carrying parentThreadId naming it. At the pinned VTA the task-consent/request document carries no threadId, parentThreadId or ceremony member, and the consent flow mints its own correlator. Our plan leaves the carrier open ('an effect or ext'). The decision is tied to the hold only by a challenge-salted payload digest that a ceremony verifier cannot see.
findings.evidence: SPEC.md:780 "It does so by carrying that exchange's threadId, or, where the evidence is supplied through a nested exchange, by that exchange carrying parentThreadId naming the held one"; SPEC.md:779 rule 2 "unless the decision identifies the held exchange"; external/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/vta-service/src/trust_tasks/consent_request.rs:111-118 (unsigned doc = id, type, issuer, recipient, issuedAt, payload only); policy_gate.rs:815-819 "A correlator of its own, not the digest"; vti2823 docs/05-design-notes/hcp.md:159 "Keyring accepts it only for the VID and threadId it scanned"; d3-plan-canvas docs/plans/agent-connect-plan/2026-11-25-bam.md:186 "the threadId in an effect or ext"
findings.keyringImpact: Keyring's rule 'accept only for the VID and threadId scanned' needs a defined carrier. parentThreadId on task-consent/request and decision is the framework's own carrier, works for ceremonies, and Keyring already sends parentThreadId elsewhere (oobSignIn.ts:376-385).
findings.askOfPR: In hcp/grants/request, add a SHOULD: the documents of the approval exchange carry parentThreadId equal to the held request's threadId (SPEC §4.9.2, §4.13.3 rule 3). Separately, ask VTI #2823 and our plan to use parentThreadId rather than an effect or ext.
findings.corrected:
The finding holds, with four corrections. Severity stays "raise", but the raise is aimed at VTI #2823 and our plan. For PR #1380 it is only an optional clarification.

(1) Version. The quoted rules are in the PR branch's SPEC.md (the framework text whose newest changelog entry is 0.7.0). SPEC.md:779 is rule 2. That rule governs this case, because a grant hold is a refer: "The act belongs to a third party, the person" (grants/request spec.md:171). Rule 2 binds a decision "on the terms of rule 3" (SPEC.md:780). The framework at our pin 2a66a0351 has no §4.13 at all.

(2) Overstated binding claim. The VTA-signed task-consent/request names the held request's issuer and type in its payload: "requester": pending.requester_did and "taskType" (consent_request.rs:88, 94). It also carries the challenge (consent_request.rs:87). So the decision is tied to the requester and the payload. The piece that is missing is the threadId, which is half of the hold's key (threadId, issuer) (grants/request spec.md:175). "A ceremony verifier cannot see" the digest should read "cannot recompute it from the spec". The task-consent spec names only the digest's inputs (spec.md:141, 165). The construction itself, with a domain tag and length prefixes, is the VTA's own (vti-common/src/task_consent/mod.rs:56, 90-112).

(3) The PR does not define an approval exchange. The spec says "The provider puts the request to the person" (spec.md:63). The demo's person approves "in the provider's app" (SCENARIO.md:195). The framework already says a nested exchange SHOULD carry parentThreadId (SPEC.md:512, 1118). It also says a producer answering a hold MUST identify the held exchange (SPEC.md:1122). So a SHOULD in hcp/grants/request would restate the framework, and should be conditional: "where the provider puts the request to the person through a Trust Task exchange". The real gap is in VTI #2823 (hcp.md:159 names no carrier) and our plan (bam.md:186, "an effect or ext"). Both should use parentThreadId on task-consent/request, with Keyring copying it onto its task-consent/decision.

(4) Keyring caveat. SPEC.md:514 says consumers "MUST NOT reject a document on the basis of parentThreadId alone". So Keyring should treat a mismatch as "not this pairing" and not show it, rather than answering with an error, in line with rule 3: "it is simply not the answer to the hold". | The core claim holds, but two parts are overstated. One part of the ask is aimed at the wrong place, and the severity should be split by target.

(1) Applicability. SPEC §4.13.3 rules 2 and 3 are normative on the PR branches' SPEC.md (tt SPEC.md:779-780). They arrived only on 2026-11-24, when SPEC.md was regenerated (bd9d5ebe5, #1364), and no changelog entry records them. They are not in our pinned framework at 2a66a0351, whose §4 ends at 4.12 Document Lifecycle. hcp/grants/request also declares "It targets framework version 0.6.0" (spec.md:69). An HCP grant hold is the refer case: the third-party person decides. So rule 2 is the rule that applies, and it binds the decision "on the terms of rule 3".

(2) What the PR scopes. hcp/grants/request leaves the approval channel to the provider: "The person reaches the decision through the provider's own modality, never through the client: a management app, a web page, a message" (spec.md:87). The suite defines no approval task, and the demo approves in-process by threadId (demo.ts:435-438). A SHOULD in hcp/grants/request cannot apply when that channel is a web page. When the channel is a Trust Task, the framework's rule 2 is already a MUST on the provider. So the ask to PR #1380 is at most a conditional, informative pointer: "where the person's decision reaches the provider as a Trust Task exchange, its documents carry parentThreadId = the held request's threadId (SPEC §4.9.2, §4.13.3 rules 2-3)". That ask is severity "note".

(3) The real gap is in VTI #2823 and our plan, and "raise" stands there. At the pinned VTA, task-consent/request carries no threadId, parentThreadId or ceremony member (consent_request.rs:111-118). The decision is matched only by its payloadDigest lookup and challenge (task_consent.rs:196). The flow mints its own correlator (policy_gate.rs:815-819; oob_sign_in.rs:1135). Our companion leaves the carrier open: "the threadId in an effect or ext" (bam.md:186). Both carriers are available: the task-consent/request schema allows `ext`, and the envelope allows parentThreadId. Only parentThreadId is the framework's named carrier.

(4) Correct "cannot see". A verifier can see the decision's challenge and payloadDigest, which the decision payload carries in the clear (decision/0.2 spec.md:188-189). What it cannot do is link them to the held grants/request. The digest construction is the executor's own: the spec says only "over the canonical payload, the task type, and challenge as salt", while the VTA adds a domain tag and length prefixes (vti-common task_consent/mod.rs:98-120). A remote_approval-style producer also hashes a synthesized {grantDigest, device, approver} payload rather than the held one (oob_sign_in.rs:1079-1084).

(5) This is a conformance and interop gap, not a security hole. The 256-bit per-pending challenge is a stronger binding than a threadId, which need not be unique.
findings.reasons:
HOLDS: Every cited line says what the claim says. SPEC.md:779-780 is on the PR branch (pr1382) and quoted correctly. consent_request.rs:111-118 at VTI pin f7b78e29d builds the unsigned document with only id, type, issuer, recipient, issuedAt and payload: no threadId, parentThreadId or ceremony. Both callers of mint_signed_requests use it: policy_gate.rs:650 and vault.rs:1869, the latter being the remote_approval path that hcp.md:94 says will be reused. policy_gate.rs:815-819 mints "A correlator of its own, not the digest", and that correlator only reaches the requester's granted notice (consent_request.rs:220, 236), never the approver. hcp.md:159 and bam.md:186 quote correctly. Keyring already sends parentThreadId (oobSignIn.ts:376-385, and also vtaClaim.ts:184/211 and vtiVetting.ts:724).

The core claim is right: nothing on the envelope links the approval exchange to the held thread, and the framework's own carrier is parentThreadId. It is overstated in two places. The payload already binds the requester and task type, so only the threadId is missing. And the digest cannot be recomputed by a third party only because its construction is the VTA's own, not because it is hidden. The ask of PR #1380 also mostly restates obligations the framework already places on nested exchanges and held-exchange evidence, because the suite deliberately leaves the approval mechanism to the provider. The ask matters most for VTI #2823 and our plan. || HOLDS: I looked for counter-evidence and found none that defeats the claim, only things that narrow it.

Confirmed: SPEC.md:780 (rule 3) and :779 (rule 2, which binds decisions "on the terms of rule 3") are on the PR branches, where hcp/grants/request answers a held request with the refer/third-party next step (spec.md:171-175). At the pin, consent_request.rs:111-118 builds the unsigned document as id, type, issuer, recipient, issuedAt and payload, with no thread members. The decision handler binds by digest and challenge only (task_consent.rs:196) and never reads threadId. Keyring sends parentThreadId elsewhere (oobSignIn.ts:383), and the plan's carrier is open (bam.md:186). The task-consent specs define no threading rule.

Narrowings:
- §4.13 is newer than our pin and than the 0.6.0 target the hcp specs declare. It was added by bd9d5ebe5 and is absent at 2a66a0351.
- hcp/grants/request deliberately leaves the person's approval channel to the provider (spec.md:87) and has no approval task. The demo approves in-process. So the SHOULD asked of the PR is misplaced or redundant: it belongs in VTI #2823, the task-consent specs and our plan.
- "A ceremony verifier cannot see" is imprecise. The challenge and digest travel in the clear in the decision payload; what a verifier cannot do is reproduce the link, because the digest construction is the executor's own.

Severity: "raise" for VTI #2823 and our plan; "note" for PR #1380.

findings.title: An abandoned hold is silently reopened; hold end states are inconsistent and allow an account probe
