findings.title: Create and revise refuse top-level entry members HCP does not define, which HCP 4.2 says a provider MUST preserve
findings.claim: The TT create and revise request roots are additionalProperties:false. So a client cannot write a top-level entry member HCP does not define, although HCP says a provider MUST preserve such members. Neither spec.md says so. The gap is only at the top level: the nested record, subject and classification are open, and record.metadata passes both sides.
findings.evidence: tt-drift/specs/hcp/entries/create/0.1/payload.schema.json:7 and entries/revise/0.1/payload.schema.json:7 '"additionalProperties": false'. hcp-spec specification.md:783 'An HCP Provider MUST preserve members of an entry that this specification does not define and MUST NOT interpret them'; :3938 A.3 'Entry member not defined by this specification | ... | Preserved and not interpreted'. Vector (vectors/out/vectors-edge.txt): 'HCP accepts TT REJECTS | create request with a member HCP does not define' with TT error 'must NOT have additional properties (https://ext.example/note)'. Control: a create with record.metadata is accepted by both.
findings.keyringImpact: Low for us today. If our agent plugin (Context Client) or Keyring ever writes vendor members, they must go under record (for example record.metadata), not at the entry top level.
findings.askOfPR: State in the create and revise field mapping that top-level custom entry members cannot be written through the carriage, and where they go instead, or open the root to them.
findings.corrected:
The finding holds, with one correction on revise, and stays at "raise". On PR branch pr1380 (94ed4200c), and unchanged on pr1381 and pr1382, the create and revise payload roots are "additionalProperties": false (payload.schema.json:7 in both). HCP's own create-request.json and revise-request.json have no additionalProperties at the root, so they are open. As a result, a top-level member that HCP does not define passes HCP's schema and fails the TT schema. Every nested shared shape is open (additionalProperties true), including record, subject, classification, assertion, content, evidence items and provenance, so record.metadata passes on both sides.

For create, HCP's rule applies directly. HCP 9.4.3 (specification.md:2182) says the create body "is an entry in the form specified in 4.2", and 4.2 (:783) says "An HCP Provider MUST preserve members of an entry that this specification does not define".

For revise, the support is weaker. HCP 9.4.4 does not call the revise body an entry. The revise half rests instead on A.2 (:3869): the Core schemas "are open: they admit members this specification does not define, which an HCP Provider preserves". Also, the vector file only tests a custom member on create; for revise, the only vector is "revise request carrying subject", so the revise half is shown by reading the schemas, not by a vector.

Neither spec.md says this, although the framework requires it. TT SPEC.md:1642 (§9.4 item 6) says: "Where some requirement of the protocol cannot be expressed in a Trust Task document, the specification MUST say which and why". Create spec.md:106 only says the shared shapes "are open, as HCP's own schemas are", which describes the nested shapes, not the closed root. The sibling read-side specs (query, confirm, set-categories, restrict-purposes) do state the preserve rule for the Entry shape.

The ask stands: state the top-level limit, and where such members go instead, in the create and revise field mappings, or open the root. | CONFIRMED at the schema level. The TT hcp/entries/create and hcp/entries/revise payload roots are additionalProperties:false and have no `ext`, so a top-level member HCP does not define is refused. HCP's Core create and revise request schemas are open and admit it, and neither TT spec.md says this. The nested objects are open: record, subject, content and assertion accept a URI-named undefined member, and so does record.metadata.

Four points narrow the claim:

(1) This does not break any HCP rule. HCP 1.5 says "A binding MAY expose a subset of an operation's fields", and HCP's own MCP binding (hcp_createEntry) also offers no way to write such members. The 4.2 MUST is a duty to preserve what the provider receives. It does not give a client the right to send these members through every binding. On the TT side, closing the root is the framework's approved way to state how unrecognized members are treated (SPEC §7.3 item 4).

(2) The 4.2 preserve rule applies directly only to create, because HCP 9.4.3 says the create body "is an entry in the form specified in 4.2". HCP 9.4.4 does not describe the revise body as an entry, and 5.2.4 gives an undefined top-level member on a revise no effect on the entry. On revise this is only a schema difference: HCP's open revise-request.json against TT's closed root, which I reproduced.

(3) "Cannot write" holds only for create and revise. TT hcp/import accepts exported entries that carry a top-level undefined member, so a Management Client such as Keyring still has a way to write one.

(4) The Keyring advice to use "for example record.metadata" is weak. record.metadata is an HCP-defined member. It is not a create request field in 5.2.3, which lists only record.provenance.* and record.relationships, and 4.1 says record is "Set by HCP Provider". So the preserve rule for undefined members does not cover it. A URI-named undefined member nested in an open object, such as record, passes both schemas and is covered by 4.2. Also, 7.4 withholds such members and record.metadata from Context Client disclosures, so our agent plugin would never read them back. That supports the low impact.

Severity: keep raise, low priority. The ask is to document the gap, not fix an interop break. SPEC §9.4 items 2 and 6 ask a carriage to map each field and to say what it cannot express. Ask the PR to state in the create and revise field mapping that top-level undefined entry members are not carried, and where they can go instead (nested members, or hcp/import).
findings.reasons:
HOLDS: Every cited line says what the claim says, and the claim is about the right branch, the PR branch.
- Both TT payload roots are closed at line 7.
- HCP's create-request.json and revise-request.json are open at the root. The only root rule HCP has on revise is a `not` that forbids subject and classification.
- HCP :783 and A.3 :3938 are quoted correctly.
- The vector output matches: vectors-edge.txt:38-40 shows the create custom member rejected only by TT, and record.metadata accepted by both.
- All shared nested defs are open, so the gap really is only at the root.
- The create and revise spec.md files on pr1380, pr1381 and pr1382 say nothing about the closed root, and pr1381's uncheckedRules do not mention it either.
- TT SPEC §9.4 item 6 requires a carriage to say which protocol requirements it cannot express, so "raise" is the right severity, and it is not a blocker for Keyring.

One overstatement: HCP 4.2's MUST covers create directly through 9.4.3, which calls the create body an entry. Revise is covered only through A.2's general statement that the Core schemas are open (:3869), and no vector tests a custom member on revise. || HOLDS: I searched for counter-evidence and found none that refutes the core claim. The roots are closed and HCP's schemas and text admit and preserve the members. I also ran the check myself: the TT revise root rejects 'https://ext.example/note' while HCP's revise-request.json accepts it, and TT also rejects an `ext` at the create root. The claim is overstated in four places, all set out in the corrected claim: HCP 1.5 lets a binding expose a subset of fields; the 4.2 preserve rule binds create directly but not revise; hcp/import gives a Management Client a way in; and record.metadata is not a create field HCP promises to keep, so it is a poor example of where to put vendor members.

findings.title: #1381 misses one placement: the disclosed-evidence credential rule in the hcp/entries/query result

findings.corrected:
The gap is real and severity "raise" is right. On pr1381 (1b3ae9ed6, which matches origin/feat/hcp-unchecked-rules), hcp/entries/query's uncheckedRules lists the VC-evidence credential rule only for the Entry branch (anyOf/1). It leaves out the Disclosure branch (anyOf/0 .../evidence/items/allOf/0/properties/credential). hcp/entries/get, create and revise all list that branch. The ask stands.

Two corrections:
(1) The Keyring impact is overstated. uncheckedRules only documents rules. Per scripts/lib/unchecked-rules.mjs:62, "The library validators do not yet surface these rules". So a TT validator also accepts a VC evidence item with no credential in hcp/entries/get, where the rule is listed. Adding the entry fixes the declaration, not validation. (2) Likely cause: the PR's build cross-check cannot catch this omission. findMarkedSchemas walks the schemas breadth-first and skips any schema it has already visited (`seen.has(node)`, line 296). In query, the shared EvidenceItem is reached first through the shorter anyOf/1 path, which is covered. Its second path through the Disclosure allOf/0 is never checked. This is worth adding to the ask: the check only proves each shared schema is covered once per payload, not once per placement. | Holds, with three narrowings. Severity stays "raise", but it is a small consistency fix. (1) The rule is not missing from hcp/entries/query altogether. Its uncheckedRules already states it word for word, but only at the Entry branch (anyOf/1, spec.md:96). Only the Disclosure-branch placement (anyOf/0 .../evidence/items/allOf/0/properties/credential) is absent, while hcp/entries/get lists both branches (get spec.md:78). (2) The framework's own convention and build check count rules per spec and per shared schema node, not per placement. That is why the build passes and gives no warning. The omission breaks the author's own practice (query lists the content, confidence and one-content-item rules in both branches) and the per-branch listing in get, create and revise. findings.title: Category, Directive.action, Delegation.relationship and AuditEvent.purpose drop format:uri
findings.claim: HCP writes these members as anyOf [slug or enum | format:uri + pattern] (AuditEvent.purpose as URI or null). TT writes a single pattern with no format:uri. So TT accepts non-URI strings that HCP refuses. Across 26 string probes the two sides agree on 19; all 7 disagreements are strings like 'x:<y>' or 'a:%zz' that TT accepts and HCP refuses. The shared PurposeCode keeps format:uri. No TT description says why.
findings.evidence: tt-drift/specs/hcp/_shared/0.1/common.schema.json:24 Category '"pattern": "^([a-z][a-z0-9_]*|[a-zA-Z][a-zA-Z0-9+.-]*:\\S+)$"' with no format; :32 PurposeCode keeps '"format":"uri"'. audit-event.schema.json:41 purpose is pattern-only. vectors/out/vectors-edge.txt: 'HCP REJECTS TT accepts | category "x:<y>"', the same for 'a:%zz', directive action, delegation relationship and audit purpose; control 'purpose code "x:<y>"': both reject.
findings.keyringImpact: Small. If Keyring or the plugin relies on a category or action being a real URI (to render or dereference it), we must check that ourselves.
findings.askOfPR: Add format:uri to these four members, as HCP has it, or say why it is left out.
findings.corrected: The claim holds, with three precisions; severity stays "raise", low priority. (1) The 7 disagreements show up only when `format` is enforced as a check. That is what ajv-formats does, and it is what the review harness (vectors/validators.mjs), TT's own CI example check (tt/scripts/lib/spec-examples.mjs:120 "addFormats(ajv)") and the TS/Go/Dart demo validators all use. Under JSON Schema 2020-12's default, where `format` is only a label, HCP's and TT's schemas both accept all 7 strings. TT's Rust validator (trust-tasks-rs/src/validate.rs:101-103) builds `jsonschema` for Draft 2020-12 with no format option. In the jsonschema 0.49.9 copy cached on this machine, that default does not check formats for 2020-12. TT pins 0.63, which is UNVERIFIED. HCP's prose decides the question: it requires an absolute URI for all four members (specification.md:981, :1733, :3325, :1580, :3932). So 'x:<y>' and 'a:%zz' are non-conforming by HCP's text, not only by its schema. (2) The ask needs to be precise. Adding `"format":"uri"` straight onto TT's single alternation pattern for Category, Directive.action and Delegation.relationship would make a format-checking validator reject the slug and enum values ('health_context', 'share'); I tested this. Those three members need HCP's anyOf split, with format:uri on the URI branch only. AuditEvent.purpose can take format:uri as it is (null still passes), or point to PurposeCode-or-null. (3) The PR's drift check cannot catch this, because it does not compare `pattern` or `format` (scripts/lib/hcp-drift.mjs:23). 0.1 is not released yet, so it can still be fixed in place. After release, a format change counts as breaking (CONTRIBUTING-SPECS.md:87). One small citation fix: PurposeCode's `"format": "uri"` is at common.schema.json:29, not :32 (:32 is its pattern). | Severity should be "note", not "raise". The facts hold only for a validator that checks `format`, as the vectors' Ajv2020 + ajv-formats does. Under the default rules of JSON Schema 2020-12, `format` only labels a value and rejects nothing, and HCP's schemas use those default rules. Keyring's own validator works the same way: it has no ajv-formats. With either, the 7 disagreements disappear: both sides accept "x:<y>" and "a:%zz". One disagreement appears the other way round: category "foo:" passes HCP (its URI branch pattern is only "^[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9+.-]*:") and fails TT. What rules out "x:<y>" is HCP's text ("MUST be an absolute URI", A.3/4.5/6.4/17.2), and the text governs. The ask cannot be done as written for 3 of the 4 members. Category, Directive.action and Delegation.relationship are one string schema whose allowed values include slugs and enum words, and format:uri on that schema rejects "share" and "health_context". Adding it needs an anyOf, and the family avoids such unions to keep its generated libraries simple. Adding format:uri also costs something in Rust. The generator (typify) turns PurposeCode (format + pattern) into a plain String with no check at all, but Category (pattern only) gets a length and regex check. So adding format would likely remove Rust's only check. Go and Dart are plain string aliases either way. Only AuditEvent.purpose (type [string,null]) can take format:uri directly. A smaller ask: give AuditEvent.purpose the PurposeCode shape (format:uri works there, since null passes) so it matches, and add one sentence on the three unions saying URI well-formedness beyond the pattern is left to the consumer. Keyring impact: none from this PR either way, because Keyring's validator ignores format. If we need a real URI we check it ourselves anyway. Our planned values are https IRIs.
findings.reasons:
HOLDS: Every quote checks out on pr1380 (tt-drift), and pr1381 and pr1382 have identical text for all four members. TT Category (common.schema.json:20-25), directive action (directive.schema.json:17-22), delegation relationship (delegation.schema.json:36-41) and audit purpose (audit-event.schema.json:41-45) are each one pattern with no format. TT's Uri and PurposeCode keep format:uri (:14 and :29). HCP's category (common.json:21-33), directive action (directive.json:11-26) and delegation relationship (delegation.json:38-54) are anyOf with format:uri on the URI branch. HCP's audit purpose (audit-event.json:126-135) is anyOf [purposeCode (format uri), null]. The vector file matches the claim: 26 string probes, 19 agree and 7 disagree, all 7 being strings TT accepts and HCP rejects, plus the purpose-code control where both reject. I re-ran an independent probe with the same ajv. It reproduces the split with format checking on, and with it off both sides accept the 7 strings. TT gives no reason anywhere: there is no uncheckedRule about URI validity in pr1381, and no spec.md text on RFC 3986 or format. TT's conventions allow format:uri (CONTRIBUTING-SPECS.md:409-413), so leaving it out is not a framework rule. The finding is right but understated: it depends on format checking, and its ask, done literally, would break the slug and enum values. || HOLDS: The core facts are CONFIRMED. HCP's schemas write these members as anyOf [slug/enum | format:uri + pattern]. TT writes one pattern and no format. With ajv-formats the vectors show 7 disagreements out of 26 probes, all cases where TT accepts and HCP rejects. I re-ran this myself and got the same result. The counter-evidence narrows the claim:
(1) HCP's schemas declare JSON Schema 2020-12 and add no rule that makes `format` reject values, so the default applies: `format` is a label, not a check. Ajv2020 configured like Keyring's validator (strict:false, no ajv-formats) warns 'unknown format "uri" ignored'. With it, HCP and TT both accept "x:<y>" and "a:%zz". HCP accepts category "foo:" and TT rejects it.
(2) Adding format:uri directly to TT's single-string Category or action schema makes them reject "health_context" and "share" (probed: false). Only AuditEvent.purpose accepts it cleanly (null passes, "x:<y>" fails).
(3) The generated Rust library checks Category's pattern but leaves format-bearing PurposeCode unchecked (Infallible FromStr), so adding format would likely weaken Rust. Go and Dart check neither.
(4) The drift check states that it does not compare `format`, so it could not have caught this. I found no TT text that explains the choice, so "no TT description says why" holds. #1381 does not list URI well-formedness among the rules a schema cannot check.

findings.title: A TT-valid object is not HCP-valid on 15 HCP schema conditionals; all are documented and listed in #1381
findings.claim: HCP's schemas check 15 conditionals that TT leaves to prose because its generators cannot express if/then/else or contains: content profile, model-inferred confidence, VC credential, one content evidence item, proposal only on contradicts, ContextEntry in type, grant expiresAt by grantType, delegation basis evidence and parent, and import rejected→reason. The edge vectors confirm HCP rejects and TT accepts in each tested case. Apart from the query gap above, #1381 lists every placement. The shared HCP objects are open on both sides, so HCP's own schemas accept TT payload sub-objects. In TT → HCP, all 38 documents that have an HCP schema pass except the Q11 hard-delete.
findings.evidence: TT descriptions, for example context-entry.schema.json Content: 'This rule is stated here and not as a schema conditional: the registry's Rust generator does not support `if`/`then`/`else`, so a validator does not check it.' vectors/out/unchecked-coverage.txt: '91 sites ... covered exactly 90 ... missing 1'. vectors/out/vectors-edge.txt: 'HCP REJECTS TT accepts | entry whose type lacks ContextEntry | #1381: listed'; the same for model-inferred, General Context without value, standing rule with neither, persistent grant with an instant.
findings.keyringImpact: Keyring's packages/trust-tasks validator will pass objects that break these rules. Cheap mitigation: run HCP's own schemas, which accept the TT shapes, as a second check on entries, disclosures and grants we receive.
findings.corrected:
The claim holds, and "note" is the right severity. Five details need correcting:

(1) The 15 are places in the TT schemas, not 15 separate HCP rules. HCP has 12 distinct conditionals TT does not carry. The VC-credential rule is counted twice (EvidenceItem and Disclosure evidence). The one-content-item rule is counted three times (Entry, the create request and the revise request).

(2) The "standing rule with neither operators nor requires" vector is not one of the 15 conditionals. That rule is HCP's anyOf of two required clauses. TT drops it from the shared StandingRule for a different documented reason ("so that the type stays fully typed in every generated library"). TT checks it only on the hcp/rules/set request root. It is allowlisted in the PR's drift check and listed in #1381.

(3) The edge vectors test 6 of the 10 rule topics: grant expiresAt (temporary and persistent), ContextEntry, model-inferred confidence, General Context value, and the VC credential on query. No vector tests these: VC Evidence forbidding value, at most one content evidence item, proposal only on contradicts, the delegation basis rules, and import rejected→reason. Those rest on the TT descriptions and #1381 alone.

(4) TT → HCP: 39 documents have an HCP schema, not 38. 38 pass and 1 fails, the Q11 hard-delete (spec.md:166, "must have required property 'status'"). This holds after the documented mapping: accessToken stripped, respondedAt renamed to timestamp, the result unwrapped.

(5) Keyring impact is conditional. Keyring has no hcp/* schemas today. Its validator.ts is a generic Ajv2020 instance: it expects cross-file $refs pre-inlined and does not load ajv-formats. Running HCP's schemas as a second check would catch the conditionals, because Ajv2020 supports if/then/else and contains/maxContains. But it means registering HCP's multi-file schemas by $id. Without ajv-formats, the format checks (uri, date-time) are skipped, so the non-URI category/action/purpose differences would still get through.
findings.reasons:

findings.title: directives: required in TT (Q42) and null for a Management Client (Q5); differs from HCP in both directions
findings.claim: In the get and query results, 'directives' absent is refused by TT and accepted by HCP. 'directives': null is accepted by TT and refused by HCP ('must be array'). HCP's own 9.4.2 example omits directives, so it fails TT unchanged and passes once directives:[] is added. TT has 11 required-and-nullable members in all. For AuditEvent.entryId, absent is refused by TT and accepted by HCP; null is accepted by both.

findings.title: The hard-delete result has no status (Q11); fails HCP withdraw-result on that one member
findings.claim: The TT hard-delete response is {entryId, hardDeleted:true, respondedAt}. HCP 9.4.5's result requires status. The PR documents this as pending Q11 and lists the side as notCompared. In TT → HCP, the PR's own example fails HCP only on 'status'. In HCP → TT, HCP's result with hardDeleted:true fails TT only on the extra 'status'. The withdraw response closes hardDeleted to false (Q10).
findings.evidence: tt-drift/specs/hcp/entries/hard-delete/0.1/spec.md:113 'result `status` | none | Absent ... pending HCP confirmation'; :162. vectors/out/vectors-tt-to-hcp.txt: 'HCP FAIL | hcp/entries/hard-delete response [specs/hcp/entries/hard-delete/0.1/spec.md:166] ... must have required property 'status''. vectors-hcp-to-tt.txt: 'must NOT have additional properties (status)'.
findings.keyringImpact: Keyring issues hard deletes as the Management Client. It must not depend on a status member in the reply.
findings.corrected: The claim holds, and "note" is the right severity. Three places need tighter wording. (1) HCP has no hard-delete result at all, neither as prose nor as a schema. The only result HCP publishes for DELETE /v2/entries is operations/withdraw-result.json, titled "Withdraw result" and defined in 5.2.5 and 9.4.5. It requires `status` (const "deleted") and `timestamp`, needs one of `ref`/`entryId`, and does not set additionalProperties:false. So "HCP 9.4.5's result requires status" means that withdraw schema, which the review applies to hard delete by analogy. That is the same analogy the PR uses and leaves open as Q11. (2) The HCP → TT case "as HCP writes it" is a vector the reviewer built: the withdraw example at specification.md:2223-2230 with hardDeleted set to true. It still carries status:"deleted". HCP never writes that document. (3) Both directions matter to Keyring. Keyring must not depend on `status`. Also, if a provider copies HCP's HTTP result and leaves status:"deleted" in, a Keyring that checks the reply against the TT schema will reject it, because TT closes the reply with additionalProperties:false. Everything else checks out: the TT response requires exactly {entryId, hardDeleted const true, respondedAt}; the drift map lists hcp/entries/hard-delete:response under notCompared, citing Q11; the TT → HCP vector fails only on 'status'; the HCP → TT vector fails only on the extra 'status'; the withdraw response sets hardDeleted to const false and marks it OPTIONAL (Q10).

The spec says what the claim says: spec.md:113 '| result `status` | none | Absent: the entry is no longer held, so it has no status, *pending HCP confirmation* ([question 11]...' and spec.md:162 'This specification takes the withdraw result's shape, with `hardDeleted` `true` and no `status`'. The response schema has additionalProperties:false, required ["entryId","hardDeleted","respondedAt"], and hardDeleted const true. scripts/lib/hcp-drift-map.json:313 reads '"hcp/entries/hard-delete:response": "HCP publishes no JSON schema for it: HCP 9.4.5 shows only the withdraw result (Q11)."'. The withdraw response is '"hardDeleted": {"type":"boolean","const":false ...}', with allowlist ref Q10 at hcp-drift-allowlist.json:131-136 and withdraw spec.md:109/203. In HCP at b790561, 9.4.5 (specification.md:2207-2231) shows only the withdraw response, with status "deleted" and hardDeleted false. withdraw-result.json has required ["status","timestamp"] and status const "deleted". The vector outputs match the claim: vectors-tt-to-hcp.txt:43-44 'HCP FAIL | hcp/entries/hard-delete response [specs/hcp/entries/hard-delete/0.1/spec.md:166] / must have required property 'status'', and vectors-hcp-to-tt.txt:11-12 'must NOT have additional properties (status)'. The validators use Ajv2020 with allErrors:true (validators.mjs:24,36), so "only on status" is accurate. The one overstatement is that the HCP → TT input is not an HCP document. It is built at vectors-hcp-to-tt.mjs:38-39 ('The example shows the withdraw; set hardDeleted.'). It is not a mistake.

findings.title: HCP → TT vectors: 22 cases from 15 HCP examples, 19 pass, 3 fail with known causes
findings.claim: Each concrete HCP example was validated against its own HCP schema (17 pass, 1 fail, 4 have no HCP schema), then mapped mechanically and validated against TT. The mapping moves the path parameter into the payload, adds accessToken, renames timestamp to respondedAt and wraps the result. 19 pass TT. The 3 failures: the get-entry result has no directives (Q42); the hardDeleted:true result has HCP's status (Q11); and the import example uses export:{}, which fails HCP's own schema too. A full export passes both. All 18 HCP templates use only member names TT declares, or sit inside objects TT leaves open.
findings.evidence: vectors/out/vectors-hcp-to-tt.txt; vectors/out/template-members.txt ('every member declared', or '[open: accepted, not interpreted]' for narrowedTo.entryIds, credential members and conversion.unmapped). hcp-spec tools/check_schemas.py:193 treats export:{} as a template.
findings.keyringImpact: Data written to HCP's examples carries over to the TT tasks unchanged, apart from the documented Q42 and Q11 points.
findings.corrected:
The claim holds and severity "ok" is right, but four details are overstated.

(1) Coverage. HCP's pages hold 24 concrete JSON blocks and 21 template blocks (out/hcp-examples.log). This track used 15 concrete blocks and 18 templates. Of the concrete blocks it left out, 8 are the MCP blocks (10.2-10.4, a separate track) and one is A.2's @context document, which no task carries. Of the templates it left out, 11.2 Content has every member declared in TT when checked. 14.10 is an attestation-authorization credential, so its members fall in a position TT leaves open. 19.2 is the discovery document, which no task carries.

(2) Six of the 22 cases are not HCP examples as written. They are built from examples: the two hardDeleted:true cases (HCP shows no hard-delete result; the "status" one comes from HCP's withdraw-result.json, which requires status const "deleted"), the directives:[] case, 11.4 wrapped as a get-entry response, and the two create bodies. Also, the 9.9 revocation SET is not a mechanical mapping. It is restructured (jti→noticeId, grantId and revokedAt lifted out of events), under the PR's declared departure Q16.

(3) "Or sit inside objects TT leaves open" is always true for shared objects. Every TT _shared object has additionalProperties:true; there is no additionalProperties:false in grant, context-entry, disclosure, export, standing-rule, directive, audit-event or delegation. So the result that matters is "every member declared". For the same reason, 4 of the 19 TT passes (9.4.2 disclosed entry, 11.4 entry, G2.2 entry, 14.2 content) would accept any extra member. A member-name check on those four found every member declared, so the conclusion stands.

(4) "A full export passes both" rests on vectors-edge.txt:51 ("HCP accepts TT accepts | import of a realistic export (control)"), not on the cited files. That export has one entry, empty rules, directives and delegations, and no versions or audit, so it is realistic rather than full.

Keyring impact, more precisely: values in HCP's examples carry over unchanged, apart from Q42 (directives required), Q11 (no status on hard delete) and the Q16 reshaping of the revocation notice. The 9.4.11 export:{} is a placeholder in HCP's own example, not a TT gap.
findings.reasons:
HOLDS: I reran the harness in a scratch copy with OUT redirected, so no review file was touched. out/hcp-examples.json, vectors-hcp-to-tt.txt and template-members.txt came out byte-identical. The counts check out:
- 22 cases from 15 example ids.
- HCP side: 17 pass, 1 fail (9.4.11), 4 not applicable. HCP has no operation schema for confirm, set-categories, restrict-purposes or the revocation SET.
- TT side: 19 pass, 3 fail, with the stated causes.

Each cause is confirmed in source:
- Q42: TT get Response requires "directives" (spec.md:172, 258), while HCP's get-entry-result.json leaves it optional.
- Q11: TT hard-delete Response is additionalProperties:false with no status (spec.md:113, 162, 225). HCP's withdraw-result requires status.
- check_schemas.py:193 reads exactly `(template if imp.get('export') == {} else validate)`.

The mappings are documented in the TT spec: query spec.md:120 (accessToken), :127 (respondedAt). The schemas are the right version. tt-drift is at pr1380 94ed420, and its specs/hcp is identical to pr1382's. pr1381 changes only spec.md files. hcp-spec is at b790561.

Controls show the checks are not vacuous:
- Adding a stray member to a request or response payload makes TT refuse it, and so does dropping accessToken or respondedAt, or leaving timestamp unrenamed.
- A planted unknown member is reported by the template member-name check.

What I found is overstatement, not error: 18 of 21 templates and 15 of 24 concrete blocks were covered, some cases are derived rather than examples as written, the "open" branch is trivially true for all shared objects, and "full export" is cited from vectors-edge rather than the named evidence. None of this changes the conclusion.

findings.title: TT → HCP vectors: 72 documents, all TT-valid; 38 HCP-valid after stripping, 1 fails (Q11), 33 have no HCP schema
findings.claim: The 10 hcp/* documents in the demo's transcript.golden.txt and the 62 example documents in specs/hcp/**/spec.md all pass their TT schema. After stripping accessToken (and ext on the import result), renaming respondedAt to timestamp and unwrapping, 38 pass HCP's schema and 1 fails: the hard-delete response, missing status (Q11). 33 sides have no HCP schema (path or query parameters, 204 answers, the SET). The transcript's query result carries two real disclosures.
findings.evidence: vectors/out/vectors-tt-to-hcp.txt: 'TT control: 72 pass, 0 fail'; 'HCP: 38 pass, 1 fail, 33 n/a'.
findings.keyringImpact: What the PR's demos and examples emit is valid HCP once the carriage members are removed.
findings.corrected: The claim holds, and "ok" is the right severity for the vector result, but it needs three corrections. (1) The reasons given for the 33 n/a sides leave a group out. Six of them are JSON request bodies that HCP describes only in prose and publishes no schema for: entries/confirm (HCP 9.4.9, {disposition, expectedVersion}), entries/set-categories and both entries/restrict-purposes examples (9.4.10), rules/set (9.4.14) and directives/set (9.4.15). The rest are path or query parameters, 204 answers, and the SET with its acknowledgement. (2) Some passes check only part of the payload. The three grants/request requests check only the access[] items against common.json#/$defs/accessDetail; expiresIn and subjectHint are checked by nothing. The export request checks only export.json#/properties/options. The grants/request response checks only `grant`. (3) The Keyring impact goes too far. "Valid HCP once the carriage members are removed" is shown only for the 38 sides that have an HCP schema. The hard-delete result is invalid against HCP's withdraw-result schema, and the PR does this deliberately as question 11. Because the TT hard-delete Response has additionalProperties:false and no `status`, a provider that answers in HCP's withdraw-result shape (status:"deleted") would fail the TT schema; that belongs with the HCP-to-TT vectors. Most of what Keyring would send as Management Client (revoke, hard-delete, confirm, set-categories, restrict-purposes, rules and directives) is in the n/a group, so this vector test gives little schema-level assurance for Keyring's own requests. Something the claim leaves out, which supports it: HCP's schemas are open-world (no additionalProperties:false outside discovery.json), so a pass by itself would not show leftover TT members. A separate walk found no member that the HCP schemas do not declare in any of the checked instances, and a control run with injected members flagged 25 sides.
findings.reasons: HOLDS: I reran a scratch copy of the vector script, and its output is byte-identical to vectors/out/vectors-tt-to-hcp.txt: 72 documents (10 transcript, 62 spec.md); TT control 72 pass, 0 fail; HCP 38 pass, 1 fail, 33 n/a. The 10 are correct: the transcript has exactly 10 hcp/* documents among its arrows (the others are discovery, next-step and error). The 62 are correct: grep finds exactly 62 hcp type lines across specs/hcp/**/spec.md. specs/hcp is identical between pr1380 (tt-drift, which the TT schemas come from) and pr1382 (tt, which the documents come from); git diff is empty. Mapping hard-delete to withdraw-result.json is justified: HCP 9.4.5 covers both withdraw and hardDelete=true, and the schema's own description cites 9.4.5. The PR documents the missing status as question 11 (hard-delete spec.md:113, 162, 225). The transcript query result has two entries, hcp-ref-0001 and hcp-ref-0002. Nothing in the claim is wrong. The parenthetical reasons for the n/a sides are incomplete, and the Keyring-impact sentence claims more than the test shows, as set out in correctedClaim.

findings.title: Edge vectors: 40 cases plus 26 string probes; HCP and TT disagree on 20 cases, and all but 4 are documented
findings.claim: Temporary grant without expiresAt: both reject. Temporary with null, and persistent with an instant: HCP rejects, TT accepts (listed in #1381). Both ref and entryId on a request: both accept (#1381 lists it, Q6). Both on the withdraw result: HCP rejects, TT accepts (listed). Entry without ContextEntry: HCP rejects, TT accepts (listed). Standing rule with neither operators nor requires: the shared object and the response are rejected by HCP and accepted by TT (listed); the rules/set request is rejected by TT. Query with empty categories: HCP accepts, TT rejects (Q42). Size: 257 categories, a 2049-character URI, 65 evidence items and a 65-character language are accepted by HCP and rejected by TT; 21 query results are rejected by both. Of the 20 disagreements, 4 are undocumented: the top-level custom create member (create-revise-root-closed), the query VC credential gap (query-unchecked-gap), and the 2048 URI and 64 language caps, which follow the framework rule but are unexplained.
findings.evidence: vectors/out/vectors-edge.txt, with the full table in notes Appendix B. For example 'HCP REJECTS TT REJECTS | temporary grant without expiresAt' (HCP: must have required property 'expiresAt'); 'HCP accepts TT REJECTS | query with empty categories | Q42' (TT: '/categories must NOT have fewer than 1 items').
findings.keyringImpact: These vectors can be reused in Keyring's own tests of the hcp/* bindings.
findings.corrected:
Severity stays "note". The edge-vector run has 66 rows: 40 edge cases plus 26 string probes, and 4 of the rows have no HCP schema to check against. 20 of the 40 edge cases disagree, and every row in the claim matches the output.

Two corrections:

(1) The string probes also disagree, on 7 of 26. For Category, Directive.action, Delegation.relationship and AuditEvent.purpose, HCP rejects "x:<y>" and "a:%zz" and TT accepts them, because TT drops `format: uri`. That is finding F4, and the PR does not document it. So across all 66 rows there are 27 disagreements and 11 of them are undocumented (the 4 named plus these 7), not "all but 4".

(2) "Follow the framework rule" overstates it. No framework rule requires a maxLength on a URI or on a language tag:
- CONTRIBUTING-SPECS "Bounds and URL members" requires maxItems on request-side arrays. That is why the 256-category and 64-evidence caps exist, and both are documented.
- SPEC §7.3 item 19 bounds free-text members only, and says constrained values are outside it.

The 2048 cap is the PR's own "framework bound" convention. The PR labels it that way on AuditEvent.purpose but not on PurposeCode, which is the query `purpose` the vector tested. The 64 cap on Content.language has no label anywhere.

Also, several of the "documented" rows rest on #1381, which is stacked and not merged. #1381 changes no schemas. For one of them, model-inferred confidence null, only #1381 states the rule.
findings.reasons:
HOLDS: I recounted vectors-edge.json without changing it: 66 total, 40 edge, 26 strings, 4 n/a, 20 edge disagreements, 7 string disagreements. I re-ran the 65-character language, the 2049-character purpose and the x:<y> category probes on their own, and the results match. The TT schemas loaded from tt-drift (pr1380) are identical to pr1382 (diff -rq is empty), and pr1381 changes only spec.md files.

How each disagreement is documented:
- Q5 and Q42 (directives null/required, categories never empty) are in the query spec's "Pending HCP confirmation".
- Q10 (hardDeleted always false) is in the withdraw spec, and Q6 (exactly one of ref/entryId) is in the get spec.
- The 256-category bound and the 64-evidence bound each carry "framework bound" in their schema descriptions.
- PurposeCode's 2048 and Content.language's 64 carry no such text.
- #1381's query uncheckedRules list the VC credential rule only for anyOf/1. Get lists anyOf/0, so the query gap is real.
- HCP's query-request has no minItems on categories, and query-result caps entries at 20.

The claim's facts hold. It leaves out the 7 undocumented string-probe disagreements, and it calls the 2048 and 64 caps a framework rule when no framework rule requires them.

findings.title: grants/request's differences from HCP's access detail are intended and consistent with HCP
findings.claim: The task carries no HCP operation, and HCP has no grant-request schema, so pairing it with accessDetail is my own approximation. The three member differences match HCP's prose. purposes is optional because HCP 6.1.5.2 lets a request name no purpose. purposes[].description is optional because the provider shows its own. notTo is not requestable because the provider sets it. The rest are bounds and closed objects on TT's own request shapes. The grant in the response is HCP's grant whole.
findings.evidence: tt-drift/specs/hcp/grants/request/0.1/spec.md:65 'This task carries no HCP operation.'; :126 'A detail that names no `purposes` is allowed: the provider MUST then ask the person to choose'. hcp-spec specification.md:1584 'Where a grant request names no purpose, the Authorization Service MUST ask'. TT OnwardSharingRequest description: '`notTo` is set by the provider, never asked for'; HCP specification.md:1705.
findings.keyringImpact: Our plugin's grant request can omit purposes, and Keyring, as the person's app, is then where the purposes are chosen.
findings.corrected:
Mostly holds, but one of the three member differences is not backed by HCP's text. Severity should be raise (minor), not ok.

What holds (CONFIRMED on pr1380, and unchanged on pr1382):
- The task carries no HCP operation (spec.md:65), and HCP has no grant-request schema. Its schemas/2.0-draft-3/operations/ holds no grant request; grant requests are left to the profiles (HCP 6.1.7, line 1606).
- purposes optional: ok. HCP 1584 says "Where a grant request names no purpose, the Authorization Service MUST ask...". HCP 12.2 (line 2882) says the same for an authenticated channel: "where the client names no purpose, the Authorizing Principal chooses one in the channel". One nuance: HCP 13.3's authorization_details form (line 2920) lists `purposes` as a required member ("actions, categories, purposes, and optionally narrowedTo"); 13.3 allows no purpose only for scope strings (line 2921). So the schema's "(HCP 6.1.5.2, 13.3)" citation for "absent" is loose. It is harmless, because this task is not 13.3.
- notTo not requestable: ok. HCP 1527 says "`notTo` is set by the HCP Provider", and HCP 1705 says the same.
- The rest: closed objects (additionalProperties false) plus bounds (actions ≤3, categories ≤256, purposes ≤32, description ≤4096, domains 1..64 of 1..253 characters), on a shape HCP does not define.
- Response grant: ok. It is HCP's grant with every member, unrenamed and open (_shared grant.schema.json:9). It adds framework bounds (maxLength, and minLength 1 on ids that HCP leaves unbounded). HCP's temporary/persistent `expiresAt` if/then is moved into prose and into #1381's uncheckedRules.

What does not hold:
- "purposes[].description is optional because the provider shows its own" is the PR's own reasoning, not HCP's text.
- HCP defines a purpose as "a code ... with a description the person can read" (1580). Its `purpose` object requires `description` (common.json). The person "MUST be shown the description of each purpose" (1583).
- HCP's extension-point table (A.3, line 3941) says an unrecognized purpose code is "Accepted; its description is what the person is shown". That is the description that travels with the code.
- HCP says the provider gives its own wording only for categories (1597, 3721), not for purposes.
- So a code-only purpose with a code the provider does not know leaves nothing to show. Nothing could then fill the response grant's required `Purpose.description` either (_shared grant.schema.json:207).
- grants/request says only "The provider shows its own description where it has one" (payload.schema.json:125). It gives no rule for the case where it has none.
- The demo papers over this case. Its toy provider uses `description: p.description ?? p.code` (examples/hcp-demo-ts/src/demo.ts:373). With `purposes` absent, `(a.purposes ?? [])` would issue a grant with no purposes, which breaks HCP 1582 ("A grant is never issued without one"). The demo always sends purposes, so that path never runs.

Ask of the PR: require `description` unless the code is one the provider describes itself, or say that a code-only purpose with an unknown code is refused with malformedRequest.

Keyring impact: the plugin may omit `purposes` (the person then chooses in Keyring). But any purpose it does send should carry a description.
findings.reasons: HOLDS: Every quote cited is accurate, and the citations point to the right PR branch (pr1380, with no grants/request change on pr1382; pr1381 only adds uncheckedRules). Two of the three member differences (purposes optional, notTo not requestable) and the "grant whole" point check out against HCP text. The third ("description optional because the provider shows its own") has no basis in HCP. HCP requires a description on every purpose, and A.3 says an unrecognized code's own description is what the person sees. The PR's relaxation is therefore its own design choice, and it leaves one case without a rule. That is an overstatement plus a small ask, not a wrong overall conclusion, so refuted=false with the severity raised from ok to raise.

findings.title: Published TT $ids do not resolve the schemas' relative $refs (affects the whole registry)
findings.claim: A payload's $id is https://trusttasks.org/spec/hcp/<slug>/0.1, with no file segment. Its refs ('../../../_shared/0.1/...') resolve correctly on disk but not against that URL. The framework's own example check works around this by registering each schema under its file URL. A validator that loads the schemas by $id will fail to resolve the shared definitions.
findings.evidence: tt-drift/scripts/lib/spec-examples.mjs:131-134 'The published `$id` names the registry URL, against which the relative on-disk `$ref`s do not resolve; the file URL does.' entries/create/0.1/payload.schema.json $id 'https://trusttasks.org/spec/hcp/entries/create/0.1' with refs to '../../../_shared/0.1/...'. vectors/validators.mjs uses the same workaround.
findings.keyringImpact: Keyring's packages/trust-tasks validator must load the hcp/* schemas from vendored files or bundles, registered by path, not fetched by $id.
findings.corrected: CONFIRMED, severity stays "note". The claim is right, but it needs three corrections. (1) This is not specific to HCP. The framework does it everywhere, and it was already there before this PR. SPEC.md's own A.2 example (SPEC.md:2018 `$id` ".../spec/acl/change-role/0.1" with SPEC.md:2059 `$ref` "../../_shared/0.1/acl-entry.schema.json") has the same mismatch. About 1435 schemas at our pin 2a66a0351 use `../` refs, and 1526 do on pr1380. The file-URL workaround in spec-examples.mjs came from upstream main #1216 (83da23ae8), not from #1380. Each relative ref resolved against a payload `$id` lands one directory too high, because the `$id`'s last segment "0.1" counts as a file name. For example, "../../../_shared/0.1/entry-write.schema.json" against `https://trusttasks.org/spec/hcp/entries/create/0.1` gives `https://trusttasks.org/spec/_shared/0.1/entry-write.schema.json`, but the real `$id` is `https://trusttasks.org/spec/hcp/_shared/0.1/entry-write.schema.json`. (2) The problem only hits a consumer that loads the raw payload.schema.json files by their `$id`. The artifacts the framework publishes for consumers are self-contained: the generated TS modules' PAYLOAD_SCHEMA and RESPONSE_PAYLOAD_SCHEMA say cross-file refs "are already inlined", and the registry bundles are described as "self-contained" (check-bundles.mjs). (3) Keyring needs no change. Its validator already takes pre-inlined schemas (validator.ts:8), so it can use the hcp/* schemas from the generated TS library (or the bundles) and does not need to register files by path. A possible framework-level clarification, not an ask of #1380: SPEC.md:2013 says "`$ref` values are relative to the schema's own position in the registry", which is not true when the base URI is the `$id`.
findings.reasons:
HOLDS: I opened every cited location on the pr1380 worktree (tt-drift, HEAD 94ed4200c) and it says what the claim says. In spec-examples.mjs, lines 132-133 say "The published `$id` names the registry URL, against which the relative on-disk `$ref`s do not resolve; the file URL does." and line 134 runs ajv.addSchema({ ...schema, $id: pathToFileURL(full).href }). The header at line 37 says the same thing. entries/create/0.1/payload.schema.json:3 has `$id` "https://trusttasks.org/spec/hcp/entries/create/0.1", and lines 16-60 hold refs to "../../../_shared/0.1/...". vectors/validators.mjs:41 uses the same file-URL workaround, but that file is our own review harness, not the PR.

I then tested it with Ajv 2020 from the vectors folder. With every specs/*.schema.json registered under its published `$id`, 22 of 28 hcp request roots and 28 of 28 response variants fail with "can't resolve reference ../../../_shared/0.1/common.schema.json#/$defs/Category from id https://trusttasks.org/spec/hcp/audit/read/0.1". The other 6 requests only compile because their roots never reach the external refs. Registered under file URLs instead, 28 of 28 requests and 28 of 28 responses compile. As a control, the shared entry-write schema compiles by `$id`: shared-to-shared sibling refs resolve because shared `$id`s include the file name.

The claim falls short in three ways. It is a framework-wide property that predates the PR, not something HCP introduces. The published bundles and generated libraries inline the refs, so only raw-file consumers are affected. And Keyring already validates against pre-inlined schemas, so its stated impact ("registered by path") is not needed. One more detail: hcp/import's `_framework` ref could not resolve by `$id` even with a file segment, because the framework's `$id` is "https://trusttasks.org/spec/trust-task/0.4/framework", which does not mirror its on-disk path. Unverified: whether trusttasks.org serves the raw schema or the bundle at the Type URI.

findings.title: HCP's own MCP tools take a different argument shape for create and revise than the TT payloads
findings.claim: HCP 10.3 publishes inputSchemas for six MCP tools. The TT request examples, stripped of accessToken, pass hcp_queryContext, hcp_getEntry, hcp_withdrawEntry and hcp_reportSharing. They fail hcp_createEntry, which requires the flat categories, declarationType and sourceContext, and hcp_reviseEntry ('/content must be string'). The split is HCP's own (HTTP versus MCP), not the PR's.
findings.evidence: vectors/out/vectors-mcp.txt: 'hcp_createEntry (required ["categories","content","declarationType","sourceContext"] ...) FAIL hcp/entries/create request ...'; 'hcp_reviseEntry ... FAIL ... /content must be string'.
findings.keyringImpact: vti-agent-connect reaches the VTA over MCP (vta-mcp). If the VTA also exposes HCP's own MCP tools, the plugin's create and revise arguments need a mapping to or from the TT payload. Query and get map directly.
findings.corrected: The claim holds, and "note" is the right severity. Three refinements: (1) The revise mismatch is wider than the one validator error. HCP's hcp_reviseEntry tool has flat `declarationType`, `confidence`, `assertedBy` and `sourceContext`. The TT revise example nests them under `assertion` and `record`. The tool schema does not set additionalProperties, so the validator ignores those nested members silently, and only "/content must be string" is reported. (2) The split is inside HCP itself. Core 5.2.3/5.2.4 and the HTTP Binding (operations/create-request.json, revise-request.json) use the nested shape that the TT payloads copy. The MCP tools in 10.3.3/10.3.4 flatten it. HCP 10.3.3 publishes the field mapping for create; 10.3.4 gives none for revise. Withdraw and reportSharing match TT member for member too, not only query and get. (3) Keyring impact: in VTI #2823 the MCP tools are a later phase (H5, V3), built in the separate vta-mcp process as an HCP 10.5 bridge ("Extend the separate `vta-mcp` process; nothing in the VTA"). So the flat-to-nested mapping would live in vta-mcp, not in the vti-agent-connect plugin, unless the plugin itself builds TT payloads from flat MCP arguments.
findings.reasons: HOLDS: Every cited quote checks out at the right commits: HCP spec at b790561, TT branch pr1382 at e163cac1d. HCP 10.3.3 requires the flat ["categories","content","declarationType","sourceContext"], and its `content` is a string. The TT create example (create/0.1/spec.md:145) nests these as classification.categories, assertion.declarationType and record.provenance.source, and content is an object. So with accessToken removed, it fails exactly the three required members that vectors-mcp.txt reports. HCP 10.3.4 types `content` as a string, but the TT revise example sends a {profile,value,language} object, so the reported error is real. The query, get, withdraw and report TT schemas have the same top-level members as the matching MCP tools, apart from accessToken and the Management Client's entryId. HCP's own Core operation schemas use the nested shape. Its MCP tools state "A tool MAY expose a subset" and give a flat-to-Core mapping table. So the difference comes from HCP's MCP binding, not from the PR. I found nothing that disproves the claim. It only understates the revise divergence, because extra nested members pass silently. The impact statement is conditional, which is fair: VTI plans HCP's MCP tools for a later phase (H5, V3) in vta-mcp.

findings.title: Governance requests require accessToken, but VTI #2823 V0 gives Keyring no token
findings.claim: Every hcp/* governance request (revoke, audit/read, disclosures/summary, grants/list, …) has accessToken in its schema's top-level required list. VTI #2823 says Keyring sends no token in V0, only DID proof plus ACL admin role. The VTA validates every payload against its published schema, so a token-less Keyring revoke would be refused malformedRequest. Neither document says what Keyring puts in accessToken in V0.
findings.evidence: tt/specs/hcp/grants/revoke/0.1/spec.md:118 "`grantId`, the grant to end, and `accessToken`, the Management Client's token. Both are REQUIRED."; schema required ['grantId','accessToken'] (also audit/read ['accessToken'], disclosures/summary, grants/list); vti2823/docs/05-design-notes/hcp.md:158 "Keyring → VTA | DIDComm authcrypt from the admin DID, a required document proof by that DID, the ACL admin role; no token (§4.4)"; hcp.md:591 "Management by DID-proven request, not an HCP token (V0)"; vti/vta-service/src/trust_tasks/mod.rs:605-633 validate_payload → trust_tasks_rs::validate::against_schema
findings.keyringImpact: As both documents are written, Keyring's V0 revoke, the agent list and the 'Telling…/was told' polling (disclosures/summary) cannot be sent schema-valid. Keyring would need a management token, or the VTA would have to run a different schema from the suite.
findings.askOfPR: Ask Brendan to resolve #2823 V0 against #1380. Options: mint a management token for Keyring at pairing in V0; or make the suite accept a DID-proven Management Client without accessToken, and say how; or state that V0's VTA uses a different schema.
findings.corrected:
The core of the claim holds, but two details are wrong and the severity should be "raise", not "blocker".

The two documents do contradict each other.
- In the PR (branch pr1382), every Management Client request in the suite puts accessToken in its top-level required list. That includes grants/revoke, audit/read, disclosures/summary and entries/create, and also grants/list.
- The suite also says the token, not the proof, is what authorizes the request. revoke spec.md:91 says the proof "is not the authorization: the token is." audit/read:109, disclosures/summary:101 and grants/list:102 say the same.
- VTI #2823 says Keyring sends no token in V0 (hcp.md:158 and §4.4:228-239) and that V0 pins the suite "as frozen at X0" (hcp.md:24; hcp-plan A1).
- The VTA validates every payload against its schema before the policy gate, on every transport, and refuses a failure with MalformedRequest (pinned mod.rs:605-645, called at :1986).
- So a revoke or a disclosures/summary poll from Keyring with no token would be refused. Neither document says what Keyring puts in accessToken. #2823 records the V0 departure only against HCP 1.6 and 5.4 (hcp.md:591), not against the suite's own required member.

Corrections:
1. Drop "the agent list". Our companion says V0 lists agents from Keyring's own record (2026-11-25-bam.md:122), and grants/list is in V2 (hcp-plan §3.4).
2. Add hcp/entries/create. It is Keyring's V0 "add a memory" (hcp.md §4.4; companion :36, C3), and its schema also requires accessToken.

Severity: "raise". Nothing is built yet (hcp-plan.md:3 "Nothing is built"), and V0 is a fork branch that is never merged. The fix is small, and the PR's own demo already shows it: the Management Client holds a token "issued at setup" (examples/hcp-demo-ts/SCENARIO.md:79, demo.ts:111). The gap is in #2823, not in #1380, and it must be settled before Keyring's client (C0) or the VTA core (A2) is written. A placeholder string would pass the schema (minLength 1) but would contradict the suite's text that the token is the authorization, so it is not a clean fix. The best option is to mint a management token at pairing in V0. | The claim holds, with one part overstated and one part missed. Severity stays blocker for V0 as written. In V0 the VTA serves six hcp/* tasks: grants/request, entries/query, entries/create, grants/revoke, audit/read and disclosures/summary (hcp-plan.md §3.2). VTI #2823 §4.4 says Keyring sends four of them with no token, authenticating as the admin DID: grants/revoke, audit/read, disclosures/summary and entries/create. All four have accessToken in the suite schema's top-level required list. The VTA pins the suite's bundles byte-identical (A1) and merges them into schema_index. Its spine checks every payload against that schema before the policy gate, not behind enforcement. So a token-less request is refused malformedRequest before any handler runs. That breaks demo step 6 (add a memory, entries/create) and step 8 (revoke, with the disclosures/summary polling). Overstated: the agent list is not hit in V0. grants/list is V2/H2 in VTI, which comes after V1's management tokens. Keyring's companion says "`grants/list` later; the demo lists from Keyring's own record". Missed: entries/create has a second mismatch. The suite says its authority is "the HCP access token for the grant", not a Management Client credential. Neither document says what Keyring puts in accessToken in V0. The suite's own demo mints a management token "issued to the person's app at setup". The ask stands: pick one of three. (a) Mint a V0 management token at pairing. (b) Make the suite accept a DID-proven Management Client without accessToken. (c) State that V0 runs a different schema, which breaks A1's byte-identical pin.
findings.reasons:
HOLDS: I opened every cited location. All four quotes are exact and in context, and each comes from the right version (pr1382, the #2823 docs, and the VTI pin f7b78e29d).

The VTI pin has no HCP schemas yet. Even so, the design pins the suite schemas unchanged and merges them into the schema index (hcp-plan A1). The cited validate_payload then refuses a missing required member with MalformedRequest. It runs before the policy gate and is not switched off by `policy.enforcement`.

Neither #2823 nor our companion says what Keyring puts in accessToken. The suite text makes this worse than a schema mismatch: it says the proof is not the authorization, the token is.

So the claim stands, with two scope errors:
- In V0 the agent list comes from Keyring's own record, and grants/list arrives in V2.
- It leaves out entries/create, which Keyring does send in V0.

I call it "raise" rather than "blocker" for three reasons. Both sides are unbuilt docs. The fix is small, and the PR's demo already shows it (a management token issued at setup). The contradiction is in #2823's design, not a defect in #1380. || HOLDS: I looked for anything that undoes the claim and found nothing. No exception in the suite: none of the 28 schemas or specs mention a DID-proven Management Client, "management token" or anything that stands in for a token. pr1381 changes nothing on revoke or list beyond uncheckedRules. The latest pr1380 commit makes it stricter: a proof is now required on any request that carries a token. No VTA bypass: validate_payload runs for every type URI that schema_index knows. It runs before the policy gate, and only ceremony tasks are exempt. A1 says hcp/* goes into schema_index with byte-identical bundles. The VTI docs, the demo plan and our own companion (D2) all say "no token" and never name an accessToken value. The HCP spec backs the suite: HCP 9.3 says "All requests MUST include a Bearer token", and 3.2.3 gives the Management Client its own credentials. The suite's demo uses MANAGEMENT_TOKEN for revoke. The one thing that narrows the claim is the agent list: grants/list is not in V0. And entries/create, which the claim leaves out, is also affected. Blocker fits the rubric for V0 as written, because the demo's revoke and memory steps cannot be sent schema-valid. But this is a mismatch between two draft documents (VTI V0 has "0 of 15 tasks done"), and there are cheap ways to fix it.

findings.title: The demo's person always approves, by a function call; no decline test or state in any port
findings.claim: In #1382 the provider holds the grant request with a next step. The person's approval is an in-memory state change in the provider that always approves. No Management Client approves or declines. Hold states are pending/approved/granted only, in TS, Rust, Go and Dart. None of the 14 shared tests declines, and none covers the unknown-person hold that must look like a decline.
findings.evidence: tt/examples/hcp-demo-ts/src/demo.ts:435-439 "The person decides, in the provider's own modality (here: approves at once)"; demo.ts:145 `state: "pending" | "approved" | "granted"`; README.md:100 "There is no consent UI. The person's decision is one function call, and it always approves what was asked."; SCENARIO.md:236-274 (14 tests); hcp-demo-go/demo.go:165-169; hcp-demo/src/lib.rs:204-211; hcp-demo-dart/lib/demo.dart:207

Neither the Trust Task spec nor HCP 6.1.6 says the provider puts the request to the Management Client. HCP 6.1.6 allows a redirect, an in-app session, messaging or an LLM-mediated dialogue. The demo already prints "in the provider's app". The accurate ask is for the README to say that a real provider puts the request to the person through its own modality, for example the person's management app (in VTI #2823 that is Keyring, via task-consent). The decline ask itself matches the spec: on the next resubmission the client gets the same fixed permissionDenied, never another next step, and no grant is issued. | The facts hold, and "raise" is the right severity for the decline test. Two of the asks are overstated, and so is the Keyring-impact line. (1) In #1382 the toy provider holds the request with a next step. The person's decision is one in-memory call that always approves (demo.ts:435-438). Every port has only the hold states pending, approved and granted. None of the 14 shared tests declines. Ask: add a decline to SCENARIO.md and every port. (2) Drop the README wording "a real provider puts the request to the person's Management Client". In HCP, approving a grant belongs to the authorization profile: the OAuth Authorization Service, or another authenticated channel (HCP 6.1.6, 12.2). findings.reasons: HOLDS: Every cited quote is accurate and comes from the PR branch (pr1382 HEAD e163cac1d; only package-lock.json is modified locally). demo.ts:435-439 approves unconditionally. demo.ts:145 and the Go, Rust and Dart lines have only the three states.
